modules.cost: [`sign_of_det2`], at most [`ITERATIONS`] passes of a few comparisons, subtractions and one Euclidean division each. [`sign_of_det3`], at most [`DET3_PASSES`] passes, each at most about 480 calls of [`sign_of_det2`]; its search keeps up to 119 lattice points in a fixed array of 2,856 bytes. No allocation, no recursion.
modules.does: [`sign_of_det2`] finds the sign of x1·y2 − y1·x2 from the four entries without ever forming a product: it compares, subtracts and divides, keeping every value within the entries' own magnitude, and [`orient2d`] applies it to the three points' translations, as the generated `orient2d` does. [`sign_of_det3`] finds the sign of a 3 × 3 determinant the same way, by a walk in the lattice its first two rows span whose every test is a [`sign_of_det2`], and [`orient3d`] applies it to the four points' translations, as the generated `orient3d` does. A product is never computed, so no value needs more bits than a few entries: the method answers in 64-bit arithmetic where the exact paths need 128 bits.
guarantees: **The exact sign.** For every four entries of magnitude at most [`ENTRY_MAX`], the result is the sign of x1·y2 − y1·x2 (tested against 128-bit products and against the generated `orient2d` in this crate's `tests/avnaim.rs`, and against big integers by geom-fuzz's `variants` target). For every nine entries of magnitude at most [`DET3_ENTRY_MAX`], the result of [`sign_of_det3`] is the determinant's sign (tested against big integers here, and against the generated `orient3d` in this crate's `tests/avnaim.rs` and geom-fuzz's `variants` target). An entry past its bound is refused with `None`, never answered.

**Checked and bounded.** Every step is a checked method. [`sign_of_det2`]'s loop runs at most [`ITERATIONS`] times: each pass either answers or replaces the second row by one whose entries are below half the first row's, so the entries halve at least every two passes. [`sign_of_det3`] runs at most [`DET3_PASSES`] passes, each with a lattice search of at most 119 doublings and 118 halvings, kept in a fixed array.
modules.job: The signs of 2 × 2 and 3 × 3 integer determinants in single-precision arithmetic, by Avnaim, Boissonnat, Devillers, Preparata and Yvinec's method: chapter 23.3's reference for the exact paths of orientation (piece G42). It lives here, in a development crate, because it is a reference to measure against, not a path the kernel ships: G42's report measured it and did not adopt it, so it is outside the foundation set's coverage and mutation gates (28.8), which its pass limits, never reached, could not meet by test.

method.text: Avnaim, Boissonnat, Devillers, Preparata and Yvinec, "Evaluating signs of determinants using single-precision arithmetic", Algorithmica 17 (1997), sections 2 and 3, doi:10.1007/BF02522822 (the authors' report: <https://inria.hal.science/inria-00090613>). Signs first: an entry of zero leaves one product, and entries of mixed signs settle the sign or are made positive by negating rows and columns. Then, with the rows ordered so that x2 ≥ x1 and y2 ≥ y1, the Euclidean step x2 = k·x1 + xr, yr = y2 − k·y1 keeps the determinant (|x1 y1; xr yr|), and the halves of the first row settle it or give a smaller second row: (xr, yr) when both lie in the lower halves, (x1 − xr, y1 − yr) when both lie in the upper, which negates the determinant. The paper writes that last determinant without the change of sign; it is −|x1 y1; xr yr|, as expanding both shows, and this module follows the expansion.

errors.name: BvhError

invariants: Every box is rounded outward to whole grid steps and never misses what it should contain; boxes around certified or Tolerant geometry are padded by their bound (19.9, 23.7).

Built top-down in one pass by the binned surface-area heuristic with integer costs; every split is a pure function of the node's contents, ties broken by entry key, so the tree is the same on any number of threads (19.9).
Answers never depend on the tree's shape: every query returns its set sorted by key (19.9, 23.7).
Traversal uses an explicit stack with a depth limit, never recursion, and checks cancellation at fixed steps (19.9, principle 13).
Parallel only through `geom-run`'s helper (23.4).
crates.job: The one tree of integer boxes, 2D and 3D.

modules.cost: constant per box; no allocation.
modules.does: an [`Aabb`] holds a lower and an upper corner of whole grid steps. It comes from `geom-math`'s grid boxes exactly ([`Box2`], [`Box3`]), or from a box of doubles in grid units rounded outward ([`Aabb::from_float`], [`FBox2`], [`FBox3`]), and [`Aabb::inflated`] pads it by its holder's class (chapter 23.7): nothing for Exact geometry, the bound ε for Certified(ε), the tolerance for a Tolerant import, each rounded up to whole steps. The tree measures a box by [`Aabb::area`], the surface-area heuristic's measure in whole numbers.
guarantees: **Never misses what it holds.** Grid boxes convert exactly. A float box's lower corner is rounded down and its upper corner up, each to a whole step, and a padding is the bound rounded up, so the result holds every point within the bound of the float box.

**Bounded, so every cost is exact.** Every coordinate lies within ±[`LIMIT`] = 2^43 (the 2^40 frame of chapter 6 with room for padding), so an extent plus one is at most 2^44 + 1 < 2^45, a 3D area (three products of two) is below 3·2^90 < 2^92, and an area times an entry count (below 2^32) is below 2^124: the tree's costs are exact in `u128`.
**Closed.** Boxes that touch overlap, as `geom-math`'s do.
modules.job: The box tree's boxes: closed boxes of whole grid steps in two or three dimensions, padded by the exactness of what they hold.

method.text: chapter 23.7 of the kernel architecture ("Boxes that never miss", padding by exactness) and section 19.9 ("Boxes are whole grid steps"); the area measure is the surface area of I. Wald, "On fast construction of SAH-based bounding volume hierarchies", IEEE Symposium on Interactive Ray Tracing (2007), <https://doi.org/10.1109/RT.2007.4342588>, counted in grid points so a point's box has a positive measure, and in two dimensions the perimeter, the plane's analogue (the chance a random line meets a convex region is proportional to its perimeter).

modules.cost: O(n·D) per level of the tree, about log₂ n levels for spread boxes and at most [`MAX_DEPTH`]; memory: the nodes, the order, one centre per entry, and per subtree task a copy of its range's order. No recursion.
modules.does: [`build`] takes the entries sorted by key and returns the tree's nodes and the order of the entries along its leaves. Each node's entries are split by the plane, among b − 1 planes per axis between b bins of their boxes' centres (b = min(entries, [`BINS`])), that minimises area(left)·count(left) + area(right)·count(right), or kept as a leaf once there are at most [`LEAF_MAX`]. The top of the tree is built on the calling thread until every unbuilt range holds at most [`GRAIN`] entries; those subtrees are then built as one phase of the helper, one task each, and spliced in task order.
guarantees: **One tree for one set of entries.** Every split is a pure function of the range's entries: the bins and the costs are whole numbers ([`crate::bound`] bounds them), ties between planes go to the lower axis and then the lower plane, and the partition is stable, so each range keeps its entries in key order. Which ranges become subtree tasks depends on their sizes alone. So the nodes, their order and the entries' order are the same for any thread count, pool and chunking, and for any input order of the same entries.

**Depth at most [`MAX_DEPTH`].** From depth [`MEDIAN_DEPTH`] = 32 on, every split is at the median in key order. A range there holds fewer than 2^32 entries, and halving reaches at most [`LEAF_MAX`] entries within 31 more levels, so no leaf is deeper than 63.
**No recursion.** Ranges wait on an explicit stack; ranges where all centres coincide are split at the median in key order.
**Charged.** Each node charges its entry count to the meter before its work, so a build stops at the same node for the same budget on every machine.
modules.job: The box tree's construction: top-down, by the binned surface-area heuristic with whole-number costs, in parallel only through `geom-run`'s helper.

method.text: I. Wald, "On fast construction of SAH-based bounding volume hierarchies", IEEE Symposium on Interactive Ray Tracing (2007), <https://doi.org/10.1109/RT.2007.4342588> (binning centroids into a fixed number of bins per axis and sweeping the bin boundaries), with costs counted in whole grid points and ties broken by axis, plane and key (section 19.9 and chapter 27's `geom-bvh` row); the subtree phase follows chapter 23.4's helper.

modules.cost: building is O(n log n): a sort by key when the input is not in key order, n codes, the runs' sorts and ⌈log₂(n/32,768)⌉ rounds of merges, with a copy of the points in key order and two buffers of n slots (24 bytes each) at the peak of a round. A search is two binary searches per cell (at most 27 cells) and one exact test per point in those cells. The pairs are one search per point.
guarantees: **The same answer everywhere.** The order (code, key) is unique for distinct keys, so the index, its bytes and every answer are the same for any input order, pool and target; every answer is sorted by key.
**Exact.** Distances are compared as squared integer distances in `i128` (each coordinate difference below 2^41 + 2^42, so the sum of squares stays below 2^88), never in floating point.
**Bounded and cancellable.** No recursion; the meter is charged one unit per point a search scans, so a cancelled or over-budget search returns an error and no keys.
**Safe.** No `unsafe`, no panics, no unchecked indexing; allocations are fallible.
modules.job: The Morton-sorted cell index (piece G55): grid points in a linear octree, for point searches such as welding and envelopes (chapter 19.9).

method.text: the Morton order (G. M. Morton, "A computer oriented geodetic data base and a new technique in file sequencing", IBM Ltd., Ottawa (1966)) and the linear octree, the leaves of an octree kept as a sorted list of location codes (I. Gargantini, "An effective way to represent quadtrees", Communications of the ACM 25(12) (1982), 905–910, <https://doi.org/10.1145/358728.358741>). The bits are spread by the mask-and-shift sequence for 21-bit coordinates, applied to the low 21 and the high 20 bits of each.

modules.cost: constant.
modules.does: [`BvhError`] names each failure of the tree's construction, refit and queries, and maps `geom-run`'s stops and phase errors onto them, so a caller sees one error type.
guarantees: **Typed, never partial.** Every failure is one of these kinds and returns no tree or answer; a tree that fails to refit is left exactly as it was before the call.
**Stops keep their reason.** A meter's stop (budget, cancellation, memory) and a phase's budget failure keep `geom-run`'s own record of it.
modules.job: Why the box tree could not build, change or answer.

method.none: an error enum and its conversions, with `geom-run`'s stops (chapter 23.10).

modules.cost: O(nodes visited + answers·log answers); memory: the answer.
modules.does: each query walks the tree from the root with an explicit stack, skipping every node whose box misses, and charges one unit of its meter per node, or pair of nodes, it visits. It collects the keys it finds and sorts them.
guarantees: **The answer of brute force.** A query returns exactly the keys (or key pairs) whose boxes meet, as testing every entry (or every pair) would, sorted ascending: a pair within one tree as (smaller key, larger key), a pair between trees as (this tree's key, the other's). So the answer does not depend on the tree's shape, a refit, a rebuild or the thread count it was built with.

**No recursion, bounded stacks.** A tree is at most [`MAX_DEPTH`] deep, so a walk of one tree holds at most `MAX_DEPTH + 1` nodes on its stack, of two trees at most `2·MAX_DEPTH + 1` pairs (each step descends one side, pushing two), and of one tree against itself at most `4·MAX_DEPTH + 1` (a node against itself pushes three). The stacks are vectors with room for [`MAX_DEPTH`] reserved, grown fallibly beyond it.
**Cancellable, never partial.** The meter polls the caller's cancellation at fixed charges; a stopped query returns [`BvhError::Stopped`] and no keys.
modules.job: The box tree's queries: the entries whose boxes meet a box, the pairs of entries whose boxes meet within one tree, and the pairs between two trees.

method.text: depth-first traversal of a bounding-volume hierarchy, and the simultaneous traversal of two hierarchies for overlapping pairs, as in G. van den Bergen, "Efficient collision detection of complex deformable models using AABB trees", *Journal of Graphics Tools* 2(4) (1997), 1–13, <https://doi.org/10.1080/10867651.1997.10487480>, with the larger node descended first; answers sorted by key (section 19.9 and chapter 23.7).

modules.cost: building as [`crate::build`], plus a stable sort by key; a refit O(updates·log n + nodes); the bytes O(entries + nodes). Memory: the entries, the nodes and the key index.
modules.does: [`BoxTree::build`] sorts the entries by key, refuses a repeated key, and builds the nodes ([`crate::build`]). The entries are then stored in leaf order, each leaf a range of them, beside an index from key to position. [`BoxTree::refit`] gives entries new boxes and passes the change up to every node. When the tree's cost ([`BoxTree::cost`], the surface-area heuristic summed over its nodes) passes [`REBUILD_FACTOR`] times the cost it was built with, the refit rebuilds the tree from its entries instead. [`BoxTree::to_bytes`] writes the tree in a canonical form, for goldens and caches.
guarantees: **A function of its entries.** A tree is built from the set of its entries alone: their input order, the pool, the thread count and the chunking change nothing, down to the last byte of [`BoxTree::to_bytes`]. A rebuild equals a fresh build of the same entries.
**Every node holds what is below it.** A node's box is the union of its children's, a leaf's the union of its entries', after a build and after a refit.
**All or nothing.** A refit checks every update before it changes anything, so a refused refit, or one stopped by its meter while rebuilding, leaves the tree as it was.
**Children after parents.** A node's children have larger indices than it has, so one pass from the last node to the first refits the tree.
modules.job: The box tree: its entries, its nodes, how it is built, refitted and rebuilt, and its canonical bytes.

method.text: section 19.9 of the kernel architecture ("Refit or rebuild"; "Answers do not depend on the tree"), with the tree's cost the surface-area heuristic of I. Wald, "On fast construction of SAH-based bounding volume hierarchies", IEEE Symposium on Interactive Ray Tracing (2007), <https://doi.org/10.1109/RT.2007.4342588>, one unit per inner node and one per entry in a leaf.

crates.sections: 14.8, 19.9 and 23.7; open questions OQ-11.2 and OQ-19.1; chapter 27 ("Who owns what"), in the kernel architecture (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/`).

crates.summary: Spare Kit geometry kernel: the one box tree.

invariants: Checks run in groups: combinatorial, geometric consistency, self-intersection and the exactness record (8.3).
Geometric consistency is certified with bounds, never sampled (8.3).
Self-intersection checks use the same certified intersections the operations do (ARCHITECTURE.md, layers).
The cheap groups run after every operation in every build; the full set runs in debug builds, in continuous integration, on every import and on request (8.3).
The checker reports what fails with the entities involved and never modifies a body (principle 4).
crates.job: The B-rep validity checker.

modules.cost: linear in the body's rows, plus the near-constant time of each set union; memory: a few words per row of each arena, reserved before use.
modules.does: the check runs in two stages, as Parasolid gates its body check. The first follows every list and ring of the body once: each region's shells, each shell's faces and each face's loops (a first child and a `next` chain, each child naming its parent), each loop's fins (a ring both ways), each edge's fins (a radial ring), and each edge's two ends. It finds a list that comes back on itself, a child listed twice or by the wrong parent or by none, a ring that does not close, a fin off its edge's ring, and an edge with one end. Only a body whose lists and rings are sound goes on to the second stage, which reads them:
guarantees: **Finite on any body.** Every walk of the first stage marks each row it visits and stops at the first row it meets twice, so it visits each row at most once, however the links are broken; the second stage walks only rings and lists the first found sound.
**The second stage reads only sound structure.** It runs only when the first found nothing, so a fault it reports is real, never an echo of a broken list.
**Every fault, in a fixed order.** The checks run in the order above, rows ascending, so the same body gives the same faults in the same order on every machine.
**Charged.** One work unit per row visited, to the caller's meter.
modules.job: Group 1 of chapter 8.3, combinatorial: every loop closes, every fin has a partner or is a boundary, shells are closed and consistently oriented, regions nest correctly, and Euler's formula holds.

method.text: Parasolid's published body check, its loop, fin and shell checks and its gating (`projects/kit/notes/G01-evidence/02-occt-parasolid-acis.md`, section 5, and the checking chapter it links, <http://www.q-solid.com/Parasolid_Docs/chapters/fd_chap.09.html>); the shell check of Open CASCADE, each edge used exactly twice in a closed shell (`BRepCheck_Shell`, linked from the same section); and the Euler–Poincaré formula for boundary representations, V − E + F − (L − F) = 2(S − G): M. Mäntylä, *An Introduction to Solid Modeling*, Computer Science Press, 1988, chapter 3. A. Hatcher, *Algebraic Topology*, Cambridge University Press, 2002, section 2.2 (the Euler characteristic of a compact surface, 2 − 2g − b), <https://pi.math.cornell.edu/~hatcher/AT/AT.pdf>. R. E. Tarjan and J. van Leeuwen, "Worst-case analysis of set union algorithms", *Journal of the ACM* 31 (1984), 245–281, <https://doi.org/10.1145/62.2160>, for the connected sets (union by size, path halving).

modules.cost: a few dozen interval operations per check; no loop. Recursion: none.
modules.does: [`carrier`] turns a face's surface into its closed form ([`Carrier`]), and each check bounds a distance from above and compares it with the body's bound b. With w = p − c, h = w · n̂ (height along the axis) and ρ = |w × n̂| (distance from it), the distance of a point from each kind is:
guarantees: **Upper bounds, certified.** Every distance is bounded from above in interval arithmetic that stays exact where the doubles are (`geom_curve::tight`), on the exact unit vectors' enclosures (`geom_curve::Frame::unit_vectors`) and certified sines and cosines of half-turns (`geom_num::Interval::{sinpi, cospi}`).

**Exact on exact data.** A grid point on a plane given by doubles, a cylinder, a sphere or a torus whose data are small integers on an axis-aligned frame is measured exactly, so a vertex exactly at the bound passes and one a step beyond fails. A circle's points come from `sinpi` and `cospi`, which widen by a step even where exact: its checks hold to that step.
**Fails closed.** A value that cannot be enclosed, a cone point whose radius may be negative, a torus that is not a ring, a surface kind without a closed form here: not certified, never passed.
**Nothing allocates; nothing is sampled.**
modules.job: Certified bounds for group 2 on every carrier it measures against: how far a grid point, a line segment or a circle can lie from a plane, cylinder, cone, sphere or ring torus, and how far a grid point lies from a circle's end. Never sampled.

method.text: the closed forms of the elementary surfaces of ISO 10303-42 as `geom_surface::analytic` parametrises them, the Lipschitz bound of the distance function, and interval arithmetic (R. E. Moore, R. B. Kearfott and M. J. Cloud, *Introduction to Interval Analysis*, SIAM 2009, <https://doi.org/10.1137/1.9780898717716>), for chapter 8.3's group 2 (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/08-topology.md`).

modules.cost: linear in the body's faces, edges and fins; no allocation.
modules.does: a body recorded [`Exactness::Exact`] must be one its geometry can make exact. Chapter 9 makes a B-rep exact for flat faces and certified for curved ones, so every face of an exact body lies on a plane, every edge on a line, and every pcurve it holds is a line; any other kind of carrier is a fault at the entity that uses it. A body recorded [`Exactness::Certified`] or [`Exactness::Approximate`] may use any carrier: its stated bound is judged against the geometry by group 2, which certifies every vertex and edge against its carriers at that bound (11.12), and the record's own arithmetic, the least exact class of the inputs with their bounds added, is `geom_num::Exactness`'s, proven there.
guarantees: **An exact record is flat.** A body recorded exact passes only when every face's surface is a plane, every edge's curve a line and every pcurve a line.
**Every fault, in a fixed order.** Faces, then edges, then fins, rows ascending.
**Charged.** One work unit per row visited, to the caller's meter.
modules.job: Group 4 of chapter 8.3, the exactness record: the body's exactness class is consistent with its geometry.

method.text: chapter 9's exactness classes and the kinds that keep a B-rep exact (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/09-representations.md`), checked as chapter 8.3's fourth group (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/08-topology.md`).

modules.cost: linear in faces, fins and edges, one meter unit each; constant work per row; nothing allocated. Recursion: none.
modules.does: [`check`] walks the faces, fins and edges in row order. A face's surface is a plane, cylinder, cone, sphere or ring torus (`crate::curved::Carrier`); any other kind is reported as [`FaultKind::Unchecked`], never passed (8.3: "certified with bounds, not sampled"). For each fin, the vertex it starts at must lie on its face's surface, and its edge's line or circle on that surface; for each edge, its vertices must lie at its line's or circle's ends. An edge on another kind of curve, and a fin's pcurve, are reported unchecked.
guarantees: **Exact on flat faces.** A plane given by integer-valued doubles (its origin and two spanning vectors within ±(2^40 − 1)) becomes the integer plane through three grid points, and a vertex passes exactly when (n · p + d)^2 ≤ b^2 · |n|^2, compared in 320-bit integers; for b = 0 that is the orient test, n · p + d = 0. A line whose ends are grid points passes the same way, end by end: a segment is never farther from a plane than its farther end, and no double holds the squared normal of a long edge's plane, so an interval could not say 0. A plane not given by integers is unchecked in a body recorded Exact, and measured in certified intervals otherwise.

**Certified on lines and curved carriers.** Every other distance is a certified upper bound (`crate::curved`, and a line's end points enclosed with `geom_curve::tight`, exact where the doubles are), so a vertex exactly on the bound passes where the data are exact and one a step beyond fails.
**Fails closed.** Every comparison whose operands cannot be formed (a value out of its range, an overflow, a cone past its apex) is a fault, never a pass.
**No sampling, nothing allocated.** Each check is an exact predicate or one interval evaluation of a closed form.
modules.job: Group 2 of chapter 8.3, geometric consistency: every vertex lies on its faces' surfaces and at its edges' curve ends, and every edge on its faces, within the bound the body is recorded with.

method.text: chapter 8.3's group 2 and its certified-bounds rule (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/08-topology.md`), on the exact integer plane of 6.3 (`geom_num::plane`, after Campen and Kobbelt 2010, <https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-8659.2009.01609.x>) and interval enclosures that stay exact where the doubles are (R. E. Moore, R. B. Kearfott and M. J. Cloud, *Introduction to Interval Analysis*, SIAM 2009, <https://doi.org/10.1137/1.9780898717716>).

modules.cost: constant time per accessor; a report holds one fault per thing found wrong.
modules.does: [`Group`] names the four groups of 8.3; [`Level`] says which run ([`Level::Cheap`] after every operation in every build, [`Level::Full`] in debug builds, in continuous integration, on every import and on request); [`Entity`] names one entity of a body by its index; [`Fault`] is one thing found wrong, of a [`FaultKind`], at one entity and possibly naming a second; [`Report`] holds the faults of one check in the order they were found (the first [`crate::MAX_FAULTS`], and a count of the rest), the groups that ran, and the groups the level asked for that this checker does not have yet.
guarantees: **Nothing hidden.** A [`Report`] passes only when it found no fault, kept or counted; a group the level asked for but which is not built yet is listed in [`Report::missing`], never counted as passed.
**One order.** Faults are listed in the order the checks find them, which is fixed (each check runs over rows in ascending order), so the same body gives the same report everywhere.
**Plain words.** Every [`FaultKind`] has a sentence saying what is wrong ([`FaultKind::what`]), and [`Fault`]'s `Display` names its entities by arena and row.
modules.job: What the checker reports: the groups of chapter 8.3, how many of them a check runs, and each fault with the entities it involves.

method.text: Parasolid's published body check, which runs in gated groups and reports each fault with the entities involved (`projects/kit/notes/G01-evidence/02-occt-parasolid-acis.md`, section 5), as chapter 8.3 sets out (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/08-topology.md`).

modules.cost: the sum of the groups run, each linear in the body's rows; it reserves [`crate::MAX_FAULTS`] faults and one scratch buffer of a few words per row (at most four per vertex and one per edge), shared by every check.
modules.does: [`check`] runs, for each group of [`Group::ALL`] the [`Level`] asks for, the group's checks on the body and the exactness the body is recorded with, and reports every fault in the order found. A group the level asks for that this checker does not have yet is listed as missing in the report, never run and never counted as passed. An operation calls it on its result before returning it, at [`Level::of_build`] (8.3; principle 4); an import, and any caller who asks, call it at [`Level::Full`].
guarantees: **Never changes the body.** The check reads the body through `&Body` only.
**The same report everywhere.** The groups run in 8.3's order and each in a fixed order, so one body gives one report on every machine and thread count.

**Stoppable.** Every row visited is charged to the caller's meter, so the caller's budget or cancellation stops a check like any operation (23.10), and a refused allocation stops it as the meter's `OutOfMemory`, never as an abort.
modules.job: One check of a body: the groups its level asks for, in chapter 8.3's order, each charged to the caller's meter, into one report.

method.text: Parasolid's body check in gated groups, reporting each fault with its entities (`projects/kit/notes/G01-evidence/02-occt-parasolid-acis.md`, section 5), as chapter 8.3 and 28.4 run it (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/08-topology.md`, `projects/engines/geometry/architecture/28-testing.md`).

modules.cost: one meter unit per face, per pair of a face's edges, per pair of faces and per edge tested against a face; quadratic in a face's edges and in the faces, as primitives have few. Nothing allocated. Recursion: none.
modules.does: [`check`] runs on a body groups 1 and 2 passed, so every face lies on a plane, cylinder, cone, sphere or ring torus and every edge is a line or a circle on its faces.
guarantees: **Exact on segments and polygons.** Their tests are integer predicates on the grid vertices (`geom_num::predicate::orient3d`, and 2D orientations in `i128`, checked).
**Certified elsewhere, and fails closed.** A pair no exact or certified test separates is a [`FaultKind::PairUnchecked`] fault, never a pass (8.3: "certified with bounds, not sampled").
**A segment is its vertices.** A line edge is tested as the segment between its vertices, which group 2 has certified within the body's bound of the line's ends.
**Nothing allocated.** Every list is walked again where it is needed.
modules.job: Group 3 of chapter 8.3, self-intersection, for primitive bodies: no face crosses itself, and no two faces cross except along shared edges.

method.text: chapter 8.3's group 3 (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/08-topology.md`), on J. R. Shewchuk's exact orientation predicates ("Adaptive precision floating-point arithmetic and fast robust geometric predicates", Discrete & Computational Geometry 18 (1997), <https://doi.org/10.1007/PL00009321>) and the segment and convex-polygon tests built on them (J. O'Rourke, *Computational Geometry in C*, 2nd ed., Cambridge University Press 1998, <https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511804120>).

modules.cost: constant time per charge and per fault; [`Sink::new`] reserves [`MAX_FAULTS`] faults.
modules.does: [`Sink`] holds the faults of one check and the caller's [`WorkMeter`]. It reserves room for [`MAX_FAULTS`] faults before the check starts, as Parasolid's body check takes a largest number of faults to return, so recording a fault never allocates; a fault past the cap is counted, not kept. Each check charges one work unit per row it visits ([`Sink::charge`]), so a check of a huge body can be stopped by the caller's budget or cancellation like any operation (23.10). The checks' scratch space is reserved once, by [`crate::check`], so a refused allocation stops the check through the meter instead of aborting ([`Sink::out_of_memory`]).
guarantees: **The first faults kept, in order, and the rest counted.** [`Sink::push`] keeps a fault while fewer than [`MAX_FAULTS`] are kept, and counts it otherwise; it never allocates.
**Never aborts on memory.** A refused reservation is the meter's [`geom_run::Stop::OutOfMemory`].
modules.job: Where a check puts what it finds, and how it pays for its work: the faults found so far, the count of those past the cap, and the caller's meter.

method.text: the work meter of chapter 23.10 (`geom_run::WorkMeter`), charged per row as `geom_topo::Builder::publish` charges per chunk (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/23-performance.md`, section 23.10), and the cap on returned faults of Parasolid's body check (`projects/kit/notes/G01-evidence/02-occt-parasolid-acis.md`, section 5).
