errors.name: CurveError

invariants: Each kind is stored as itself, exactly, in a closed enum: arcs stay arcs, never converted to NURBS behind the caller's back (7).
Conversion to NURBS is on demand and returns the NURBS, whether it is exact, and its maximum error (7).
Every kind gives evaluation, derivatives and conservative bounds on value and derivatives over any parameter interval; derivatives are never taken by finite differences (7, 12.1, 13.21).
Projection and inversion return enclosures with proofs, never bare numbers (12.4).
Spirals evaluate Certified, by quadrature with a proven bound whose panel count depends only on the segment's parameters (17.8).
A transform that changes a kind, such as a non-uniform scale turning a circle into an ellipse, does so explicitly (7).
crates.job: Every curve kind in 2D and 3D, spirals included: evaluation, bounds, projection, conversion.

modules.cost: twelve products and sums per point in doubles and in intervals; nothing allocates.
modules.does: [`Entries::of`] reads a [`TypedTransform`]: an exact grid transform and a rational one through their exact integer entries (m / d), a certified one through its own doubles. [`Entries::image`] maps a homogeneous point w·P (weight w) to M·(w·P) + w·t, once in doubles in a fixed order and once in intervals, and returns the doubles with the distance between them, an upper bound on how far the double image lies from the exact image under the exact transform.
guarantees: **Exact entries enclosed.** An integer entry whose double is not exact (beyond 2^53) is widened by its rounding; each quotient m / d is an outward-rounded interval division; a certified transform is exact in its own doubles (`geom-math`'s `transform` header).

**The image's error bounded.** The interval image holds the exact image of the exact point, and the double image is computed from the doubles of the same entries, so the returned distance bounds their difference.

**Exact images report 0.** When every entry is exactly its double (grid and certified transforms), each coordinate is also summed exactly, as exact products in `geom-num`'s superaccumulator, and an image equal to its double reports an error of 0: interval arithmetic widens every result and could never say so.
modules.job: Typed transforms applied to control points, with a certified bound on the rounding: the entries of each `geom-math` transform variant as doubles and as interval enclosures of their exact values, and the image of a homogeneous point in both.

method.text: affine invariance of B-splines and NURBS under affine maps of their control points (The NURBS Book, 2nd ed., properties P3.10 and P4.10, <https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-59223-2>), with the weights unchanged, and interval arithmetic for the bound.

modules.cost: constant.
modules.does: [`Axes`] holds the two vectors u and v of an ellipse, hyperbola, parabola or involute, and [`HelixAxes`] the three of a helix. The `Frame` form gives lengths along an exact [`Frame`]: u = a·x̂, v = b·ŷ (and w = (pitch/2)·n̂ for a helix), so the semi-axes, the focal length or the radius are exact numbers of the data. The `Vectors` form stores u, v (and w) directly: it is what a transform that is not a similarity makes of the `Frame` form, with the same parameter, because principal axes found again would shift the parameter by an angle no double holds (chapter 7: "a non-uniform scale turns a circle into an ellipse", explicitly).
guarantees: **Checked.** Lengths are finite and positive; `Vectors` are finite and u and v independent, decided exactly.
**Exact reversal.** Reversing negates v (and w): on a frame, by negating its normal, which negates ŷ and n̂ exactly.
**Transforms keep the form when they can.** A similarity maps a `Frame` form to a `Frame` form (lengths times the scale, a helix's pitch negated by a mirror); any other transform gives `Vectors`.
modules.job: How an analytic kind stores its vectors: lengths on an exact orthonormal frame, or the vectors themselves when the kind is the affine image of one.

method.text: the conjugate-diameter form of an ellipse, c + cos θ·u + sin θ·v, the image of the unit circle under the affine map taking the axes to u and v, of which the principal-axis form is the case u ⟂ v; and its analogues for the other kinds. Chapter 7 asks for the kind change to be explicit (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/07-geometry-types.md`).

modules.cost: one match per call.
modules.does: [`Basis`] is a closed enum with one variant per leaf kind (NURBS, the analytic kinds, the bulge polyline, the transition), dispatching the kind contract to each, with the conversions to and from [`CurveKind`]. The kinds that hold curves hold a `Basis`, never a `CurveKind`, so no kind contains itself: no recursive type, no recursive call, nothing for WebAssembly's stack to bound (chapter 28.8).
guarantees: **The same behaviour as the kind.** Every method is the leaf kind's own.

**Leaves stay leaves.** Every leaf's reversal and transform is a leaf (a circle may become an ellipse, a bulge polyline or a scaled transition its NURBS form); a split of a bulge polyline is a trimmed one, so the trimmed kind splits by its interval instead.
modules.job: The leaf curve kinds: the kinds that hold no other curve, which the trimmed, composite and offset kinds and curves on surfaces are built on.

method.text: the storage-and-behaviour split chapter 7 decides, closed enums for storage and traits for behaviour (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/07-geometry-types.md`); a leaf's breaks are a NURBS curve's knots (where its smoothness may drop, The NURBS Book, 2nd ed., P2.5, <https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-59223-2>), a polyline's vertices and the middle of a Helmert transition.

modules.cost: O(k) per evaluation of order k; a bound O(1) per segment the span meets; conversion O(n) for n segments.
modules.does: [`BulgePolyline`] stores 2D vertices, one bulge per segment (b = tan(θ/4) for an arc of sweep θ, positive turning anticlockwise; 0 for a straight segment) and optionally a start and end width per segment. Segment i runs over parameters [s + i, s + i + 1] (s, the start, is 0 for a new polyline). Each segment is exactly the rational quadratic its bulge defines, in homogeneous form with p₀ and p₂ its ends and w = (1 − b²)/(1 + b²): h₁ = ((1 − b²)·m + b·(d.y, −d.x))/(1 + b²), with m the chord's middle and d = p₂ − p₀, so C(v) = (B₀p₀ + B₁h₁ + B₂p₂)/(B₀ + B₁w + B₂) with v the parameter within the segment. Every value is a rational function of the stored doubles: a bulge arc is stored exactly, a semicircle (w = 0) and a major arc (w < 0) included, whose denominator stays at least (1 + w)/2 > 0.
guarantees: **Exact definition, certified evaluation.** Points, derivatives of every order (Leibniz's rule on W·C = A) and bounds over spans are interval evaluations of those rational functions.

**An exact NURBS form.** The segments are rational quadratic Bezier pieces on the same parameter; an arc whose middle weight is low (a semicircle or more) is first halved, or quartered, by de Casteljau's algorithm at dyadic parameters, which keeps every weight positive. The deviation bounds only the rounding of the pieces' points and weights.

**Transforms change the kind explicitly.** A similarity keeps a bulge polyline (vertices mapped, widths scaled, bulges negated by a mirror); any other transform makes its NURBS form. A grid transform that moves every vertex exactly is exact: deviation 0 (chapter 7; piece G69).
**Splits are trimmed polylines.** A split leaves the polyline untouched and trims it (`crate::trimmed`); a reversal reverses the vertices and negates the bulges, exactly.
modules.job: The bulge polyline kind: lines and arcs through vertices, each arc given by its bulge, with optional widths, as DXF's LWPOLYLINE stores them.

method.text: the bulge of DXF's LWPOLYLINE (chapter 14's polyline row, `projects/engines/geometry/architecture/14-2d-drafting.md`), written as the rational quadratic form of a circular arc (L. Piegl and W. Tiller, *The NURBS Book*, 2nd ed., section 7.3, <https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-59223-2>) with the middle point carried homogeneously, so the semicircle's point at infinity is a finite h₁.

modules.cost: evaluation is a binary search over the starts plus the segment's; a bound is the bounds of the segments it meets; the conversion is linear in the Bezier pieces, each O(p²·D).
modules.does: [`Composite`] stores segments (trimmed curves, so a segment is any leaf kind on any interval) and starts s₀ < s₁ < … < sₙ: segment k runs over [sₖ, sₖ₊₁] of the composite's parameter, mapped affinely onto its own interval [aₖ, bₖ], so the joints sit at the starts exactly. A new composite starts at 0 and gives each segment its own length, sₖ₊₁ = sₖ + (bₖ − aₖ), rounded, which the affine map absorbs. Consecutive segments must meet: the end of one and the start of the next must have certified enclosures that overlap (chapter 14: "ends must be the same exact point"; there is no join fuzz), and each joint keeps a certified bound on its gap, 0 when both ends are the same exact point.
guarantees: **Exact definition.** Evaluation at a parameter whose segment parameter is exact is the segment's; otherwise the segment parameter is enclosed and the segment bounded over it, so enclosures stay certified; derivatives carry the affine map's factor.

**Certified conversion.** The deviation adds, per segment, the segment's conversion, elevation and Bezier extraction, the joint's gap and weight rescaling (the rational bound of `crate::rational`), and the rounding of shifted knots (a Bezier piece reparametrised by e at its ends moves by at most |N′|·e).

**Exact operations where they can be.** A split at a joint, a reversal and a split whose segment parameter is exact change no point; a transform moves each segment with its own deviation, the joints' gaps recomputed within it.
modules.job: The composite curve kind: trimmed curves joined end to end into one curve, and its conversion to one NURBS curve.

method.text: STEP's `composite_curve` (ISO 10303-42) with segments on parameter trims, joined as chapter 14 asks (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/14-2d-drafting.md`); conversion by degree elevation (A5.9) and Bezier decomposition (A5.6) of L. Piegl and W. Tiller, *The NURBS Book*, 2nd ed. (<https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-59223-2>).

modules.cost: constant per evaluation; conversion O(n) in its pieces (at most 5 for a circle or ellipse, 1024 for a hyperbola).
modules.does: [`Circle`] is c + r·cos πt·x̂ + r·sin πt·ŷ on an exact [`Frame`], t in half-turns over at most one turn (a full circle is [0, 2]). [`Ellipse`] is c + cos πt·u + sin πt·v, by its parameter (the eccentric angle), not by polar angle (chapter 7), with u and v principal semi-axes on a frame or any conjugate pair ([`Axes`]). [`Hyperbola`] is c + cosh t·u + sinh t·v, one branch. [`Parabola`] is c + t²·u + t·v; on a frame with u = f·x̂ and v = 2f·ŷ it is the parabola of focal length f with its vertex at c, as ISO 10303-42 defines it. Each implements the kind contract through the shared analytic form (`crate::form`).
guarantees: **Stored as themselves.** An arc stays an arc: its center, radius and frame are the stored doubles, exactly (chapter 7).

**Exact NURBS forms.** Circles, ellipses and hyperbolas convert to rational quadratics on the tangent half-angle parameter (`crate::rational`), parabolas to a quadratic on the same parameter; each with a certified deviation, 0 when the doubles hold the conversion exactly.

**Transforms change kinds explicitly.** A similarity keeps a circle a circle (radius times its scale, frame carried); any other transform makes it an [`Ellipse`] with conjugate axes, on the same parameter; principal axes on a frame stay principal under a similarity. A grid transform that moves the centre exactly is exact: deviation 0 (chapter 7; piece G69).
**Exact split and reversal.** A split changes only the domain; a reversal negates the domain and v (a frame's normal), exactly.
modules.job: The conic kinds: circle and arc, ellipse and elliptical arc, hyperbola and parabola, each stored as itself.

method.text: the parametric conics of ISO 10303-42 (`circle`, `ellipse`, `hyperbola`, `parabola`), with angles in half-turns, the kernel's proven angle form (chapter 6); their conversion from L. Piegl and W. Tiller, *The NURBS Book*, 2nd ed., chapter 7 (<https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-59223-2>).

modules.cost: for each parameter, a few enclosures and bounds of the kind, a split, a reversal and a transform: the kind's own costs, a few dozen times.
modules.does: [`check`] runs a kind through every law of [`Law`] at the parameters given and returns the first law broken, with where. The laws compare certified objects with each other: two enclosures of one exact value must overlap, so a bound, an enclosure, a conversion, a split, a reversal or a transform that is wrong by more than its own stated error is caught wherever a sample lands on it. Evaluation in doubles is compared with the certified enclosure within 2^−30 of the largest value at that parameter, which catches a wrong formula, not rounding.
guarantees: **Sound.** A law reported broken is broken: two certified enclosures of one exact value that do not overlap (after widening by the stated deviations) prove that one of them is false, and a refusal the law requires that did not come is a broken refusal.
**Deterministic.** The checks run in the order of the parameters given, each law in the order of [`Law`]; the same kind and parameters give the same verdict.
modules.job: The kind contract: the laws every curve kind must keep, as a check any kind's tests run (`projects/engines/geometry/AGENTS.md`, "How to add a geometry kind").

method.text: property checks of the trait's contract (chapter 28.2's contract laws, applied to the behaviour chapter 7 lists): consistency of certified enclosures, as interval methods check inclusion (R. E. Moore, R. B. Kearfott and M. J. Cloud, *Introduction to Interval Analysis*, SIAM (2009), <https://doi.org/10.1137/1.9780898717716>, the inclusion property of chapter 5).

modules.cost: a few machine words; nothing allocates.
modules.does: [`CurveError`] names the failure of an operation of a curve or surface kind (the surface kinds of `geom-surface` share it, a span there being a box): a parameter or span outside the domain, a transform a 2D curve cannot take, a refusal from the NURBS algorithms underneath, a result that is not finite, or a budget that stopped the work. [`ContractError`] names the law of the kind contract (`crate::contract`) a kind broke, and where.
guarantees: **Typed, never silent.** No operation clamps a parameter into the domain or returns a best-so-far result beside an error (chapter 29.7).
**Comparable and stable.** Every variant holds plain values, so errors compare with `==` and print the same on every target.
modules.job: The one error type of the curve kinds: what a kind refuses, and why.

method.none: error enums and their `Display` and `Error` implementations.

modules.cost: a few interval evaluations of g, one `atan2` and at most sixteen evaluations per family; the pieces' route at most 64 × 9 evaluations of g and of g′.
modules.does: [`Scalar`] names the functions the analytic kinds are made of, one coordinate of one derivative at a time, each with interval coefficients (enclosures of the exact ones the stored data define), and the closed form of the zeros of its derivative:
guarantees: **Certified.** The result holds g(t) for every t of the span and every coefficient in its enclosure. A function continuous on a closed span takes its extremes at the ends or where g′ is zero; every such zero inside the span lies in one of the enclosures evaluated (the table's closed forms in interval arithmetic: `geom-num`'s proven `atan2`, `ln`, `sinpi` and `cospi`, π between its neighbouring doubles), and g over an enclosure holds g there.

**Few evaluations however long the span.** Periodic critical points come in families t = c + 2m, each one period of cos πt apart. Along a family the values of g are constant (`Wave` with q = 0) or step by the same amount from one member to the next (2q for `Wave`, ±2πR for `Involute`), so the extremes over the members inside the span are at the first or the last of them. So at most four members of a family are evaluated: the first two and the last two whose enclosure meets the span, since an enclosure narrower than a period may reach into the span while its member lies just outside, and the next member then lies inside.

**Undecided cases are refined, not guessed.** Where the coefficients' enclosures leave a closed form undecided (a and b enclosing the origin without both being zero, \|q\| enclosing πR, r or a + b enclosing zero without being zero, a family wider than half a period, a span or critical point beyond 2⁵⁰), and for `Modulated`, which has no closed form, the span is cut into monotone pieces: at most 64 pieces of at most a quarter of a half-turn; a piece whose derivative's enclosure has a certain sign contributes g at its two ends, any other is cut in eight and tested again, and a piece still undecided contributes the intersection of g's interval extension over it and its mean-value form g(m) + g′·[−r, r] about its middle m. That is sound too, and only a little wider.
**Deterministic.** The same function and span give the same bits on every target.
modules.job: Closed-form extents: the range of one function of one parameter over a span, from its values at the span's ends and at its critical points, each critical point in closed form.

method.text: the extreme value theorem with the critical points in closed form, the amplitude and phase form R·cos(π(t − φ)) of a·cos πt + b·sin πt, and interval arithmetic for every closed form (R. E. Moore, R. B. Kearfott and M. J. Cloud, *Introduction to Interval Analysis*, SIAM (2009), <https://doi.org/10.1137/1.9780898717716>: the natural interval extension, and the monotonicity test and the mean-value form of chapter 6 for the pieces).

modules.cost: a few dozen floating-point operations per evaluation and derivative order; a bound one closed-form extent per coordinate, a few evaluations each.
modules.does: [`Shape`] names the scalar functions (f₁, f₂, f₃) of each kind, with angles in half-turns, the kernel's proven angle form (chapter 6):
guarantees: **Certified.** An enclosure holds the exact value of C⁽ᵏ⁾ at every parameter of the interval: `geom-num`'s proven `sinpi`, `cospi` and `exp` enclosures, π between its two neighbouring doubles, and interval arithmetic that is exact where it can be (`tight`).

**Derivatives in closed form.** The k-th derivative of each scalar function is its formula, never a finite difference (chapter 7): cos and sin of πt shift by a quarter turn per derivative and gain a factor π, cosh and sinh trade places, and the involute's terms follow d^k(θ·cos θ) = θ·cos⁽ᵏ⁾θ + k·cos⁽ᵏ⁻¹⁾θ.

**Closed-form extents.** A bound holds every value of C⁽ᵏ⁾ over the span, and is the hull of its values at the span's ends and at the critical points of each coordinate inside it (`crate::extent`'s guarantees).
**Refused outside.** A parameter or span outside the domain, or not finite, is an error.
modules.job: The certified evaluation the analytic kinds share: every one of them is C(t) = c + f₁(t)·u + f₂(t)·v + f₃(t)·w, fixed vectors times scalar functions of the parameter.

method.text: direct evaluation of the closed forms, in interval arithmetic for the enclosures (R. E. Moore, R. B. Kearfott and M. J. Cloud, *Introduction to Interval Analysis*, SIAM (2009), <https://doi.org/10.1137/1.9780898717716>, the natural interval extension); the extents of chapter 12.3's analytic row, from the ends and the closed-form critical points (`crate::extent`).

modules.cost: two cross products and three norms; constant, nothing allocates.
modules.does: a [`Frame`] stores a reference vector x and a normal n, any two finite vectors that are not parallel. They define, exactly, the orthonormal frame x̂ = ((n × x) × n) / |(n × x) × n|, ŷ = (n × x) / |n × x|, n̂ = n / |n|: x̂ is the unit vector along the part of x across n, and ŷ = n̂ × x̂ completes a right-handed frame. Because the stored doubles define the frame, rather than approximate one, a circle on it is exactly a circle of exactly its radius, whatever rounding made x and n. A 2D frame has x in the plane and n = (0, 0, k) with k ≠ 0: ŷ is x̂ turned a quarter turn anticlockwise when k > 0 and clockwise when k < 0. [`Frame::reversed`] negates n, which negates ŷ and n̂ exactly and keeps x̂, as reversing a kind needs.
guarantees: **An exact definition, certified enclosures.** The unit vectors come in doubles and as enclosures of their exact values, exact points wherever the arithmetic is exact (an axis-aligned frame, or one whose lengths are whole, such as 3-4-5).
**Refused when degenerate.** Parallel x and n (decided exactly), a 2D normal with x or y components, and entries that are not finite are errors.
modules.job: Orthonormal frames defined exactly by two stored vectors: where a kind starts and which way it turns.

method.text: the derived axes of an axis placement, as ISO 10303-42 builds them for `axis2_placement_3d` (its `build_axes` function, <https://downloads.steptools.com/docs/stp_aim/html/t_build_axes.html>: the axis normalised, the reference direction's projection across it, then their cross product), with the projection taken exactly as (n × x) × n so that no stored vector needs to be of unit length or perpendicular.

modules.cost: constant per evaluation; conversion O(n·p²) for n eighths of a turn.
modules.does: [`Helix`] stores a center on its axis, a frame whose normal is the axis, a radius and a pitch (the rise per full turn, positive for a right-handed helix), or, as the affine image of one, the vectors u, v and w themselves ([`HelixAxes`]). It is a 3D kind; any length of domain, many turns included. Neither STEP nor IFC has a helix (chapter 7), so it is stored as itself here and exchanged as a NURBS approximation with its certified error.
guarantees: **Exact.** The stored doubles define the helix; evaluation is certified through the shared analytic form (`crate::form`, shape `Helical`).

**A certified NURBS form.** A helix is not a rational curve, so it converts by Taylor pieces of degree 9, each an eighth of a turn, on the same parameter, with the remainder bounded by its tenth derivative (`crate::taylor`): about 2.4·10⁻¹⁴ times (|u| + |v|) per piece, plus rounding.

**Transforms change it explicitly.** A similarity keeps it a circular helix (radius and pitch times the scale, the pitch negated by a mirror, which turns a right-handed helix into a left-handed one); any other transform gives the `Vectors` form on the same parameter.
**Exact split and reversal.** Reversal negates v and w (the frame's normal) and the domain, and keeps the pitch: a helix traversed backwards keeps its hand.
modules.job: The helix kind, exactly: c + r·cos πt·x̂ + r·sin πt·ŷ + t·(pitch/2)·n̂, t in half-turns.

method.text: the circular helix in its standard parametrisation, with angles in half-turns, stored exactly as chapter 7 asks (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/07-geometry-types.md`: "Helix (exact; neither STEP nor IFC has one)").

modules.cost: constant per evaluation; conversion O(n·p²) for n eighths of a turn.
modules.does: [`Involute`] stores the base circle's center, radius and frame (the involute leaves the circle at x̂ when t = 0 and unwinds towards ŷ for t > 0, the other way for t < 0), or, as the affine image of one, the vectors u and v themselves ([`Axes`]). The point t = 0 is a cusp: the derivative vanishes there, and the bounds say so. Gear teeth flanks are its common use.
guarantees: **Exact.** The stored doubles define the involute; evaluation is certified through the shared analytic form (`crate::form`, shape `Involute`), whose derivatives of every order are closed forms.

**A certified NURBS form.** The involute is not a rational curve; it converts as the helix does, by Taylor pieces of degree 9 an eighth of a turn wide on the same parameter (`crate::taylor`), the remainder bounded by its tenth derivative.
**Transforms change it explicitly.** A similarity keeps it the involute of a circle (radius times the scale); any other transform gives the `Vectors` form on the same parameter.
**Exact split and reversal.**
modules.job: The circular involute kind: the path of the end of a taut string unwound from a circle, c + r·(cos θ + θ·sin θ)·x̂ + r·(sin θ − θ·cos θ)·ŷ with θ = πt, t in half-turns.

method.text: the involute of a circle in its standard parametrisation by the unwinding angle (for gears, F. L. Litvin and A. Fuentes, *Gear Geometry and Applied Theory*, 2nd ed., Cambridge (2004), <https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511547126>), with angles in half-turns.

modules.cost: O(K) for a sum, O(K²) for a product, quotient or root.
modules.does: a [`Jet`] of order K holds enclosures of f(t), f′(t)/1!, …, f⁽ᴷ⁾(t)/K! at every parameter t of an interval (a point, for an enclosure; a span, for a bound). Sums, products, quotients and square roots of jets are the jets of the sums, products, quotients and roots, by the recurrences of automatic differentiation, so a jet of an offset curve's formula gives its derivatives to order K from the basis curve's derivatives to order K + 1.
guarantees: **Certified.** If each input coefficient encloses its function's coefficient at every t of the interval, so does each output coefficient: every recurrence is a polynomial or a quotient in the inputs, evaluated in interval arithmetic (inclusion isotonicity).
**Refused where undefined.** A quotient by, or a root of, a jet whose value may be zero (or, for the root, negative) is an error, never a guess.
modules.job: Truncated Taylor series in interval arithmetic: the derivatives of a formula built from curves' derivatives, enclosed, without differentiating the formula by hand.

method.text: the Taylor-coefficient recurrences of automatic differentiation (A. Griewank and A. Walther, *Evaluating Derivatives*, 2nd ed., SIAM (2008), <https://doi.org/10.1137/1.9780898717761>, on univariate Taylor propagation), evaluated in intervals as in Taylor-model and interval AD methods (R. E. Moore, R. B. Kearfott and M. J. Cloud, *Introduction to Interval Analysis*, SIAM (2009), <https://doi.org/10.1137/1.9780898717716>).

modules.cost: constant per evaluation; conversion and transforms constant.
modules.does: [`Line`] stores an origin o, a direction d (any nonzero vector) and a domain whose ends may be infinite: finite for a segment, one infinite end for a ray, both for an infinite line ([`Extent`]). It implements the kind contract through the shared analytic form (`crate::form`, shape `Linear`). A ray or infinite line has no finite NURBS form and no bound over an infinite span; both are refused, never clamped.
guarantees: **Exact storage.** The doubles o and d define the line; [`Line::segment`] from two points says how far its stored direction is from the exact difference (0 when it is exact, as it is for grid points).
**Exact operations.** Split and reversal (o kept, d negated, the domain negated) change no bit; conversion of a segment is the degree-1 NURBS curve through its ends.

**Bounded or refused.** A transform of a ray or infinite line whose direction's image is not exact would drift without bound along it, so it is refused with [`CurveError::Unbounded`]; trim the line to a segment first.
modules.job: The line kind: a segment, a ray or an infinite line, P(t) = o + t·d.

method.text: the parametric line of ISO 10303-42 (`line`: a point and a vector), with the segment, ray and infinite line distinguished by the domain, as DXF's LINE, RAY and XLINE are; the kinds chapter 7 lists (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/07-geometry-types.md`).

modules.cost: a binary search over the breaks and a few interval operations.
modules.does: [`NurbsForm`] is what [`crate::ParamCurve::to_nurbs`] returns: the NURBS curve and the [`ParamMap`] taking a parameter t of the kind to the parameter u of the NURBS curve at the same point. Most kinds convert with the same parameter. The conics cannot: a circle traced uniformly in angle is not a rational curve in its angle, so its exact NURBS form, the rational quadratic, runs on the tangent half-angle substitution instead. [`ParamMap::enclose`] encloses u for any t, so a caller (and the kind contract) can compare the kind and its NURBS form at the same point.
guarantees: **Certified.** The enclosure holds the exact u: τ is enclosed with `geom-num`'s proven `sinpi`, `cospi` and `exp` enclosures, and the result is cut to the piece's span, which holds the exact u because τ is increasing.
**Refused outside.** A parameter outside the breaks is an error.
modules.job: A kind converted to NURBS, and the map from the kind's parameter to the NURBS curve's.

method.text: the rational quadratic form of a conic and its parametrisation (L. Piegl and W. Tiller, *The NURBS Book*, 2nd ed., sections 7.2 and 7.3, <https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-59223-2>), where u is the stereographic (tangent half-angle) parameter of the circle and, for the hyperbola, of the unit hyperbola.

modules.cost: the classification (a few dozen interval operations), then twelve products per image.
modules.does: [`Motion::of`] reads a [`TypedTransform`] for a kind of dimension D: its entries (`crate::affine`), its certified classification (`geom-math`), which decides whether circles stay circles (a similarity) and whether it mirrors, and the scale factor a similarity applies to lengths (exactly 1 when it keeps lengths). Its images of stored data are doubles; its image of a kind's form encloses the exact image, so a kind compares the curve it builds with the exact image of the curve it had.
guarantees: **Planar kinds see the plane.** For a 2D kind the classification is of the transform's 2×2 block, so a uniform scale of the plane keeps a circle a circle.

**Typed.** A degenerate transform (singular, or too close to it to decide) is refused for the analytic kinds, whose definitions need independent vectors; a 2D kind takes only a transform acting in the plane.

**Normals carried, not reflected.** A normal maps by n ↦ sign(det M)·M·n, so the frame built from the images, x̂′ along M·x and ŷ′ = n̂′ × x̂′, is exactly the image of x̂ and ŷ under a similarity M = s·R: (R·a) × (R·b) = det R · R·(a × b) for an orthogonal R.

**Exact where the arithmetic is.** The enclosed images use `tight`, so an exact transform of exact data gives exact points, and [`Motion::exact_for`] says when a grid transform moves a kind's stored points exactly, so that the kind rebuilt from them is exactly its image.
modules.job: A typed transform as the analytic kinds apply it: its entries, its classification, the images of stored points, vectors and normals, and the exact image of a kind's vectors for the deviation.

method.text: affine images of points and vectors, and the cross-product identity above for orthogonal matrices; the classification is `geom-math`'s (G03), and the rule that a transform changes a kind explicitly is chapter 7's (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/07-geometry-types.md`).

modules.cost: an enclosure or bound runs Bezier extraction in intervals, O(s·p²·D) for s spans, plus O(p²·D) per piece and derivative order; a split O(n·D); a reversal or transform O(n·D).
modules.does: implements [`ParamCurve`] for [`Curve`]. Points and derivatives are A3.1, A3.2 and A4.2 (`geom-nurbs`). Enclosures, bounds and derivative bounds come from the curve's Bernstein forms in interval arithmetic (piece G59): the piece holding the parameter, or each piece meeting the span cut down to it by de Casteljau subdivision at interval parameters, its box from the convex hull; derivatives from hodographs, and for a rational curve by Leibniz's rule on W·C = A, C^(k) = (A^(k) − Σ C(k, i)·W^(i)·C^(k−i)) / W, in interval boxes, with C over a span taken from the piece's convex hull rather than from the boxes of A and W, which are far wider when the weights spread (chapter 19.3, piece G68). Conversion to NURBS is the curve itself, exactly. A split inserts the parameter until its multiplicity is the degree (A5.1) and parts the control points there. Reversal negates and reverses the knots, which is exact. A transform maps the control points (affine invariance) with the weights kept.
guarantees: **Certified.** Every enclosure and bound holds the exact value; a split's deviation is the certified rounding of the knot insertion; a transform's is the largest certified error of a control point's image, which bounds the curve's because a NURBS point is a weighted average of its control points with weights `N_i`·`w_i` ≥ 0 (The NURBS Book, P4.3 and P4.4).
**Exact where the operation is.** Conversion and reversal change no bit (deviation 0).
**Refused outside the domain.** A parameter or span outside it is an error, never clamped.
modules.job: The NURBS curve kind: `geom-nurbs`'s [`Curve`] under the kind contract.

method.text: The NURBS Book, 2nd ed. (<https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-59223-2>): A3.1, A3.2, A4.2, A5.1, de Casteljau subdivision (section 1.3), hodographs (section 3.3) and affine invariance (P4.10), on `geom-nurbs` (pieces G56 and G59).

modules.cost: an evaluation of order k is the basis's of order k + 1 plus O(k²) interval operations; the cache is the Taylor conversion of `crate::taylor`, eight to 128 pieces per smooth interval of the basis, narrower pieces tried where wider ones cannot bound the offset's derivatives.
modules.does: [`Offset`] stores a trimmed basis curve C and an [`OffsetLaw`]:
guarantees: **Certified, or refused.** Where the normal may vanish (a cusp of the basis, or a span too wide to separate it from zero) a derivative bound is `Unbounded` and an enclosure is refused, never guessed; a bound on the points still holds there, from the basis's bound widened by the offset's largest size.
**Exact split and reversal.** A split trims the basis; a reversal reverses the basis and negates the distances (the left normal of the reversed curve is the right normal).

**Transforms keep the kind only when exact.** A grid transform of an offset whose basis moves exactly gives an offset (a mirror negating the side); any other transform gives the moved NURBS cache, with both deviations.
modules.job: The offset curve kind: a basis curve moved along its normal, in 2D, in 3D against a reference direction, or by distances that vary along it, with a certified NURBS cache.

method.text: offset curves as defined in ISO 10303-42 (`offset_curve_2d`, `offset_curve_3d`) and IFC 4.3 (`IfcOffsetCurveByDistances`), evaluated with automatic differentiation in interval arithmetic; offsets of conics and splines are neither conics nor splines (R. T. Farouki and C. A. Neff, "Analytic properties of plane offset curves", Computer Aided Geometric Design 7 (1990), <https://doi.org/10.1016/0167-8396(90)90023-K>), hence the certified cache.

modules.cost: the NURBS kind's costs on the cache.
modules.does: [`OnSurface`] stores the pcurve (a trimmed 2D curve in the surface's (u, v) space), an opaque [`SurfaceRef`] into the geometry pool that holds the surface (chapter 8.1: geometry attaches by index into a body's pools), and the 3D curve as a NURBS cache on the pcurve's parameter with a certified bound on its distance from S(pcurve(t)). `geom-curve` sits below `geom-surface` and cannot see surfaces (chapter 27), so, as chapter 12 lays out for the intersection curve, it evaluates, bounds, splits and converts the kind through its cache alone: the kind's curve is the cache, and [`OnSurface::error`] says how far the surface's own curve may be from it. The surface crates build the cache and its bound, and evaluate S on the pcurve when they need the exact curve.
guarantees: **The contract on the cache.** Every evaluation, bound, split and transform is the NURBS kind's on the cache, certified for the cache; the error carries over: a split adds its deviation to each half's error, and a transform scales the error by an upper bound on the transform's stretch (its linear part's Frobenius norm) and adds its deviation.
**Exact pcurve.** The pcurve is never approximated here: a split trims it, a reversal reverses it, a transform leaves it (the surface moves with the pool, its parameters do not).
modules.job: The curve-on-surface kind: a curve in a surface's parameter space (a pcurve), the surface held by reference, and its 3D curve as a certified NURBS cache.

method.text: the pcurve and its 3D cache of chapter 8 (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/08-topology.md`, fins and their pcurves) and the cache-only evaluation chapter 12 gives the intersection curve (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/12-intersections.md`).

modules.cost: none here; each kind's implementation states its own.
modules.does: [`ParamCurve`] is the trait chapter 12.1 names for this behaviour, implemented by each kind and by [`CurveKind`], the storage enum with one variant per kind, which dispatches to it. Operations that make a new curve (split, reverse, transform) return a [`CurveKind`], because a transform may change a kind (a non-uniform scale turns a circle into an ellipse, chapter 7), wrapped in `geom-nurbs`'s [`Changed`]: the result and a certified bound on how far it lies from the exact result of the operation on the exact input, 0 when it is exact.
guarantees: **Certified, or refused.** Every bound and enclosure holds the exact value for the curve the stored data define; every [`Changed`] deviation bounds the distance between the returned curve and the exact result. A kind that cannot bound a derivative over a span says [`DerivativeBound::Unbounded`] rather than guess.
**One family for 2D and 3D.** The trait is generic over the dimension D, so planar and spatial curves share every kind and every rule (chapter 7, principle 8).
**Closed and exhaustive.** [`CurveKind`] lists every kind built; matching on it is exhaustive, and adding a kind is a new variant (the playbook in `projects/engines/geometry/AGENTS.md`).
**Typed transforms.** A transform is a `geom-math` [`TypedTransform`]: exact, rational or certified, and the result's deviation accounts for its entries as the variant holds them.
modules.job: The behaviour every curve kind has (chapter 7): evaluation, derivatives, certified enclosures, conservative bounds on the value and its derivatives over any span, conversion to NURBS with an error, split, reverse and transform; and the closed enum that stores every kind.

method.text: the operations of chapter 7 and the trait names proposed in chapter 12.1 (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/12-intersections.md`); the storage-enum-and-behaviour- trait split chapter 7 decides ("Storage uses closed enums ... Behaviour uses traits").

modules.cost: O(n·D) per evaluation and derivative order; O(n²·D) per bound.
modules.does: [`Polynomial`] stores the coefficients a₀ … aₙ (degree 1 to `geom-nurbs`'s `MAX_DEGREE`) and a finite domain, as IFC 4.3's `IfcPolynomialCurve` stores one per coordinate. It evaluates by Horner's rule, bounds a span by the centred form about its middle, converts to a single Bezier piece of its own degree on the same parameter, and transforms by mapping a₀ as a point and the others as vectors, which is exact for every affine map.
guarantees: **Certified.** Enclosures and bounds hold the exact values, in interval arithmetic that is exact where it can be (`tight`); a derivative of order above the degree is exactly zero.
**Exact NURBS form up to rounding.** The Bezier form of the same polynomial, with only the rounding of its control points in the deviation (`crate::taylor`, whose remainder is zero for a polynomial).
**Exact split and reversal.** A split changes the domain only; reversal negates the odd coefficients and the domain.
modules.job: The polynomial curve kind: P(t) = Σⱼ aⱼ·t^j, a vector coefficient per power.

method.text: Horner's rule and its derivatives (D. E. Knuth, *The Art of Computer Programming*, vol. 2, 3rd ed., section 4.6.4), and the centred form of a polynomial over an interval (R. E. Moore, R. B. Kearfott and M. J. Cloud, *Introduction to Interval Analysis*, SIAM (2009), <https://doi.org/10.1137/1.9780898717716>, the centred or Taylor form).

modules.cost: O(n) for n pieces (at most 5 for an ellipse, 1024 for a hyperbola), a few dozen interval operations each.
modules.does: [`conic`] cuts the domain into pieces of at most a quarter turn (an ellipse, t in half-turns) or a parameter width of 1 (a hyperbola), and writes piece [t₀, t₁] as the rational quadratic with control points C(t₀), the meeting point of the end tangents, C(t₁), and weights 1, 1, λ, where, with h = (t₁ − t₀)/2 and σ = tan πh (ellipse) or tanh h (hyperbola), λ = 1 + σ² (ellipse) or 1 − σ² (hyperbola) and the middle control point is C(t₀) + σ·C′(t₀)/π (ellipse) or C(t₀) + σ·C′(t₀) (hyperbola). That is the conic exactly, on the tangent half-angle parameter of [`ParamMap`]. Odd pieces run the other way (weights λ, 1, 1, the middle point from the far end), and each piece's weights are scaled so neighbours share their joint's weight: the weights then alternate and stay bounded. A whole quarter turn has σ = 1 and λ = 2, so a circle on an axis-aligned frame with an exact center and radius converts with weights 1, 1, 2, 1, 1, 1, 2, 1, 1 and every control point exact: deviation 0.
guarantees: **Certified.** Every control point and weight is first enclosed exactly, then stored as a double. The stored piece differs from the exact one by at most max |Pᵢ − Qᵢ| + 2ε/(1 − ε)·max |Qᵢ − Q₀| (stored points P, exact points Q, weights within a relative ε): a rational Bezier point is Σ Rᵢ·Pᵢ with Rᵢ ≥ 0 summing to 1, and a relative change ε in the weights changes each Rᵢ by at most 2ε/(1 − ε) of itself.
**Exact where the doubles are.** With the enclosures exact points, the deviation is 0.
modules.job: The exact NURBS form of a conic: an ellipse (circles and arcs included) or a hyperbola as rational quadratic pieces, with a certified bound on the rounding of its control points and weights.

method.text: the conic as a rational quadratic Bezier (L. Piegl and W. Tiller, *The NURBS Book*, 2nd ed., sections 7.2 and 7.3, <https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-59223-2>), with the weights in the non-symmetric standard form (1, 1, λ) reached from the symmetric (1, cos α, 1) by a rational reparametrisation (section 7.2's weight invariant w₀w₂/w₁² = λ = 1/cos² α), so a quarter circle's weights are exact doubles.

modules.cost: per piece, one enclosure of p derivatives, one derivative bound of order p + 1 and O(p²·D) interval operations; n pieces.
modules.does: [`same_parameter`] cuts a kind's domain into n equal pieces and, on each piece [a, b] with middle m, takes the Taylor polynomial of degree p at m from the kind's certified derivative enclosures, rewrites it in Bernstein form on [a, b] in interval arithmetic, and replaces its two end coefficients by the kind's enclosed points at a and b, so neighbouring pieces share their joint. The pieces become one NURBS curve of degree p with each interior knot repeated p times (a C⁰ join at the exact curve points).
guarantees: **Certified.** On each piece the distance from the curve to the stored NURBS is at most R + E + Z: R = M·ρ^{p+1}/(p+1)!, Taylor's remainder, with M the norm of the kind's bound on its (p + 1)-th derivative over the piece and ρ the farthest the piece reaches from m; E the change from replacing the end coefficients (a Bernstein end basis function is at most 1, and the two together at most 1); Z the rounding of the stored coefficients. A kind whose (p + 1)-th derivative bound is exactly zero is a polynomial of degree p at most, and then R and E are 0: the Taylor polynomial is the curve.
**Same parameter.** The NURBS curve at t is within the deviation of the kind at t.
modules.job: NURBS forms on the same parameter by Taylor polynomials with a certified remainder: the conversion of the kinds that have no exact rational form (helix, involute), and of the polynomial kinds, for which it is exact up to rounding.

method.text: Taylor's theorem with the Lagrange remainder in its vector form (the integral form, whose norm is bounded by the derivative's), the power-to-Bernstein change of basis (R. T. Farouki, "The Bernstein polynomial basis: a centennial retrospective", Computer Aided Geometric Design 29 (2012), section 3, <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cagd.2012.03.001>), and Bezier pieces as a NURBS curve with p-fold knots (L. Piegl and W. Tiller, *The NURBS Book*, 2nd ed., section 2.3, <https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-59223-2>), all in interval arithmetic.

modules.cost: a few floating-point operations per call more than the interval operation.
modules.does: each function is the `geom-num` interval operation of the same name, except that when both operands are single doubles and the exact result is a double too, it returns that double as a point interval instead of widening it. So a circle of integer radius on a grid center, evaluated at a quarter turn, is enclosed by its exact point, and two constructions of one exact value compare equal: a conversion or transform that is exact reports a deviation of 0, which widened intervals never could. [`meet`] intersects two enclosures of one value.
guarantees: **Certified.** A point result is the exact value, decided by an error-free transformation (`geom-num`'s `two_sum` and `two_prod`, whose error is finite and zero exactly when the operation was exact); every other result is the widened interval of `geom-num`, which encloses the exact range.
**Deterministic.** The same operands give the same bits on every target.
modules.job: Interval operations that stay exact when they can: the analytic kinds' arithmetic.

method.text: error-free transformations (T. J. Dekker, "A floating-point technique for extending the available precision", Numerische Mathematik 18 (1971), <https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01397083>; J. R. Shewchuk, "Adaptive precision floating-point arithmetic and fast robust geometric predicates", Discrete & Computational Geometry 18 (1997), <https://doi.org/10.1007/PL00009321>) as exactness tests, with `geom-num`'s interval arithmetic otherwise.

modules.cost: construction O(P·n) evaluations of the heading for P panels of n nodes, with up to twelve ellipses tried per panel; each evaluation n evaluations of the heading and of its sine and cosine, and O(k²) more operations for the k-th derivative; a bound O(1) per panel the span meets; the NURBS form O(m·p²) per attempt for m pieces of degree p, the attempts doubling m; a split or reversal copies the panels, and a transform keeping lengths builds them again.
modules.does: [`Transition`] holds a parent curve and the part of it the curve covers. The parent is a start point, a start direction, a length L and a [`CurvatureLaw`], parameterised by its station, the arc length σ from 0 to L; positive curvature turns left. The part is a window of stations [σ₀, σ₁] and a sense, as IFC 4.3's `IfcCurveSegment` trims a parent curve with its `SegmentStart` and `SegmentLength`, the length's sign giving the sense: run forward, the curve's parameter is the station, on [σ₀, σ₁]; reversed, it is minus the station, on [−σ₁, −σ₀]. [`Transition::new`] makes the whole parent, forward, and [`Transition::segment`] any part of it. The laws are decision 32.33's closed set. From a start curvature κ₁ to an end curvature κ₂, with ξ = σ/L: the clothoid, Helmert, Bloss, cosine and sine transitions and the cant-coupled transition, IFC 4.3's CLOTHOID, HELMERTCURVE, BLOSSCURVE, COSINECURVE, SINECURVE and the curve IFC calls VIENNESEBEND. And IFC's parent spirals, read from a station along them: `IfcClothoid` and the second-, third- and seventh-order polynomial spirals, `IfcCosineSpiral` and `IfcSineSpiral`. It is a curve kind of chapter 7 ([`ParamCurve`], `CurveKind::Transition`): points and derivatives in doubles and certified enclosures of them, bounds on the point and on each derivative over any span, conversion to NURBS with a certified error, split, reversal and typed transforms; and certified enclosures of the turn of the heading and of the curvature at any station of the parent.
guarantees: **Exact heading.** The heading is the closed-form integral of the law's curvature: in half-turns, a polynomial of degree at most 8 in ξ plus at most one sine or cosine of an affine argument, its coefficients enclosed from the stored doubles. No quadrature touches it.

**Certified positions.** The position is the start plus the integrals of the cosine and sine of the heading, each by the [`NODES`]-point Gauss–Legendre rule on panels of equal width in ξ. Each panel's remainder is bounded by Trefethen's theorem for integrands analytic in a Bernstein ellipse, the integrand's size on the ellipse bounded in interval arithmetic; the panel count is the smallest power of two (from 1, or 2 for Helmert's two halves) whose remainders sum to at most L·2⁻⁵⁶. An enclosure holds the rounding of every step and the remainders of every panel it passes.
**Deterministic.** The panel count, and so every result, depends only on the stored doubles.

**Located exactly.** A station is placed in its panel by an exact comparison, so an enclosure never mixes two panels, or Helmert's two halves. Helmert's middle, where the fourth derivative jumps, is evaluated on the half its side asks for.
**Never a guess.** A law that needs more than [`MAX_PANELS`] panels is refused ([`CurveError::TooManyPanels`]), never evaluated with a bound it does not meet.

**Exact split and reversal.** A split narrows the window and a reversal flips the sense; the parent and its panels are untouched, so each part, and the reversed curve at −t, evaluate as the original does at the same station, bit for bit (a reversed derivative of odd order negated), with deviation 0.

**Bounds from the panels.** A span's box is the union, over the panels it meets, of the point at the panel's start (or the span's) moved by up to the panel's length along any tangent the heading's enclosure allows there: no sampling. A derivative's box is the interval evaluation of its closed form over the span, from both sides at Helmert's middle.

**A certified NURBS form.** Taylor pieces of degree 9 on the same parameter (`crate::taylor`), each piece's remainder bounded by the box of the tenth derivative, cut at Helmert's middle. The pieces double, from one per smooth part, while each doubling more than halves the certified deviation: the remainder falls about a thousandfold a doubling, so the refining stops where rounding, which no doubling reduces, has taken over: the width of the enclosures the pieces start from and of the stored control points, a few dozen steps of the coordinates. At most [`MAX_PANELS`] pieces.

**Typed transforms.** A transform that keeps lengths keeps a transition: the start point and direction move, a mirror negates the law's curvatures, and the deviation bounds the rounding of both and how far the transform is from the rigid motion they define, over the window. Any other transform gives the moved NURBS form, since the parameter is arc length, which a scale does not keep; its deviation is the conversion's times a bound on the transform's stretch, plus the move's.
modules.job: The transition kind: a plane curve whose curvature follows a law along its length, the transition curves (spirals) of road and rail alignments.

method.text: the heading as the exact integral of curvature and the position by certified Gauss–Legendre quadrature (chapter 17.8). The laws are IFC 4.3's (`IfcAlignmentHorizontalSegmentTypeEnum` and the `IfcSpiral` subtypes, in the record below). An `IfcSineSpiral` is read by its heading, as `IfcSpiral` defines the curve (x = ∫cos Θ dl), where its printed curvature disagrees with the heading's derivative. The remainder bound is L. N. Trefethen, "Is Gauss quadrature better than Clenshaw–Curtis?", SIAM Review 50 (2008), <https://doi.org/10.1137/060659831>, Theorem 4.5: on [−1, 1], |I − Iₙ| ≤ (64/15)·M·ρ⁻²ⁿ/(ρ² − 1) for f analytic in the open ellipse Eρ with |f| ≤ M there; for f = cos πh or sin πh, M ≤ cosh(π·sup |Im h|). The ellipse of a part of a panel lies inside the panel's, so the panel's bound holds for every station in it. No code from the Clothoids library's `Fresnel.cc`: the clothoid uses this same evaluator. A part of the parent is `IfcCurveSegment`'s trimming; the NURBS form is `crate::taylor`'s Taylor pieces with the Lagrange remainder. A rigid motion keeps a plane curve's signed curvature at each arc length and a mirror negates it, and the curvature with the start point and direction fixes the curve (the fundamental theorem of plane curves), so the image of a transition under one is the transition of the moved start and direction with that law.

modules.cost: the series about 20 terms (about 2 µs), the expansion at most 64 (about 2 µs); between, up to about 35 panels of 8 evaluations each, with five of Trefethen's bounds per panel (a few hundred µs: the slow range, which a clothoid near its inflection point never reaches).
modules.does: [`fresnel`] encloses C and S over an interval of arguments. Both are odd, so the work is at |x|, at the double m nearest the interval's middle, in one of four ranges:
guarantees: **Certified.** Each enclosure holds C(x) and S(x) for every x of the interval: every series and expansion summed in interval arithmetic with its remainder bound added, π between its neighbouring doubles, the angle πx²/2 taken from x² split exactly into two doubles (`geom-num`'s two-product) so `geom-num`'s proven `sinpi` and `cospi` see it exactly however large x is, and the quadrature's remainder bounded, never estimated.
**Tight.** About 10⁻¹⁵ wide on the expansion's range, a few times that on the series', and a few times 10⁻¹⁴ between (the rounding of a few dozen panels).
**Deterministic.** Fixed ranges, a fixed series stop, panels fixed by their position alone: the same bits on every target.
modules.job: The Fresnel integrals C(x) = ∫₀ˣ cos(πt²/2) dt and S(x) = ∫₀ˣ sin(πt²/2) dt, enclosed: the clothoid's own functions, by series and asymptotic expansion with their remainder bounds, and by the transition kind's certified quadrature between them; and a clothoid's point by them, [`Transition::enclose_fresnel`] (piece G67).

N. Trefethen, "Is Gauss quadrature better than Clenshaw–Curtis?", SIAM Review 50 (2008), <https://doi.org/10.1137/060659831>, Theorem 4.5). modules.does: [`Trimmed`] stores a [`Basis`] (any leaf kind: NURBS, analytic or bulge polyline) and an interval [a, b] inside its domain, and is the basis on that interval, on the basis's own parameter. Trimming keeps the basis exactly as stored: a NURBS curve trimmed at a crossing keeps its knots and control points, where cutting it would insert knots and round (chapter 14: "a trimmed spline is section 7's trimmed curve, the original curve on an implicit parameter interval"). Composite and offset curves and curves on surfaces are built on trimmed curves, so the kinds that hold curves hold only leaves: no kind contains itself.
guarantees: **Exact.** Evaluation, enclosures and bounds are the basis's, inside the interval; a split changes only the interval; a reversal or transform is the basis's, with its deviation.
**Refused outside.** A parameter or span outside the interval is an error, though the basis would take it.
**Converted by cutting.** The NURBS form is the basis cut at the interval's ends (exact for the analytic kinds, by knot insertion for NURBS), then converted; the deviations add.

invariants: Canonical bytes: deterministic CBOR (RFC 8949, section 4.2), a pure function of the stored value on every machine and thread count (24.1, 24.3).
Never stores decimal text or rounds a number twice; NaN and infinities are refused both ways (24.3, 24.13).
Reads untrusted bytes through the `no_std` byte-source traits, checks every length before allocating, walks nesting with an explicit stack and never panics (24.7).
An unknown required record stops the reader with `UnsupportedRecord`; an unknown optional record is skipped and listed (24.2).
Readers for every old version are kept, and a file opens without replaying anything (24.6, 26.2).
Never depends on an exchange crate or on a recipe's owner (24.4).

modules.cost: linear in the record; values are copied once.
modules.does: [`attributes_record`] writes a model's [`Definitions`] and its [`Attributes`] as one required record (tag [`ATTRIBUTES_TAG`]): each definition with its owner, name and version, the kinds of entity that may carry it, its value schema and its behaviour at section 8.4's events; then each attribute's values by name, a value as the owner's opaque bytes, or the values a merge combined. [`read_attributes`] reads them back: definitions, and attributes whose classes come from their definitions, so `geom-name`'s attribute step can carry the values through later edits without ever decoding them.
guarantees: **No owner needed** (24.4; piece G95): a value is the owner's bytes, kept as they are; what a value does at each event is in its definition, which every reader reads.
**Every value has its definition**: a value whose attribute the record does not define is refused, and a definition is checked as `Definition::new` and `Definitions::define` check it.
**One encoding**: the record is read and encoded again, and the bytes must be the stored ones.
modules.job: The attributes record: every attribute definition a model holds, and every value keyed by the persistent name of the entity that carries it, readable by a program that does not know the attribute's owner.
