modules.cost: linear in the body: one pass over each table to write, one to read, one SHA-256 pass over every chunk; memory for one chunk's payload at a time plus the body itself. [`BodyVersion::next`] is linear in the chunks it checks and the rows of the name tables, and encodes and hashes only the chunks that changed, plus the index.
modules.does: [`write_body`] turns a `geom_topo::Body` into a [`StoredBody`]: one chunk record (type 4) per run of [`CHUNK_ROWS`] rows of each table, in arena order, and the index record (type 3) listing every table's row count and its chunks' content IDs in order. [`read_body`] reads them back through `geom_topo::Builder`, which checks the topology again before it publishes, so a stored body is never trusted further than a built one. The tables, by code in [`table`], are the arenas of chapter 8.2: regions, shells, faces, loops, fins, edges and vertices; the geometry pools (points, surfaces, curves and pcurves); and, for a body published by name, the names of its regions, faces, edges and vertices. A [`BodyVersion`] is a body with each chunk's content ID: [`BodyVersion::next`] writes a new version, encoding and hashing only the chunks it does not share with the one before (23.8). Its [`BodyVersion::geometry_id`] is the root of the same tree without the name tables, which a name-free cache key takes (23.8).
guarantees: **Index for index.** A body read back equals the one written (`PartialEq`), every arena in the same order, so the next operation on either gives the same bits (24.3).

**Chunks are a pure function of their rows.** The runs are geom-topo's own chunks (`geom_topo::CHUNK_ROWS`, 4,096), so a chunk whose rows did not change encodes to the same bytes and the same content ID, whatever else changed: an edit to 1% of a body's rows rewrites only the chunks those rows are in.

**A new version hashes only what it changed, and gets the same IDs.** [`BodyVersion::next`] reuses a chunk's ID only where every column of the chunk is the very chunk the version before holds (`Column::shares_chunk`) or, for a name table, where the rows are equal, so its index is byte for byte [`write_body`]'s. The version holds the earlier body's columns, so a chunk it compares against is never freed and its address reused.

**References are checked.** Every reference is stored as its row plus one, 0 for none; a required reference of 0, a row count that disagrees with the chunks, a chunk of the wrong table or position, or a content ID that does not match its chunk is refused before anything is built, and the builder then checks the topology itself.
modules.job: Body records: a body stored as one index record and a chunk record for every 4,096-row run of each of its tables, so a body's content ID is the root of a hash tree and a new version writes only the chunks that changed (24.2, 24.3).

method.text: chapter 24.2 to 24.4 of the kernel architecture, `projects/engines/geometry/architecture/24-file-format-exchange.md`, and the arenas of chapter 8.2, `projects/engines/geometry/architecture/08-topology.md`; Merkle's hash tree, <https://doi.org/10.1007/3-540-48184-2_32>, for the content ID of the index over its chunks.

modules.cost: a key is one encoding and one SHA-256 pass over it: linear in the path's labels and the number of inputs. A store lookup, insertion or eviction is O(log n) in the entries held.
modules.does: [`CacheKey::new`] is the SHA-256 of the canonical encoding of `[edition, name, version, path, precision, [input content IDs]]`: the kernel edition, the operation's name and version from its schema, its `OpPath` (every name the operation creates holds it, 20.2), its precision (a preview and a final result never share a key, 23.6) and the content ID of each input, in the operation's order. [`CacheKey::name_free`] is the same without the path, for the operations whose schema says their geometry does not depend on names; its inputs are then the content IDs of their geometry without names. [`CacheEntry`] holds a result with the budget its run had and what the run used. [`MemoStore`] is the caller's store of entries: bounded by bytes, it forgets the entry used longest ago first, and it is a value the caller owns. [`restamp`] turns a name-free entry into the entry of one call: it fills in the path and the input names and recomputes every `NameId`, through a result's own [`Restamp`].
guarantees: **A hit is the same bits as a fresh run.** [`CacheEntry::answer`] answers only when a fresh run under the caller's budget would give exactly the stored answer: a stored result, or a stored deterministic error, when the budget covers everything the run used (a run stops only when a charge passes its cap, and charges only add); a stored budget failure only under the same budget, since a smaller one can stop the run sooner with other numbers. Every other call misses, and the caller's own run gives the exact `BudgetExceeded`.
**What is never stored.** [`CacheEntry::new`] refuses `Cancelled`, `OutOfMemory` and a batch's total: none is the operation's deterministic answer (23.10).
**Name-free only where the schema says so.** [`CacheKey::name_free`] gives no key for an operation whose schema does not set `name_free`. A body enters such a key by `BodyVersion::geometry_id`.

**A restamped hit is the same bits as a fresh run, names included.** Names go through `Stamp`, a body is published again by its new names, so its arenas take the new order. A stored error holds paths and names only the run knows, so [`restamp`] gives no entry for one: the call misses, and the caller's own run gives it.

**One encoding.** A key is `geom-op`'s canonical encoding and SHA-256 (32.20), and its path is written by [`OpPath::encode`], as names write it. Every field changes the key; a key with a path and a name-free key differ in length, so they never collide by construction.

**Bounded, and deterministic.** A [`MemoStore`] never holds more than its byte bound. Which entry it forgets depends only on the order of the calls made on it, never on time, addresses or a hash seed. It holds no global state (principle 7).
modules.job: Cache keys and the reference memo store: an operation's result named by everything it depends on, so that a hit is the same bits as running the operation again (23.8).

method.text: chapter 23.8's `CacheKey`, `CacheEntry` and memo store (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/23-performance.md`), with the content IDs of 24.2 (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/24-file-format-exchange.md`) and SHA-256 by NIST FIPS 180-4, <https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/180-4/upd1/final>, through `geom_op::hash`. 23.8 fixes only that the store is bounded by bytes and owned by the caller; forgetting the entry used longest ago first is this piece's choice, deterministic because its clock counts calls.

modules.cost: see each module.
modules.does: SKG's bytes are deterministic CBOR (RFC 8949, section 4.2.1) with the rules of 24.3. [`decode`] reads them head by head and refuses any other encoding; [`column`] reads the `i64` and `f64` columns coordinates and reals are stored in; [`text`] writes the diagnostic text form of 24.6, and [`parse`] reads it back into the same bytes. The canonical encoder that writes SKG's bytes from values is `geom-op`'s (piece G86), so that `NameId` hashing below this crate uses it too (30.5, "Placed to keep the crate graph acyclic").
guarantees: **One encoding per value.** The decoder accepts exactly the bytes the canonical form gives a value, so equal accepted values are equal bytes, and a content hash over them is a hash of the value (24.2, 24.3).
**Text and bytes convert both ways, bit for bit.** For every input the decoder accepts, the text form reads back to the same bytes.
modules.job: SKG's CBOR subset: the strict decoder that refuses anything but deterministic CBOR, its columns, and the lossless text form.

method.none: it declares its modules and states the subset they share.

modules.cost: O(n) time in the column's bytes, in one pass over chunks of [`SCAN_BYTES_PER_CHARGE`]; one reservation of exactly the values appended. Recursion: none.
modules.does: [`int_column`] and [`float_column`] read the byte string a tag 79 or tag 86 holds (RFC 8746) into values, appending to the caller's vector, after reserving the memory through the caller's work meter. 24.3 stores grid coordinates as `i64` columns and other reals as `f64` columns.
guarantees: **Exact.** Each value is the little-endian reading of its eight bytes, bit for bit.
**Finite reals only.** A NaN or an infinity in a float column is refused with the offset of its first byte, and nothing of that column is appended.
**A whole number of values.** A byte string whose length is not a multiple of eight is refused.

**Metered and fallible.** The memory is reserved from the meter and from the allocator before anything is appended; a refused reservation stops the meter rather than aborting. Each [`SCAN_BYTES_PER_CHARGE`] bytes charge the meter one unit.
modules.job: Columns: the little-endian `i64` and `f64` arrays SKG stores coordinates and other reals in, read into vectors.

method.text: RFC 8746 section 2's typed arrays, tags 79 (signed 64-bit, little endian) and 86 (binary64, little endian), <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8746#section-2>, read with Rust's `from_le_bytes`, which every target computes the same way; SKG's columns, `projects/engines/geometry/architecture/24-file-format-exchange.md` (24.3).

modules.cost: O(n) time in the input's length, one pass; no allocation but the explicit stack, which holds one small frame per open container or tag, at most the caller's depth limit. Recursion: none.
modules.does: a [`Decoder`] walks one data item and hands out its heads as [`Item`]s, in the order the bytes hold them, borrowing strings from the input. Before handing out a head it checks every rule of 24.3's canonical form that the head, and the bytes so far, can break. [`check`] walks one whole item and refuses trailing bytes; [`item_len`] walks the first item of a CBOR Sequence and says where it ends.
guarantees: **Canonical or refused.** The decoder accepts bytes only if they are the one encoding SKG's canonical form gives their value; any other input is refused with the offset of the item at fault and the rule it breaks. So two accepted inputs that decode to the same items are the same bytes.

**Never panics, never reads past the input.** Every length and count is checked against the bytes left before it is used: a string must fit in them, an array of n items needs n bytes and a map of n pairs 2n.
**Bounded nesting without recursion.** Containers and tags are walked with an explicit stack no deeper than the caller's limit; deeper input is refused, never recursed into (24.7).

**Metered.** Every head charges the caller's work meter one unit, and every [`SCAN_BYTES_PER_CHARGE`] bytes of text or column it scans charge one more, so a budget or a cancellation stops a read within a bounded amount of work, and the same input stops at the same charge on every machine.
**Independent of how the input arrives.** The decoder reads a byte slice and nothing else; the items, the errors and the offsets depend only on the bytes.
modules.job: The strict decoder: reads one item of SKG's deterministic CBOR, head by head, and refuses any byte that is not in the one canonical encoding of its value.

method.text: RFC 8949 (Concise Binary Object Representation), sections 3 (encoding), 3.4.3 (bignums), 4.1 (preferred serialization) and 4.2.1 (core deterministic encoding requirements), <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8949>; RFC 8746 (typed arrays as byte strings), section 2, <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8746#section-2>; and SKG's canonical bytes, `projects/engines/geometry/architecture/24-file-format-exchange.md` (24.3, 24.7). A head's argument is in its shortest form when additional information 24, 25, 26 or 27 carries a value that would not fit in the next shorter one (RFC 8949, section 4.2.1, first rule). Map keys are compared as the byte slices of their encodings, which is the bytewise lexicographic order of section 4.2.1; RFC 7049's length-first order is not used.

modules.cost: a few machine words; nothing allocates.
modules.does: [`CborError`] carries the byte offset of the head at fault and a [`CborErrorKind`]; [`TextError`] carries the line and column of the text at fault and a [`TextErrorKind`]. Every refusal of the decoder and of the text form is one of these, never a panic (24.7).
guarantees: **One kind per rule.** Each rule of 24.3's canonical form that bytes can break has its own kind, so a test can tell which rule refused an input.
modules.job: Why bytes or text were refused as SKG's deterministic CBOR, and where.

method.none: it defines error types and their `Display` and `Error` implementations.

modules.cost: a few integer and float operations; nothing allocates; no loops.
modules.does: [`half_to_f64`] and [`single_to_f64`] read a half or single precision float into the double that holds it exactly. [`shortest`] says which of the three widths is the shortest that holds a double exactly, with its bits: the one width RFC 8949's preferred serialization allows for a float (section 4.1), which section 4.2.1's deterministic form requires and SKG keeps (24.3).
guarantees: **Exact both ways.** A half or single precision value reads as the double of exactly the same value, `−0.0` included; [`shortest`] gives bits that read back to the same double, bit for bit.
**The shortest width.** [`shortest`] gives half precision whenever a half holds the value, otherwise single precision whenever a single holds it, otherwise double precision.
**Finite only.** A NaN or an infinity has no width here: the reads return `None` for them, and [`shortest`] refuses them.
modules.job: Half, single and double precision floats: reading each width exactly, and finding the shortest width that holds a value.

method.text: IEEE 754-2019's binary16, binary32 and binary64 interchange formats, and RFC 8949 section 4.1's preferred serialization of floats (<https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8949#section-4.1>). A half's 15 magnitude bits, shifted up 13 places, are the bits of the single precision float `2^−112` times its value, for normal and subnormal halves alike (the exponent biases differ by 127 − 15 = 112, and both formats' subnormals sit one step below their least normal exponent), so a half is read through the exact conversion of that single and one exact scaling by `2^112`. Whether a single holds a double is Rust's round-to-nearest conversion compared with the double, bit for bit; whether a half holds it is the same map read backwards.

modules.cost: an `Item` is a few words; strings borrow the input and copy nothing.
modules.does: [`Item`] names what each head of SKG's CBOR subset says (24.3). A container's head carries its count, and its contents follow as later items, so a decoder hands out one `Item` per head in the order the bytes hold them, and never builds a tree.
guarantees: **One variant per kind of head the subset allows.** Indefinite lengths, `undefined` and every other simple value have no variant, because the subset refuses them (24.3).
modules.job: One CBOR data item as the decoder yields it: a head and, for strings, the bytes it holds.

method.none: it defines a type and nothing that computes.

modules.cost: O(n) time and memory in the text: one list of heads, then the bytes, then one decoder pass. Recursion: none.
modules.does: [`from_text`] reads the one item of the text into a flat list of heads, in three passes: it parses the text with an explicit stack, counting each array's items and each map's pairs as their brackets close; it writes every head in its shortest form and every float in the shortest width that holds it; and it checks the bytes with the strict decoder, so whatever the decoder refuses (keys out of order, a repeated key, a tag outside the subset, a bignum that fits in 64 bits, a column of the wrong length) is refused here too, at the line and column of the item at fault.
guarantees: **Canonical bytes or an error.** What it returns is accepted by the strict decoder at the same depth: the one encoding SKG's canonical form gives the items the text describes.
**Lossless.** `from_text(to_text(bytes))` gives back `bytes` for every input the decoder accepts, floats bit for bit, −0.0 included.
**Exact or refused.** A number is never rounded: an integer out of range or a float no double holds is an error.
**Never panics, no recursion.** Nesting is walked with an explicit stack no deeper than the caller's limit; every error carries the line and column where it was found.
modules.job: Reading the text form back: diagnostic notation with hexadecimal floats, turned into SKG's deterministic CBOR bytes.

method.text: RFC 8610 Appendix G (extended diagnostic notation), with G.5's hexadecimal floats and G.6's comments, <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8610#appendix-G>; RFC 8949 section 8 (diagnostic notation), <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8949#section-8>; JSON's string escapes, RFC 8259 section 7, <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8259#section-7>; and RFC 8949 sections 3, 4.1 and 4.2.1 for the bytes written. A hexadecimal float m·2^e, m an integer, is a double exactly when, with its trailing zero bits moved into e, m has at most 53 bits, e is at least −1074 and its leading bit's exponent is at most 1023 (IEEE 754-2019, binary64).

modules.cost: O(n) time in the input and the text, which is at most about three bytes per input byte (hexadecimal) plus the indentation; the text is built in one `String`. The formatting stack holds one entry per open container or tag, at most the depth limit. Recursion: none.
modules.does: [`to_text`] decodes one item with the strict decoder and writes it as text. The layout is fixed, so equal bytes give equal text:
guarantees: **Lossless.** For any bytes the strict decoder accepts, `from_text(to_text(bytes))` is the same bytes, floats bit for bit.
**One text per item.** The layout depends only on the bytes.
**Refuses what the decoder refuses.** Bytes that are not SKG's deterministic CBOR give the decoder's error and no text.
modules.job: The text form: SKG's deterministic CBOR written as extended diagnostic notation, with every float a hexadecimal float, for diffs, fixtures and AI agents; never for storage (24.6).

method.text: RFC 8949 section 8 (diagnostic notation), <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8949#section-8>, and RFC 8610 Appendix G (extended diagnostic notation; G.5, hexadecimal floats), <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8610#appendix-G>; text escapes as JSON's, RFC 8259 section 7, <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8259#section-7>. A hexadecimal float writes a double's 52 fraction bits as 13 hexadecimal digits after `0x1.` and its unbiased exponent after `p`; a subnormal is first scaled by 2^64, exactly, to read its leading bit as a normal double's.

modules.cost: linear in the input, one table read per byte; the table is a constant built at compile time, and nothing is allocated.
modules.does: [`crc32c`] is the CRC-32C (Castagnoli) of a byte string, computed by the `crc` crate with its catalogue entry `CRC_32_ISCSI`: polynomial 0x1EDC6F41, reflected input and output, initial value and final XOR 0xFFFFFFFF.
guarantees: **The checksum RFC 7143 and RFC 3720 define.** The tests check the catalogue's check value (the CRC of `123456789` is 0xE3069283) and RFC 3720's appendix B.4 examples.
**The same value on every target.** The crate is table-driven integer code with no processor paths, so the bits depend only on the input.
**No panic, no `unsafe`.** The crate forbids `unsafe` code, and its table reads are bounded by its loop guards and an 8-bit mask (its audit, cited in `deny-no-std.toml`).
modules.job: CRC-32C, the cheap check every record carries so damage is found before its bytes are trusted (24.2).

method.text: CRC-32C as RFC 3720 appendix B.4 and RFC 7143 section 13.1 specify it, <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc7143>, computed by the `crc` crate (MIT OR Apache-2.0, a dependency, not a port); chapter 24.2 of the kernel architecture, `projects/engines/geometry/architecture/24-file-format-exchange.md`.

modules.cost: constant time, no allocation.
modules.does: [`CHUNK_ROWS`] is the run length; [`chunk_count`] says how many chunks a table of `rows` rows takes, and [`chunk`] gives the rows of one. Body records (G94) write one chunk record per run and an index listing their content IDs.
guarantees: **Fixed runs.** Every chunk but the last holds exactly [`CHUNK_ROWS`] rows; the last holds the rest, at least one; an empty table has no chunk. The chunks cover the table once, in order.
**No panic, no overflow**, for every `usize` length.
modules.job: Chunks: every table of a body is cut into fixed runs of 4,096 rows, so chunk boundaries are a pure function of the table's length, never of how memory was shared (24.2).

method.text: chapter 24.2's chunk rule (4,096 rows, proposed and fixed by the specification) in `projects/engines/geometry/architecture/24-file-format-exchange.md`.

modules.cost: one SHA-256 pass over the payload for [`ContentId::of_payload`]; the digest is copied.
modules.does: a [`ContentId`] is `[alg, digest]`. Algorithm 1 is the SHA-256 of the payload's bytes (owner action G79, 32.20), computed by `geom-op`'s hash, so names and content share one implementation. An ID of another algorithm is kept as read, so a file written once a stronger hash joins as algorithm 2 still carries its IDs through this reader byte for byte.
guarantees: **Algorithm 1 is SHA-256 of exactly the payload's bytes**, its digest 32 bytes; an ID that says algorithm 1 with any other length is refused when read.
**One encoding.** [`ContentId::item`] writes `[alg, h'digest']` in `geom-op`'s canonical encoding.
modules.job: Content IDs: a record's payload named by its hash, behind an algorithm code (24.2).

method.text: chapter 24.2's content-id rule, `content-id = [alg: uint, digest: bstr]`, in `projects/engines/geometry/architecture/24-file-format-exchange.md`; SHA-256 by NIST FIPS 180-4, <https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/180-4/upd1/final>, through `geom_op::hash`.

modules.cost: linear in the file for [`write`] and [`read`], one SHA-256 pass over it; [`salvage`] tries a record at each byte of a damaged span, so a span of `d` bytes costs up to `d` attempts, each charged to the meter.
modules.does: [`write`] lays out RFC 9277's 12-byte label (`d9 d9 f8`, the protocol tag `da 53 4b 47 46`, "SKGF", owner action G77, 32.18, and the byte string `43 42 4f 52`), the header record, the records, and an END record whose payload is `[count, h'sha256']`: how many records came before it, the header's included, and the SHA-256 of every byte before it, the label included. [`read`] reads such a file from a [`ByteSource`] (or a [`RangeSource`] through [`RangeCursor`]), record by record, and [`salvage`] keeps every intact record of damaged bytes and names the damaged spans.
guarantees: **The read does not depend on how the bytes arrive.** [`read`] takes every byte through `read_exact`, so a source that returns one byte a call gives the same result, error offsets included, as one that returns everything at once (the tests split reads at random).

**Unknown records are handled as 24.2 says.** A record the caller's registry does not know stops the read with [`FileError::UnsupportedRecord`] (tag, schema, byte offset) if it is required, and is skipped and listed in [`ReadFile::skipped`] if it is optional.
**Every length is checked before anything is allocated:** a string head longer than [`PAYLOAD_CAP`], or a record longer than [`RECORD_CAP`], is refused before its bytes are read.
**The END record is checked**: its count and digest must match what was read, nothing may follow it, and a file without one is refused.
**Salvage keeps what is intact**: every record that decodes with a matching check is kept with its offset, and each run of bytes between them is named as damaged.
**No panic, no recursion**: nested items are counted with an explicit counter.
modules.job: A standalone `.skgf` file: the label, the header record, the records and the END record (24.2), written, read from any source however it splits its reads, and salvaged when damaged.

method.text: chapter 24.2 and 24.5 of the kernel architecture, `projects/engines/geometry/architecture/24-file-format-exchange.md`; RFC 9277's labelled CBOR Sequence, <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9277>, and RFC 8742's CBOR Sequences, <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8742>; the item lengths of RFC 8949 section 3.

modules.cost: linear in the payload; a few small allocations for the ladder and the program's name.
modules.does: a [`Header`] holds the format version, the kernel edition, the `NameScheme`, the tolerance ladder in grid steps, the Unicode version of hashed text and the writing program, and ends with an extension map (24.3). [`Header::v1`] fills it for this kernel from `geom_num::ladder`'s rungs; [`Header::record`] writes it as a required record of type 1; [`Header::read`] reads a payload back. Its CDDL is `format/cddl/header.cddl` in the kernel's tree:
guarantees: **One encoding** for every header: written by `geom-op`'s canonical encoder, keys ascending.

**A reader refuses what it cannot honour**: a major format version other than 1 ([`HeaderError::Format`]), and an extension key with its must-understand bit (bit 0) set that this version does not know ([`HeaderError::MustUnderstand`]). An unknown key without that bit is skipped and listed in [`Header::ignored`]. A newer minor version is read.
**The ladder is the kernel's**: [`Header::v1`] takes every rung from `geom_num::ladder`, so a file records exactly the bounds its geometry was made under.
modules.job: The header record, the first record of every file: what a reader must know before it reads anything else (24.4).

method.text: chapter 24.3 and 24.4 of the kernel architecture, `projects/engines/geometry/architecture/24-file-format-exchange.md`; the ladder of chapter 6.5, `projects/engines/geometry/architecture/06-numbers.md`; CDDL by RFC 8610, <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8610>.

modules.cost: linear in the record; the history is decoded and encoded once.
modules.does: [`history_record`] writes an operation's history as one required record (tag [`HISTORY_TAG`]) whose payload is `geom-op`'s canonical encoding of it ([`History::encode`]): the operation's path, its records in output-name order, its deleted inputs and its topology changes. [`read_history`] reads one back.
guarantees: **What is read is what was written**: a payload is read into an `OpPath` and a `History`, which is encoded again; the bytes must be the stored ones, so a record out of order, a set out of order, an unknown origin or change, or any second spelling is refused.
**The history's own forms hold**: two records of one output, a modification from nothing or a merge of one are refused, as `History::new` refuses them.
modules.job: The history record: one operation's origins, deletions and topology changes (chapter 20.3), stored so that a reloaded model resolves its references through exactly the history it had.

method.text: chapter 20.3's records and 24.4's names and history record (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/20-naming-history.md`, `projects/engines/geometry/architecture/24-file-format-exchange.md`), read by decoding and encoding again, as the names record is.

modules.cost: linear in a kind's values, plus, for an offset stored with its cache, the cost of fitting it again.
modules.does: [`write_curve`] and [`write_surface`] append one kind to an encoder; [`read_curve`] and [`read_surface`] read one back from a decoder, rebuilding it through the kind's own constructor, so a stored kind is checked as a built one is. The codes are in [`curve`] and [`surface`]; the fields of each are the values its constructor takes, in the order `format/cddl/kinds.cddl` gives them. Doubles are written in their shortest exact width, lists of doubles as RFC 8746 `f64` columns (tag 86), an absent value as `[]`, a present one as `[value]`, and a flag as 0 or 1.
guarantees: **Value for value.** A kind read back equals the one written (`PartialEq`), every double with its bits, a negative zero included: a kind keeps what defines it, never a refit.

**Caches are rebuilt, not stored.** An offset's fitted NURBS cache is a function of the offset; the item says whether it was there and reading computes it again (`Offset::cached`), which gives the same bits on every target (23.1). A curve on a surface keeps its 3D curve, which defines it.
**Infinite ends.** A parameter interval's end may be infinite only on its own side (a ray or line); it is written `[]`.

**Bounded.** Every kind nests at most [`DEPTH`] containers deep: a surface offset at most `geom_surface::offset::MAX_NESTING` (4) times, over a swept surface whose profile is a conic on axes on a frame.
modules.job: Geometry kinds as canonical items: every curve and surface kind a body's pools hold, written as `[code, fields…]` and read back to the same value (24.2, 24.3).

method.text: chapter 24.2 and 24.3 of the kernel architecture, `projects/engines/geometry/architecture/24-file-format-exchange.md`; the kinds are those of chapter 7, `07-curves-surfaces.md`.

modules.cost: linear in the record; each node is decoded, encoded and hashed once.
modules.does: [`names_record`] writes a name graph's nodes as one required record (tag [`NAMES_TAG`]): an array of `[id, name]` pairs in `NameId` order, each name in its canonical encoding (32.19). [`read_names`] reads one back into a fresh name graph. [`read_topo_name`] reads one canonical `TopoName` item.
guarantees: **Every `NameId` is verified under the recorded scheme** (24.4; piece G95): a file whose header names a scheme other than `NameScheme v1` is refused, and every node's id must be the hash of its own stored bytes, or the record is refused with the node's offset. A name is never trusted because a file says so.

**One encoding per name**: a node is read into a `TopoName` and encoded again, and the bytes must be the stored ones, so a set out of order, a repeated name, a non-NFC role or any other second spelling of a name is refused; the graph refuses a second node under one id.
**Order is name order**: nodes are in strictly increasing `NameId` order, or the record is refused.
modules.job: The names record: every name node a file keeps, each `NameId` checked against its bytes under the file's `NameScheme` as it is read.

method.text: chapter 24.4's names record and decision 32.19's canonical encoding and hash (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/24-file-format-exchange.md`, `projects/engines/geometry/architecture/32-decisions.md`), read by re-encoding, the way RFC 8949 section 4.2's deterministic encoding is checked: decode, encode, compare (<https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8949#section-4.2>).

modules.cost: linear in the record; the parameters are checked once and copied once.
modules.does: an [`Operation`] is one authored operation (piece G96): its path (the permanent `OpId` from the log, and labels), its name and version in the operation schemas, its inputs by content ID and `NameId`, its parameters in SKG's canonical CBOR as its schema writes them, and the work and logical-memory budget it runs under (23.10: a budget that can fail an operation in a shared model is fixed by its version or recorded in the log). [`operation_record`] writes one as a required record (tag [`OPERATION_TAG`]); [`read_operation`] reads it back.
guarantees: **Versioned twice**: the record type has its schema, and every record names the operation's own version, which fixes its results, its charge schedule and its error details (26.2).
**Parameters are canonical**: they are one item of SKG's canonical CBOR, checked on writing and on reading, so equal parameters are equal bytes and a log replays to the same bits.
**One encoding**: a record is read and encoded again, and the bytes must be the stored ones.
**No clock, no preview**: nothing timed and no precision is recorded; only final operations are logged, and a cancelled run writes nothing (10.1, 23.10).
modules.job: The operation record: one entry of an operation log, everything a replay needs to run the operation again and get the same bits.

method.text: chapter 21's replay and chapter 28.13's operation logs, with the recipe envelope's inputs (24.4) (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/21-determinism.md`, `projects/engines/geometry/architecture/28-testing.md`).

modules.cost: linear in the payload; nothing is copied but the names it returns.
modules.does: a [`Reader`] steps through a payload that is already known to be canonical CBOR (the record layer checks it), one head or one whole item at a time, and turns a wrong shape into [`PayloadError::Shape`] with the byte offset and what was expected. The name, history, recipe and attribute records (piece G95) read their payloads with it.
guarantees: **Every failure names its byte**: the offset in the payload of the item that did not fit, and what the record needs there.
**Containers are read head by head**, so a reader never holds more than one item at a time, and every whole item it returns is exactly the bytes the decoder measured.
modules.job: Reading a record's payload field by field: the next head, a whole item's bytes, names, and the end of the payload, each failure naming its byte.

method.text: SKG's canonical CBOR (`projects/engines/geometry/format/SPEC.md`, section 3) read with this crate's decoder, as the header record's reader reads its payload (chapter 24.3, `projects/engines/geometry/architecture/24-file-format-exchange.md`).

modules.cost: constant per value; a column is one pass; [`plane`]'s divisor takes at most a few hundred remainder steps on 128-bit values. No allocation, no recursion.
modules.does: a file can pass every checksum and still hold a coordinate near 2^50, and release builds wrap integers silently. So every reader checks: grid coordinates within ±(2^40 − 1) steps ([`grid`], [`grid_column`]); doubles, control points included, finite and within the same range ([`real`], [`real_column`]); and planes reduced, with normals within 83 bits and offsets within 125 ([`plane`]). A failure is [`RangeError::OutOfRange`] with the record, the byte offset, the field and how many bits the value needs, or [`RangeError::Malformed`] for a plane that is not reduced.
guarantees: **Exactly the frame.** [`grid`] accepts a value exactly when `geom_num::grid::Coord::new` does, `|v| ≤ 2^40 − 1`, proven by Kani for every `i64` (`proofs`), and tested at ±(2^40 − 1) and one beyond.
**Exactly the finite doubles of the frame.** [`real`] accepts `x` exactly when it is finite and `|x| ≤ 2^40 − 1`, proven by Kani for every `f64`.

**The bits the predicates assume.** [`plane`] accepts a plane exactly when its normal is not zero, each normal component needs at most 83 bits and the offset at most 125 (the bounds of `geom_num::plane`, from 40-bit coordinates), and the greatest common divisor of the four is 1.
**No panic, no overflow**: magnitudes are taken with `unsigned_abs`, offsets with checked arithmetic.

modules.does: [`check`] takes three grid points a, b, c and computes [`reference`], the determinant of the 3 × 3 matrix whose rows are (a.x, a.y, 1), (b.x, b.y, 1) and (c.x, c.y, 1), expanded along its third column in `i128`: (b.x·c.y − b.y·c.x) − (a.x·c.y − a.y·c.x) + (a.x·b.y − a.y·b.x). That determinant is orient2d's definition (Shewchuk 1997, section 4.1); this module computes it with no code shared with `geom-num`, and by another formula than `geom-num`'s (b − a) × (c − a), so the two agree only if both are right. Against it, `check` holds `geom-num` to three claims:
guarantees: **Any bytes are a case.** Every byte string, the empty one included, decodes to three valid grid points, reading at most [`MAX_INPUT_BYTES`] = 73 bytes; the bound is derived on the constant and a unit test builds the input that reaches it.

**The oracle cannot overflow on the grid.** Each coordinate has magnitude at most M = 2^40 − 1, so each of the six products is at most M² < 2^80, each 2 × 2 minor at most 2M² < 2^81, and the determinant at most 6M² < 2^83, far inside `i128`. Every step is a checked method all the same, and a step that failed would be reported as a [`Finding`] naming this harness as the defect, never a panic and never a wrapped value.

**A wrong answer is a [`Finding`]**, naming the claim, the points, the reference value and what `geom-num` gave. An error from the predicate, or a `None` from the exact path, is a finding too, never read as a sign: `geom-num` proves every grid input answers.
**A panic is a failure.** Nothing is caught: a panic in `geom-num` fails the run, and the engine reports the input.

**What is proven and what is tested.** For every case [`proof_case`] can give with bound [`PROOF_BOUND`] (every coordinate within `PROOF_BOUND` steps of 0 or of an edge ±(2^40 − 1) of the frame, in any combination), Kani proves that all three claims hold and that nothing on the way panics or overflows (`tests/orient2d.rs`, `orient2d_proof`; Kani checks every arithmetic step, index and unwrap by default). Near the edges the filter's products round, so the proof covers the filter's error bound, not only exact arithmetic. Everywhere else in the frame the claims are tested, by fuzzing and the property tests, not proven.
modules.job: Fuzz target and bounded proof: `geom-num`'s orient2d agrees with the exact determinant of its definition, computed here from scratch.

method.text: an exact oracle for a predicate, the first of chapter 28.6's checks (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/28-testing.md`), with bounded Kani proofs of sign agreement with an exact integer reference, as evidence report 08 recommends for predicates (`projects/kit/notes/G01-evidence/08-standards-coverage-testing.md`, "Recommended test architecture", item 1). The reference is the 3 × 3 determinant of the definition, expanded by cofactors along the column of ones, in Shewchuk's paper: J. R. Shewchuk, "Adaptive Precision Floating-Point Arithmetic and Fast Robust Geometric Predicates", *Discrete & Computational Geometry* 18 (1997), 305–363, <https://doi.org/10.1007/PL00009321>.

modules.cost: 4 + 3 + 6 + 6 + 10 = 29 predicate calls per input, each constant time, and at most [`MAX_INPUT_BYTES`] bytes read.
modules.does: [`decode`] turns a fuzzer's bytes into grid points with `geom-test`'s [`GridSampler`] (four 2D points, then five 3D points). [`check`] calls every exact predicate on them: `orient2d`, `incircle`, `orient3d` and `insphere`. For each, it checks that the predicate answers, then swaps every pair of points and checks that the sign flips, `Zero` staying `Zero`. [`harness`] is `decode` then `check`, the function every fuzzing engine drives (the crate README sets out the layout).
guarantees: **Any bytes are a case.** Every byte string, the empty one included, decodes to valid grid points (magnitude at most 2^40 − 1), aimed at the hard cases: extremes of the frame, repeated and one-step-apart points, collinear points and coarse sub-grids (see `geom_test::grid`).
**A bounded input.** [`decode`] reads at most [`MAX_INPUT_BYTES`] bytes; longer inputs only add bytes nobody reads. The bound is derived below and a unit test builds the input that reaches it.
**A panic is a failure.** The harness does not catch panics: a predicate that panics fails the run, and bolero reports the input and its seed.

**An error is a failure.** Each predicate returns `Result<Sign, NumError>`, and `geom-num` proves that for grid points it is always `Ok`: its bit budgets are derived for every grid input and checked when it compiles, so `NumError::BudgetExceeded` can only be a defect in `geom-num` (`geom_num::predicate`'s module documentation). Every point the harness decodes is a grid point, so an error, on the first call or after any swap, is a [`Finding`] naming the predicate, the error and the points. It is never read as a sign, so a defect can never pass for an exact degeneracy or for a sign that flipped.
**A broken law is a [`Finding`]** naming the predicate, the swap and the points.
modules.job: Fuzz target: `geom-num`'s exact predicates never panic, and swapping two points flips their sign.

method.text: the algebraic laws of section 28.6 of the kernel architecture (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/28-testing.md`, "Swapping two points flips the sign"). Each predicate is the sign of a determinant with one row per point (the points lifted onto the paraboloid z = |p|² for in-circle and in-sphere), as in Shewchuk, "Adaptive Precision Floating-Point Arithmetic and Fast Robust Geometric Predicates", Discrete & Computational Geometry 18, 1997 (<https://doi.org/10.1007/PL00009321>), which `geom_num::predicate` follows. Exchanging two points exchanges two rows, and by the Leibniz formula an exchange of two rows negates a determinant, so every transposition must flip the sign. The board names orient2d's swap; the same law is checked on the other three predicates, whose points the harness decodes anyway.

modules.cost: linear in [`DESIGNS`]: one or two operations a design.
modules.does: a typed error is legal, but an error where a person would expect success is a gap, and a crash hunt does not count gaps. [`tally`] runs [`DESIGNS`] designs per family, each the same on every run and target, through the kernel's operations, and counts the successes. `src/robustness.txt` records them; `tests/robustness.rs` fails if a count falls.
guarantees: **The same designs every time.** Each design comes from a fixed seed through `geom_test::SplitMix64`, so a count moves only when an operation's answer moves.

**Plain designs, not the fuzzer's.** A design is what a person would draw: sizes in whole millimetres, near the origin, on the sub-grids. The fuzzer's hard cases are mostly refused for good reason; counting those would measure the generator. A design accepts no loss of exactness, so a scale of a curved body, which would widen its bound, counts as refused, as it is until the caller accepts it.
modules.job: Robustness, counted: of a fixed, seeded set of generated designs per operation family, how many succeed (chapter 28.5).

method.text: chapter 28.5's "Robustness is counted, not only crashes" (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/28-testing.md`).

modules.cost: one isolation, one Brent search and one quadrature of a polynomial of degree at most [`MAX_ROOTS`], each bounded; at most [`MAX_INPUT_BYTES`] bytes read.
modules.does: [`decode`] turns a fuzzer's bytes into a [`Case`]: a polynomial in one unknown, the product of x − rᵢ for up to [`MAX_ROOTS`] roots on a grid of quarters (repeated roots included), a domain, the Newton operator to use, and a bracket's half-width. [`check`] holds three laws, decided exactly from the roots (the sign of the polynomial at a double is the product of the signs of x − rᵢ, each an exact comparison):
guarantees: **Any bytes are a case.** Roots are quarters in [−8, 8], so repeated roots, roots on the domain's ends and roots on the engine's split lines come up often.
**A panic is a failure; a broken law is a [`Finding`]**; every typed error is legal.
**No hang.** Each call runs under a work meter of [`WORK`] units, or an evaluation cap.
**A bounded input.** [`decode`] reads at most [`MAX_INPUT_BYTES`] bytes.
modules.job: Fuzz target: the root engine misses no root and proves none twice, and Brent's method brackets its zero, on any bytes.

method.text: the engine's and Brent's stated guarantees (`geom_num::isolate`, `geom_num::brent`), checked against the exact roots, as `geom-num`'s `tests/attack_g53.rs` does on seeded systems, driven by coverage-guided fuzzing (chapter 28.5, `projects/engines/geometry/architecture/28-testing.md`).

modules.cost: `cases` runs of the harness, plus one `SplitMix64` word per eight bytes drawn and one or two words per length.
modules.does: [`run`] resolves a seed with `geom_test::seed::resolve` (the test's default, or `SPAREKIT_SEED`; printed as `seed: <hex>`), then for each case draws a length in `0..=max_len` and that many bytes from `geom-test`'s `SplitMix64`, and runs the harness on them.
guarantees: **The same cases every run.** One seed gives the same byte strings on every target, so a pull request runs a fixed set of cases (28.17) and any failure replays exactly with the printed seed.

**A failure says how to keep it.** [`Failure::Finding`] carries the case number, the seed, the bytes in hexadecimal and the broken law. Saved as a file in the target's `tests/__fuzz__/<target>/crashes` folder, the bytes become a case bolero's test mode replays on every run (28.16).
**Panics are not caught.** A harness that panics fails the test, and the seed line printed before the first case shows which seed to replay.
**Every seed is printed**, by [`run`] as `geom_test::seed::resolve` prints it and by [`run_with_seed`] as `geom_test::seed::fixed` does, before the first case.
modules.job: The seeded leg: a harness run on byte strings drawn from a printed seed.

method.text: the fixed-seed property runs of section 28.17 of the kernel architecture (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/28-testing.md`: "Unit and property tests with fixed seeds" on every pull request, "fresh, logged seeds" nightly), over the byte strings a fuzzer would give, so the one harness function serves fuzzing and fixed-seed testing alike, the arrangement bolero's own test mode uses (<https://github.com/camshaft/bolero>).

modules.cost: at most [`MAX_OPERATIONS`] operations, each checked in full, then two replays and one replay under a cut budget; at most [`MAX_INPUT_BYTES`] bytes read.
modules.does: [`decode`] turns a fuzzer's bytes into a [`Case`]: up to [`MAX_OPERATIONS`] operations on the hard cases of chapter 28.5, each transform on any earlier result, each new primitive free to start exactly on a point of an earlier one or one step from it, some patterns of [`MANY_COPIES`] copies. The first operation is always a primitive, and half of them are tamed to sizes the grid can hold, so a log gets past its first step and its later laws run. [`check`] runs it through the kernel's replay, one operation at a time, and holds each to chapter 28.5's oracle stack; then it writes the operations that succeeded as a log and replays that. [`harness`] is `decode` then `check`.
guarantees: **Any bytes are a case**, and [`decode`] reads at most [`MAX_INPUT_BYTES`] bytes, derived below; a unit test builds the input that reaches it.

**A panic is a failure; a broken law is a [`Finding`]** naming the law and the case: a log the kernel refuses; a defect, or an error no schema lists; a result without names, or one the full checker rejects; a history that breaks its laws, alone or composed along a chain; a class that rises; an input that changes; a log that does not read back as written; a replay of the log that gives another hash; a budget that changes a result instead of stopping it.

**Not yet in the stack:** a thread-count rerun waits for the first parallel operation, since none of the operations a log can hold uses the helper, and an imported Tolerant body waits for the first importer.
modules.job: Fuzz target: whole operation logs. On any bytes, a log of primitives, transforms and patterns, each on any earlier result, replays to the same hash, and every step keeps every law.

method.text: chapter 28.5's sequence target and oracle stack (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/28-testing.md`), run through chapter 28.16's replay.

modules.cost: linear in the input, three parses and two writes at most.
modules.does: [`harness`] reads the fuzzer's bytes as text and hands them to `geom_sketch::text::parse`. A text it accepts must write, read back equal, and write the same text again.
guarantees: **Never a panic.** `parse` returns a sketch or a typed refusal on every input.
**Round trip.** What parses, writes; what it writes parses to the same sketch; and that writes the same text.
modules.job: The fuzz target of the sketch text form (piece G217): any bytes at all are refused cleanly or read as a sketch that writes back to one fixed text.

method.text: the property-based fuzzing of 28.5 (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/28-testing.md`), on the grammar of section 15.13 (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/15-sketches.md`).

modules.cost: one kind built and one contract check per input, each bounded by [`WORK`] work units; at most [`MAX_INPUT_BYTES`] bytes read.
modules.does: [`decode`] turns a fuzzer's bytes into a [`Case`]: a surface kind (one of the 11 of `geom_surface::SurfaceKind`), the doubles it is built from, up to four parameter pairs in its domain and a typed transform. [`check`] builds the kind and runs `geom_surface::contract::check` on it, the kind contract kit every surface kind is held to (piece G60, with G68's derivative laws), under a bounded work meter. [`harness`] is `decode` then `check`, the function every fuzzing engine drives (the crate README sets out the layout). It reaches pieces G60 and G65 to G68 (Gate 2, 32.44).
guarantees: **Any bytes are a case.** Every byte string, the empty one included, decodes to a case, through the same rule bytes as the `curves` target: 0, ±1, whole numbers and quarters on a coarse grid, tiny and huge powers of two, or a double read from the input.

**What is a finding.** A law of the contract broken with no error behind it, or any call failing as `CurveError::Defect`, is a [`Finding`]; a kind that refuses to be built, or a call that refuses with a typed error (an overflow, a normal that cannot be separated from zero, a budget stop), is legal. A panic fails every engine.
**No hang.** Every call runs under a work meter of [`WORK`] units; running out is a typed stop, which is legal.
**A bounded input.** [`decode`] reads at most [`MAX_INPUT_BYTES`] bytes, derived below; a unit test builds the input that reaches it.
modules.job: Fuzz target: every surface kind keeps the kind contract on any bytes.

method.text: the kind contract of chapter 7 as `geom_surface::contract` states it, driven by coverage-guided fuzzing (chapter 28.5), with inputs aimed at the hard cases 28.5 lists (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/28-testing.md`).

modules.cost: a handful of transform applications and one decimal parse per input; at most [`MAX_INPUT_BYTES`] bytes read.
modules.does: [`decode`] turns a fuzzer's bytes into a [`Case`]: a grid point, two grid transforms (signed permutations with whole-step translations), a rational transform (p ↦ (M·p + t)/d with small integers), a rational rotation (an integer quaternion), and a short text. [`check`] holds four laws, each decided exactly in rationals:
guarantees: **Any bytes are a case.** Coordinates are drawn through rule bytes that make the frame's limits ±(2^40 − 1), 0 and ±1 common; a transform the constructors refuse, or an image out of the frame's range, is a typed error and legal.
**A panic is a failure; a broken law is a [`Finding`].**
**A bounded input.** [`decode`] reads at most [`MAX_INPUT_BYTES`] bytes, derived below.
modules.job: Fuzz target: the typed transforms move grid points exactly as their definitions say, and decimals round-trip, on any bytes.

method.text: each transform's definition in `geom-math` (chapter 7's typed transforms, `projects/engines/geometry/architecture/07-geometry-types.md`), evaluated exactly in dashu's rationals, and round-half-to-even read from the exact quotient; coverage-guided fuzzing (chapter 28.5).

modules.cost: per input, the registered descriptions parsed and evaluated once each in big integers, and three exact-path calls per predicate; at most [`MAX_INPUT_BYTES`] bytes read.
modules.does: [`decode`] turns a fuzzer's bytes into the inputs the predicates take: six 2D and five 3D grid points from `geom-test`'s [`GridSampler`], and twelve plane-normal coordinates of 83 bits and four plane offsets of 125 bits, each an extreme, zero, a small value or a value of a random bit length. [`check`] evaluates each registered predicate's description (geom-gen's `PREDICATES`, read by its `predicate_lang::parse`) on those inputs in big integers, and compares the shipped `value`, the plain-`i128` variant (`geom_num::generated::plain`) and the width-aware limb variant (`geom_num::generated::limbs`) with that exact value, and Avnaim et al.'s signs of orient2d and orient3d (`geom_bench::avnaim`) with its sign. [`harness`] is `decode` then `check`, the function every fuzzing engine drives (the crate README sets out the layout).
guarantees: **Any bytes are a case.** Every byte string, the empty one included, decodes to inputs inside every predicate's domain: grid points (magnitude at most 2^40 − 1), aimed at the frame's extremes and at degenerate configurations, and rounded inputs within their declared bits.
**A bounded input.** [`decode`] reads at most [`MAX_INPUT_BYTES`] bytes; longer inputs only add bytes nobody reads.

**An independent oracle.** The exact value is the description's own arithmetic in `num-bigint`'s arbitrary-precision integers, read from the description's text, not from the generated code or the fixed-width integers it uses.
**A wrong or missing value is a [`Finding`]** naming the predicate, the variant, the inputs, what the variant returned and the exact value. Every input is in the domain, so a `None` is a finding too.
modules.job: Fuzz target: every variant of every generated exact path returns the exact value (chapter 23.3; piece G42).

method.text: differential testing against an exact oracle, as chapter 23.3 asks of every variant ("the differential fuzzer checks every variant against a rational oracle"), `projects/engines/geometry/architecture/23-performance.md`, with `num-bigint`'s integers; the descriptions' integer values need no rational.

modules.cost: one operation on `Wide` and one on `BigInt` per input, at most O(L²) for a product of L ≤ 12 limbs, plus up to seven `resize` targets; at most [`MAX_INPUT_BYTES`] bytes read.
modules.does: [`decode`] turns a fuzzer's bytes into a [`Case`]: a width, an operation and two operands of that width (and, for `resize`, a second width). [`check`] runs the operation on `geom_num::wide::Wide` and on `num-bigint`'s `BigInt`, an arbitrary-precision oracle that shares no code with it, and compares: the exact result when it fits the width and `None` exactly when it does not, for `checked_add`, `checked_sub`, `checked_neg` and `checked_mul`; the order (`Ord`, `==`); the sign (`signum`, `is_negative`, `is_zero`); `resize` to every other width; and the `i128` conversions both ways. [`harness`] is `decode` then `check`, the function every fuzzing engine drives (the crate README sets out the layout).
guarantees: **Any bytes are a case.** Every byte string, the empty one included, decodes to a case. Each limb is read through a rule byte that makes the values at every width's limits common: 0, 1, −1, the top bit alone, all bits but the top one, a copy of the limb below, or a word read from the input. So the most negative and most positive values, their neighbours, and carries that run the whole length come up all the time, not once in 2^64.

**Every width the kernel uses, and the two reserved ones.** `I128` as `Wide<2>`, `I256`, `I320`, `I384`, `I512`, and `Wide<9>` and `Wide<12>`, the 576- and 768-bit widths chapter 6.2 reserves for later predicates (the board's G26; whether they are named is an owner's decision, G240), through the same generic code.
**A bounded input.** [`decode`] reads at most [`MAX_INPUT_BYTES`] bytes, derived below; a unit test builds the input that reaches it.
**A panic is a failure; a disagreement is a [`Finding`]** naming the operation, the width, the operands and both answers.
modules.job: Fuzz target: `geom-num`'s wide integers agree with a big-integer oracle on every operation.

method.text: differential testing against an independent arbitrary-precision implementation, the big-integer oracle chapter 29.3 names for the wide integers (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/29-sources-licences.md`), here `num-bigint` 0.4.8 (<https://docs.rs/num-bigint/0.4.8/num_bigint/struct.BigInt.html>). Two's complement in `L` limbs holds exactly −2^(64L−1) ..= 2^(64L−1) − 1 (the module header of `geom_num::wide`); the oracle reads a `Wide`'s limbs with `BigInt::from_signed_bytes_le`, the same two's-complement reading, computes exactly, and writes a result that fits back with `to_signed_bytes_le`.

crates.summary: Spare Kit geometry kernel, development only: the fuzz harnesses.

invariants: **Pure generators.** A generator reads nothing (no files, no environment, no clock) and gives the same bytes on every target, so `check` means the same everywhere; `tests/purity.rs` checks the generator modules' source, and each generator's unit test compares its output with the committed file on every target CI runs, wasm32 included. A generator's seed is fixed in the registry; `SPAREKIT_SEED` never applies to generators, whose outputs are committed and must reproduce.

**Exact.** Generators compute with integers and exact fractions ([`exact`], and [`bignum`]'s naturals and polynomials in the unit roundoff), never with rounded floating point, unless an output is defined as rounded (the filter constant, rounded up once).
**Bytes, exactly.** Outputs use `\n` line ends, and each generated folder's `.gitattributes` turns off line-ending conversion for them, so a Windows checkout compares the committed bytes.
**Development only**, so it may use `std` (chapter 27); `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`; no `unwrap`, `expect`, `panic!` or indexing outside tests.
crates.job: several chapters generate code or data that is checked in (predicate filters and their certificates, subdivision tables, EXPRESS tables, the native format's field tables, `MAP.json`, `PROVENANCE.md` and `NOTICE`)

modules.cost: linear in the number of limbs for addition and shifts, quadratic for multiplication; the generator's numbers have at most a few dozen limbs.
modules.does: [`Nat`] is a natural number of any size (little-endian 64-bit limbs) with exact addition, multiplication, shifts, comparison and a decimal form; the predicate generator's bit-range certificate holds every bound as one. [`UPoly`] is a polynomial in u with non-negative whole coefficients: every bound of the filter's error analysis is one, because the analysis only adds, multiplies, and multiplies by u or by 1 + u. [`UPoly::round_up_to_f64`] gives the smallest `f64` at least the polynomial's exact value at u = 2^-53, as its bits, and [`Nat::nearest_f64`] the `f64` nearest a natural number, as the number it is: the largest a rounded input's `f64` copy can be.
guarantees: **Exact or nothing.** Every operation is exact. One whose result would not fit (a coefficient beyond `u128`, a shift beyond `u32` bits, a value beyond the largest `f64`) returns `None`, never a rounded or wrapped value; nothing panics.
**Canonical.** A [`Nat`] has no zero top limb and a [`UPoly`] no zero top coefficient, so equal values compare equal and print the same.

**Rounded only on purpose.** [`UPoly::round_up_to_f64`] rounds towards +∞, so the `f64` it gives is never below the exact value; [`Nat::nearest_f64`] rounds to nearest with ties to even, exactly as the filters convert a rounded input. Nothing else here rounds.
modules.job: Exact numbers for the predicate generator: natural numbers of any size, and polynomials in the unit roundoff u = 2^-53 with whole coefficients.

method.text: schoolbook addition and multiplication on limbs with 128-bit intermediates (Knuth, *The Art of Computer Programming*, volume 2, section 4.3.1, <https://www-cs-faculty.stanford.edu/~knuth/taocp.html>); decimal digits by repeated short division by 10^19 (Knuth 4.4). The `f64` encoding is IEEE 754-2019's binary64 (<https://standards.ieee.org/ieee/754/6210/>): a normal value is m · 2^e with 2^52 ≤ m < 2^53, stored as the biased exponent e + 52 + 1023 above the 52 fraction bits of m.

modules.cost: O(log n) steps for each greatest common divisor; a decimal is O(number of digits).
modules.does: [`Ratio`] is a non-negative fraction of two `u128`s, always in lowest terms, with checked multiplication and division. [`Ratio::decimal`] writes its exact decimal expansion when it has a finite one, and [`Ratio::fraction`] writes it as `n/d`.
guarantees: **Exact or nothing.** Every operation is exact; one whose result does not fit in `u128` returns `None`, never a rounded or wrapped value. A decimal is written only when it terminates, and then with every digit.
**Canonical.** Lowest terms and a positive denominator, so equal values compare equal and print the same.
modules.job: Exact non-negative fractions for generators, and their exact decimal form.

method.text: Euclid's algorithm for the greatest common divisor (Knuth, *The Art of Computer Programming*, volume 2, section 4.5.2, Algorithm A; <https://www-cs-faculty.stanford.edu/~knuth/taocp.html>), with cross-cancellation before multiplying (Knuth 4.5.1), so intermediate products stay as small as the result allows. A fraction in lowest terms has a finite decimal expansion exactly when its denominator is 2^a × 5^b, and then it has max(a, b) digits after the point (Hardy and Wright, *An Introduction to the Theory of Numbers*, section 9.2); the unit tests check both facts on every denominator that divides 6,400.

modules.cost: linear in the schemas' fields.
modules.does: [`api`] writes Markdown, one section per operation of `engine_geometry::operations::OPERATIONS`: its name, version, family and tier, what it does, its inputs and outputs (each with its type, unit and whether it may be left out), the roles it names, the errors it can return (each detail with its base kind and its data), the warnings it can give, the exactness classes it can return, its charge schedule, whether it has a batch entry, and its example. [`mcp`] writes JSON: the MCP protocol version the descriptions follow ([`MCP_VERSION`]) and one `Tool` per operation, as MCP's `tools/list` describes a tool: its `name`, `title` and `description`, an `inputSchema` and an `outputSchema` in JSON Schema 2020-12 (MCP's default dialect) built from its fields, `annotations` (a kernel operation is pure, 10.1: it reads nothing outside its inputs and changes nothing, so it is read-only, idempotent and closed-world to the program that calls it), and the kernel's own data under `_meta` (`org.spareware/kernel`: version, family, tier, exactness classes, errors with base kinds, warnings, charges, batch entry, roles). The command layer that serves the tools adds the program's side (sign-in scopes, the program's units), as EXTENDING.md, section 2.2, sets out.
guarantees: **From the schemas, never by hand.** Both files hold only what the operation list says, so the documentation and the tools cannot drift from the kernel; CI fails until the committed files are regenerated after the list changes.

**Valid tool descriptions.** Every tool's `name` is the operation's name, which `engine-geometry`'s tests hold to MCP's rule for tool names; every `inputSchema` is an object schema, which MCP requires, closed to fields the schema does not name.
**Deterministic.** Operations in the list's order (name order); JSON objects with their keys sorted (`serde_json`'s ordered map); `\n` line ends; nothing read from the world.
modules.job: Generators `facade-api` and `facade-mcp`: the facade's API documentation and its MCP tool descriptions, from every operation's schema (piece G100; chapter 22, "Every operation is described as data").

method.text: MCP's tool description, version 2026-07-28 (<https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28/server/tools>; the `Tool` interface in <https://github.com/modelcontextprotocol/modelcontextprotocol/blob/271ecc9accafdd9b83a3c869fa67c22953b2af80/schema/2026-07-28/schema.ts>), with JSON Schema 2020-12 (<https://json-schema.org/draft/2020-12/json-schema-core>) for the inputs and outputs, written with `serde_json`.

modules.cost: every generator once, plus reading or writing each output and listing each generated folder (at most [`MAX_FOLDER_DEPTH`] folders deep, without recursion). Validation compares every pair of outputs and of folders: O(n²) in their number, times their length.
modules.does: [`validate`] checks a registry's rules. [`write()`] produces every output and writes each one whose bytes changed. [`check`] produces every output in memory and compares it with the file, byte for byte, reporting each as current, different (with the first line that differs) or missing. Both also report every orphan: a file in a generated folder that no generator owns. Both work on a workspace root given by the caller, so tests can use a scratch copy.
guarantees: **Byte for byte.** `check` compares bytes, not text: a changed line end, a trailing space or a missing final newline is a difference.

**Validated and generated before anything is written.** `write` validates the registry and runs every generator before it writes any file, so a broken registry or a failing generator leaves every file as it was. An I/O error part-way (a full disk, a folder where a file should be) can leave the outputs before it written; `write` returns the error, and running it again once the cause is fixed finishes the job, because it rewrites only what differs.
**Every file is reported.** `check` does not stop at the first difference: the report names every output that differs or is missing, and every orphan.

**No orphans.** Every output lies inside one of the registry's generated folders ([`Folder`]), and every file in such a folder must be the output of a registered generator or on the folder's keep list. So the old output of a renamed or removed generator is reported as [`Status::Orphan`] until someone deletes it. Neither `write` nor `check` deletes anything.

**One file per output, on every system CI runs.** An output path is relative, uses `/`, and has only plain components of the portable filename character set (`A`–`Z`, `a`–`z`, `0`–`9`, `.`, `_`, `-`), none longer than 255 bytes, none starting with `-` or ending with `.`, and none a Windows device name (`CON`, `PRN`, `AUX`, `NUL`, `COM0`–`COM9`, `LPT0`–`LPT9`, in any case, with or without an extension); the whole path is at most [`MAX_OUTPUT_LEN`] bytes. No two outputs are equal when letter case is ignored (Windows and macOS file systems ignore it), and no output lies inside another. So two generators can never write one file on any runner, and every output can be a file.
modules.job: Writing every generator's output, and checking that every committed output is current.

method.text: regenerate-and-compare, the way CI keeps generated code honest (chapter 27 of the kernel architecture, `projects/engines/geometry/architecture/27-crates-folders.md`: "CI reruns every generator and fails on any difference"). File names follow POSIX's portable filename character set (<https://pubs.opengroup.org/onlinepubs/9699919799/basedefs/V1_chap03.html#tag_03_282>) and Microsoft's file naming rules (<https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/windows/win32/fileio/naming-a-file>).

modules.cost: whatever the generator's function costs.
modules.does: [`Generator`] describes a generator; [`Generator::run`] produces its output in memory; [`Generator::seed_line`] is the line every command prints for it.
guarantees: **A seed is explicit, and printed.** A generator that uses randomness is [`Generate::Seeded`], with its seed fixed beside it in the registry, and its function receives that seed. One that uses none is [`Generate::Plain`], and its function receives no seed. Every command prints every generator's line, `seed: <16 hex digits>` or `seed: none`, before it runs any generator.

**No hidden seed: a checked rule, not a type rule.** Rust's types cannot stop a generator's function from building its own seed, because `geom_test::Seed` and `geom_test::SplitMix64` are public. So `tests/purity.rs` reads the source of every generator module and fails if one names a seed, builds a generator or another source of randomness, or reads the environment, a file or a clock; only `registry.rs` may write a seed, and only as a `Generate::Seeded` entry.
**Pure.** The function is a plain `fn` with no captured state: the same bytes every call.

method.text: the committed-output pattern of chapter 27's proposed `geom-gen` rule (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/27-crates-folders.md`, "Generated code and data have one home"), with the seed discipline of sections 28.5 and 28.17 (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/28-testing.md`).

modules.cost: constant; a few hundred exact operations.
modules.does: [`generate`] writes a Markdown file, [`OUTPUT`], with three tables:
guarantees: **Exact.** Integers and exact fractions only ([`crate::exact`]); a decimal is printed only when it terminates, with every digit, and a fraction otherwise. Every integer operation is a checked method or an exact fraction operation, so an overflow is an error, never a wrapped value.

**From the code.** Every number comes from `GridStep::quarter_nm`, `grid::COORD_MAX`, `grid::COORD_BITS`, the unit constants (`grid::QUARTER_NM_PER_MM` and the others), the `ladder` constants and `ladder::quarter_nm`, or from the exact unit definitions below. The steps are found by walking `GridStep::coarser` to the coarsest step and then `GridStep::finer` to the finest, so a new step gets its row and column without an edit here. `geom-num` has no list of its unit and ladder constants, so `UNITS` and [`LADDER`] name them, and `tests/drift.rs` reads `geom-num`'s `ladder.rs` and `grid.rs` and fails if any public constant there is missing from the output.

**Checked against the code.** The generator fails rather than print a table that contradicts `geom-num`: each step's name is `Q<rung>`; each step is 25 times finer than the one above, as `grid.rs` states; each unit constant is its unit's exact size, and `GridStep::steps_per` gives exactly the whole counts the table shows, and `None` where the table says "not whole"; each ladder length agrees with `ladder::quarter_nm`; each commit-distance ceiling bounds the exact distance committing can move a point, √n half steps in n dimensions; `ladder::ANGULAR` is exactly 2^`ladder::ANGULAR_LOG2`, bit for bit; and the angular bound is the fit bound divided by 2^`grid::COORD_BITS`.
**No randomness**, no input, `\n` line ends: the same bytes on every target. A unit test compares the output with the committed file, built into the test, on every target CI runs, wasm32 included.
modules.job: Generator `grid-steps`: the grid steps, common units on each step, and the tolerance ladder, exactly, from `geom-num`'s own constants.

method.text: the definitions. 1 mm = 10^6 nm = 4,000,000 quarter-nanometres. The inch is 25.4 mm exactly and the US survey foot 1200/3937 m exactly, as NIST Special Publication 811 (2008 edition), appendix B, states (<https://www.nist.gov/pml/special-publication-811>). An `f64` is exactly 2^e (for a normal e) when its fraction bits are zero and its biased exponent is e + 1023, by the binary64 format of IEEE 754-2019 (<https://standards.ieee.org/ieee/754/6210/>). A point whose n coordinates each move by at most h moves by at most √n · h, by Pythagoras: √(n · h²).

modules.cost: one run of every generator and one read or write of each output ([`geom_gen::files`]), or a listing of the registry.
guarantees: every command prints each generator's seed (`seed: <hex>`, or `seed: none` for a generator that uses no randomness) before it runs any generator, so the seeds are printed even when a generator fails. `--root` names the workspace root to work in; by default it is the workspace this binary was built in. Exit codes: 0 success; 1 an output differs or is missing, or a generated folder holds an orphan (`write` too reports orphans, and never deletes them); 2 a usage, registry, generator or file error.

method.none: it parses its arguments and calls [`geom_gen::files`], whose module header carries the method.

modules.cost: linear in the description's steps times the ways its scale's larger-ofs resolve (one per case); no allocation beyond the text.
modules.does: a generated filter computes the description's steps in `f64` on its inputs (coordinates, their differences, and the `f64` copies of wider integers), the scale S from the groups' maxima, and the bound `fl(C · scale)`, and answers when the computed value is beyond the bound. [`gappa_problem`] states exactly that computation in Gappa's binary64 with rounding to nearest, beside the same steps evaluated exactly, on whole-number inputs bounded by their groups' maxima, and asks Gappa to prove that the error is within K · S and the computed bound within a relative error R of C · S, with K = C · (1 − R): together, |error| ≤ K · S ≤ bound, so an answer has the exact sign. Where the result's scale has several monomials (the larger of `m_x^3 m_y` and `m_x m_y^3`, say), one problem cannot state it: [`gappa_case_problem`] states one problem per case ([`gappa_cases`]), the case where one group's maximum is the largest when the monomials share one degree, and otherwise where one monomial is the largest of the result's, each with S that monomial and the hypotheses the case implies. [`fptaylor_problem`] states the normalised problem for `FPTaylor`, each step divided by its scale S(v), the largest of its monomials at the group maxima, so every input is in [−1, 1] and the result's scale is 1, with a ratio parameter in [0, 1] where a sum's operand has a smaller scale set; one problem covers every input, with the same K, which HOL Light compares the certificate's bound with. [`proof_sentence`] is the label: proven, naming the problems, when the Gappa problems state the filter in every case, and otherwise "checked, not proven" with the open issue [`UNPROVEN`] gives it. Every problem carries Gappa's hints and HOL Light's bound in its text, so the tools' runs need nothing else.
guarantees: **The shipped steps.** Each problem holds one rounded definition per operation of the filter, in the generated code's order, with its operands and operation, and the constant and the scale's product order as the code has them; `tests/certificate_problems.rs` holds the committed problems to the committed filters statement by statement.

**Every input covered, nothing assumed that fails.** A filter's cases together cover every input, one problem for each way its scale's larger-ofs resolve, and each hypothesis holds for every input of its case; `tests/certificate_problems.rs` justifies each one independently.

**Exact numbers.** R = (k + 1)u, for the k roundings between the maxima and the bound, bounds the bound's relative error ((1 + u)^k − 1 < (k + 1)u for u = 2^−53), and K = C · (1 − R) is computed exactly from the constant's bits: both are dyadic, written exactly. A rounded input's largest copy is its bound rounded to the nearest `f64`, exactly ([`crate::bignum::Nat`]).

**Refused, never approximated.** A filter the Gappa problems cannot state (a scale term formed from more than two inputs, say) is refused with the reason, and its label says "checked, not proven" with its issue; with no issue in [`UNPROVEN`] its module cannot be generated.

**Ratios, never more.** Each ratio parameter of an `FPTaylor` problem is S(operand) / S(sum) for the pairs of scale sets named in the problem's header, each the same ratio once their common factor is cancelled, and every use of it is one of those pairs: the problem's box holds every input's normalised values, never fewer.
modules.job: The problems that machine-check a predicate filter's error bound (chapter 28.6 of the kernel architecture; pieces G35 and G40): the filter's claim stated for Gappa, whose proof Rocq checks, and for `FPTaylor`, whose certificate HOL Light checks; and the label each generated module carries, proven or "checked, not proven".

method.text: Melquiond and Pion's certified semi-static filters, Gappa proofs of a homogeneous predicate's error as a multiple of the product of its inputs' maxima (*Formally certified floating-point filters for homogeneous geometric predicates*, RAIRO Theoretical Informatics and Applications 41 (2007), <https://doi.org/10.1051/ita:2007005>), with Gappa's `LIN` predicate (`a // b`) in place of their special rounding operators, which current Gappa no longer has, and a case split for a scale that takes a larger-of; and `FPTaylor`'s symbolic Taylor forms on the normalised problem (Solovyev et al., *Rigorous Estimation of Floating-Point Round-off Errors with Symbolic Taylor Expansions*, ACM TOPLAS 41 (2018), <https://doi.org/10.1145/3230733>).

modules.cost: linear in the number of steps, times the size of the numbers (a few limbs, a few dozen coefficients) and of the scale sets (a few monomials).
modules.does: [`derive`] takes a description ([`crate::predicate_lang`]) and returns a [`Derivation`]: for every step, a [`StepCert`] (the bound on its exact value over the input domain, its bits, the integer type the exact path computes it in, and the filter's scale, unit bound and unit error for it), the scale expression the filter evaluates at run time, the number of roundings in it, and the error constant, exactly and as the `f64` the filter uses.
guarantees: **The certificate.** For every input in the domain (grid coordinates |v| ≤ 2^40 − 1 = `geom_num::grid::COORD_MAX`; rounded inputs |v| ≤ 2^bits − 1), every step's exact value v has |v| ≤ `bound` < 2^`bits`, and its exact-path type holds every value of that magnitude.

**The filter.** With M(g) the largest |x̃| over the computed scale variables x of group g, S the largest product Π M(g)^e(g) over the monomials e of the result's scale, and ṽ the result computed in `f64` in the steps' order: |ṽ − v| ≤ E · S, where E is the result's unit error. The generated filter computes S in `f64`, at least S · (1 − u)^r with r = [`ScaleExpr::roundings`] (every product's rounding and its operands', since relative errors multiply), and multiplies it by the constant, one more rounding: k = [`Derivation::roundings`] = r + 1. The constant is at least E · (1 + 2u)^k, so the computed bound is at least E · S, and a computed value beyond it in magnitude has the exact value's sign. If S is zero the exact value is zero.

**No overflow, no underflow, no NaN.** Every value the filter computes is a whole number (inputs are whole numbers or `f64` copies of them, and the correctly rounded sum or product of whole numbers is whole), so none is subnormal; and every computed magnitude, and the bound, is checked here to stay below 2^1000, far from `f64::MAX`.
modules.job: The derivation behind each generated predicate: the bit-range certificate of every intermediate, the width of the exact path, and the filter's error constant, all exact.

method.text: Meyer and Pion, *FPG: A code generator for fast and certified geometric predicates*, Real Numbers and Computers 2008 (<https://inria.hal.science/inria-00344297>), as Geogram's PCK uses it (Lévy, *Robustness and efficiency of geometric programs: the Predicate Construction Kit (PCK)*, Computer-Aided Design 72, 2016, <https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cad.2015.10.004>; generated headers such as <https://github.com/BrunoLevy/geogram/blob/16843b4804de35f14ef54667950ab4c8acdd0062/src/lib/geogram/numerics/predicates/orient3d.h>, BSD-3-Clause, read for method; no code is ported). Shewchuk's stage-A bounds (<https://www.cs.cmu.edu/afs/cs/project/quake/public/code/predicates.c>, `exactinit`) are the comparison in the generated headers.
