modules.cost: linear in the number of steps.
modules.does: [`predicate_module`] writes a predicate's module from its [`Derivation`]: a header with the description, the bit-range certificate and the error analysis, the error constant, `filter` (the `f64` evaluation and its decision), and `value` and `exact` (the checked integer evaluation). [`parent_module`] writes the module that declares them and holds the helpers they share. Both are formatted as rustfmt formats them, so `cargo fmt --check` passes on the committed files. [`verus_twin`] writes a Verus-annotated twin of a predicate's exact path (chapter 28.7; piece G36): a model of the grid's types, the description's value over the integers, and `value` written by the same function as the module's, with a `#[verus_spec]` attribute and a `proof!` hint before each product, so with those removed it is the shipped `value` token for token.
guarantees: **The code is the derivation.** `filter` performs exactly the derivation's steps, in their order, one `let` per step, so the error analysis is about the code that runs; it computes the scale by the derivation's scale expression, whose roundings the constant accounts for. `value` performs the same steps, each in the integer type the certificate gives it (the narrowest of `i64`, `i128`, `I256`, `I320`, `I384` and `I512` that holds its bound), with operands widened to that type and checked arithmetic (`checked_add`, `checked_sub`, `checked_mul`, and `resize` between `Wide`s), so a certificate that was wrong would show as `None`, never as a wrapped value. A product in a `Wide` whose operands fit `i128` is `product_i128`, and one with one such operand `checked_mul_i128` (piece G29): the same exact product or `None`, without widening the narrow operand to every limb. The certificate's rows name the same steps.

**Width-aware, as chapter 23.3 asks.** A step that fits 63 bits is computed in `i64`, so a product of two such steps is `i128::from(a).checked_mul(i128::from(b))`: two sign-extended 64-bit operands, whose product the compiler proves cannot overflow `i128` and emits as one 64 × 64 → 128-bit multiply, where a product of two general `i128`s is a long overflow-checked sequence. The value is the same either way; only the cost differs.

**Only the domain the analysis assumes.** A point input is a `P2` or `P3`, whose coordinates are within the grid, so no caller can pass a value outside it. A rounded input is passed as its exact integer, an `i128` (a description's rounded input of more than 127 bits is refused here: no correctly rounded conversion of a wider integer to `f64` exists in `geom-num` yet); `filter` converts it to its nearest `f64` and both functions return `None` for one outside its declared range, before any bound is relied on.

**Names that cannot collide.** Every name the module binds is checked here against every other and against the module's items, imports and Rust's keywords, so a description that slipped past the language's rules ([`crate::predicate_lang::reserved`]) is refused, never emitted as code that shadows a value or does not compile.

**Kernel rules.** No native integer arithmetic and no casts beyond the exact conversion of a grid coordinate to `f64` and the correctly rounded conversion of a rounded input (each with its reason written beside it), no `unsafe`, no panics, no allocation; every public item documented.

method.text: the straight-line predicate programs of Meyer and Pion's FPG input language (a subset of C with `group` declarations; Meyer and Pion, *FPG: A code generator for fast and certified geometric predicates*, Real Numbers and Computers 2008, <https://inria.hal.science/inria-00344297>) and of Geogram's PCK `.pck` files (BSD-3-Clause; for example <https://github.com/BrunoLevy/geogram/blob/16843b4804de35f14ef54667950ab4c8acdd0062/src/lib/geogram/numerics/predicates/orient2d.pck>), cut down to what the kernel's predicates need: one expression per line, no preprocessor, no symbolic perturbation. modules.cost: a few seconds natively: for every node, a few hundred halvings, each an exact evaluation of a polynomial of degree at most 2n + 1 ≤ 61 at a dyadic point.
modules.does: writes `geom-num`'s `src/quadrature_rules/mod.rs`, the tables `geom_num::quadrature` integrates with: the Gauss–Legendre rules of 1 to [`GAUSS_MAX`] points, and the Gauss–Kronrod rules of 2n + 1 points that extend the n-point Gauss rule for each n of [`KRONROD_N`] (QUADPACK's six). Every number is computed in exact rational arithmetic and rounded to the nearest `f64`, ties to even, only once an exact enclosure of it lies inside one rounding cell, so each entry is the correctly rounded value of the true node or weight.
guarantees: **Correctly rounded.** Every node and weight is the `f64` nearest to the exact value, ties to even (dashu-ratio's `to_f64`, which its documentation guarantees correctly rounded, and the unit tests check against both neighbours), decided from an exact enclosure, never from an approximation.

**Exact or nothing.** Every step is exact rational arithmetic; a bracket that does not round to one value within [`MAX_HALVINGS`] halvings, or an isolation that fails, is an error, never an approximate table.
**Pure.** No input but the constants here; the same bytes on every target.
modules.job: Generator `quadrature-rules`: the Gauss–Legendre and Gauss–Kronrod rules on [−1, 1], computed exactly and each node and weight rounded once to the nearest `f64` (piece G51; chapters 12 and 29.4).

method.text: G. H. Golub and J. H. Welsch, *Calculation of Gauss quadrature rules*, Mathematics of Computation 23 (1969), <https://doi.org/10.1090/S0025-5718-69-99647-1>; G. H. Golub and C. F. Van Loan, *Matrix Computations*, 4th ed., Johns Hopkins (2013), section 8.4.1 (bisection by Sturm count); A. S. Kronrod, *Nodes and Weights of Quadrature Formulas*, Consultants Bureau (1965); G. Szegő, *Über gewisse orthogonale Polynome, die zu einer oszillierenden Belegungsfunktion gehören*, Mathematische Annalen 110 (1935), <https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01448041> (the interlacing); the rule set is QUADPACK's (R. Piessens et al., *QUADPACK*, Springer (1983), <https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-61786-7>).

modules.does: [`REGISTRY`] lists every generator ([`GENERATORS`]) and every generated folder ([`FOLDERS`]). Adding a generator means adding its module and one entry here, with the one file it owns, inside a generated folder, and, if it uses randomness, its fixed seed; CI then checks its output on every pull request. Removing or renaming one leaves its old output an orphan, which `check` reports until it is deleted. errors.name: IntersectError

invariants: Every part of an answer is returned with a proof, or as a flagged region that says why it could not be proven; nothing is dropped, guessed or silently trimmed (12).
Every point and parameter returned is an enclosure, never a bare number; an "exactly zero" decision is made by exact arithmetic, by identity of the defining data, or not claimed (12).
Canonical operand order, fixed traversal and per-pair budgets: intersect(A, B) and intersect(B, A) give the same items with the roles swapped, on any thread count (12.15).
Derived caps are errors: never a best-so-far point, never success on a truncated trace (12.15).
Thresholds are in grid steps from the tolerance ladder, never a fraction of a surface's size (12.15).
crates.job: Certified curve-curve, curve-surface and surface-surface intersection; level curves, isoclines and contour generators; closed-form distances.

modules.cost: constant.
modules.does: [`IntersectError`] names each failure of a pair. Every pair of kinds is supported, so there is no "unsupported" error. A flagged region is not one of these: it is part of a complete, honest answer.
guarantees: **Never a partial answer.** A failure returns no items: every error replaces the whole result.
**A stop keeps its reason.** A meter's stop is [`IntersectError::Cancelled`] or [`IntersectError::BudgetExceeded`], so a caller can tell a request from a limit.

modules.cost: a key is one conversion to NURBS, charged to the meter; ordering a pair compares two keys, linear in their lengths. Recursion: none.
modules.does: a [`CanonicalKey`] orders operands by kind, then by a kernel-internal encoding of their defining data: each kind's NURBS form, which is a function of that data alone, or, for a line or plane that has no such form because it may be unbounded, the data itself. [`pair`] puts two [`Operand`]s in that order, runs a method on them and gives its answer back in the caller's roles. [`pairs`] does so for many pairs on the kernel's parallel helper, each under an equal share of the budget, in canonical pair order.
guarantees: **The same items with the roles swapped.** A method only ever sees the canonical order, so `pair(a, b)` and `pair(b, a)` make the same call, and differ only in which operand's unknowns come first in each item's enclosure.

**No address and no file format.** The key reads the defining data's values and nothing else, so it never depends on memory addresses, nor on file-format bytes, whose version can change independently (12.15). It is versioned with the kernel edition (26.2).

**The same answers on any thread count.** Pairs run in chunks fixed by [`PLAN`], each under its own budget, and come back in the caller's order. A pair's budget never depends on the others' costs, only on how many pairs there are, so the shares of 12.15 are the same in any order.
modules.job: The canonical order of a pair: which operand goes first, and how a batch of pairs runs (12.15).

method.text: chapter 12.15's canonical operand order and per-pair budgets (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/12-intersections.md`), on `geom-run`'s batch rule.

modules.cost: O(n log n) comparisons to order n items, then a sweep to prove them disjoint: for each item, one comparison per later item of its kind that starts before it ends in the first unknown, n²/2 at worst and each charged to the meter. Recursion: none.
modules.does: an [`Intersection`] is the items of one pair in canonical order, with its [`Coverage`], its diagnostics and the work it took. An [`Item`] is a point, a curve, an overlap or a flagged region, each with its enclosure on the operands' parameters and in space. A [`ParamBox`] holds one interval per unknown of the pair, the canonical first operand's first, so [`Intersection::swapped`] gives the same items with the roles changed.
guarantees: **One order.** [`Intersection::new`] sorts the items by kind, then by their enclosure on the parameters: lower corner, then upper corner, coordinate by coordinate, compared exactly (12.15). Two items of one kind whose enclosures overlap are refused: distinct items are disjoint, so the order is total.
**Nothing unproven is called certified.** [`Coverage::TopologyCertified`] with a flagged item is refused: a flagged region is what such a result does not have.
**One shape of box.** Every item of an intersection has as many unknowns as the pair, and a [`ParamBox`] has two, three or four.
**Flagged items carry no class.** The type gives them none (12.2).
**Swapping twice is nothing.** [`Intersection::swapped`] moves the unknowns and keeps the items' order, the order of the canonical pair, whichever way round the caller asked.
modules.job: What an intersection returns: its items, how each pair meets, and how much of the answer is proven (12.2).

errors.name: LinalgError

invariants: Bit-identical results on every target and thread count: plain scalar loops in a fixed order, no SIMD chosen at run time, no `mul_add`, and no threads inside one factorisation (15.6, 21).
Least-squares steps come from QR or the complete orthogonal decomposition, never from the normal equations, which square the condition number (15.6).
The least-change step is the limit of the damped steps as damping goes to zero, so an under-determined system never jumps to a pivot-order basic solution (15.6).
Column ordering follows COLAMD (Davis, Gilbert, Larimore and Ng 2004), written in safe Rust, with ties broken by variable order (15.6).
No platform maths: every maths function comes from `geom_num::math` (21).
crates.job: Deterministic dense and sparse linear algebra: QR, the complete orthogonal decomposition, triangular solves, column ordering.

modules.cost: as charged in the worst case, and near linear in z on the matrices a sketch makes; O(z + n) memory for the lists. No recursion.
modules.does: [`colamd`] orders the columns of a matrix A for the Cholesky factor of Aᵀ·A, which is the R of its QR, without forming Aᵀ·A. Each row of A is a clique of the columns it touches. The column of least approximate degree is eliminated; the rows it touches merge into one new row, the pivot row, whose columns get new scores; rows the pivot row covers are absorbed, and columns left with the same rows merge into one supercolumn and are ordered together. [`symmetric`] orders a symmetric matrix the same way, through a matrix with one row for each pair of neighbours.
guarantees: **Structure only.** The order depends on the pattern alone, so it is computed once for every matrix of one pattern (chapter 15.7).
**Deterministic.** The least score goes first and a tie goes to the lowest variable; supercolumns are found by sorted comparison, and no hash or address decides anything (chapter 15.6).
**A permutation.** Every column appears once, and the empty columns and the dense ones last, in variable order.
**Charged first.** It charges (z + n)·(n + 1) multiply-adds before it starts, z the stored entries and n the columns: each elimination visits each column's rows at most.
modules.job: Column ordering by approximate minimum degree: the order to eliminate a sparse matrix's columns in, so that the factors of its QR or Cholesky decomposition stay sparse.

method.text: T. A. Davis, J. R. Gilbert, S. I. Larimore and E. G. Ng, "A column approximate minimum degree ordering algorithm", ACM TOMS 30(3) (2004), doi:10.1145/1024074.1024079: its scores, its row absorption, its supercolumns and its dense rows, in our own words and in safe Rust, with ties broken by variable order (chapter 15.6). It is written from the paper, not from `colamd.c`, so its lists are plain vectors and it has no packed workspace and no garbage collection. It leaves out the paper's final postorder of the assembly tree, which changes neither the fill nor the work.

modules.cost: one allocation of len · count doubles; access is constant time, copies linear.
modules.does: [`Cols`] holds `count` columns of `len` doubles each, one after another, so a column is one contiguous slice and two columns can be borrowed together for a rotation. [`Cols::to_matrix`] copies chosen columns, in a chosen order, into a row-major [`Matrix`].
guarantees: **No panic, no abort.** Every index is checked and every index sum and product too; a bad one is [`LinalgError::Defect`]. The storage is allocated fallibly.
**Exact copies.** Moving values between [`Cols`] and [`Matrix`] copies them unchanged.
modules.job: Matrices stored by columns, for the factorisations that work column by column (the SVDs and the symmetric eigensolver), and checked index arithmetic for them.

method.text: column-major storage as LAPACK uses it (E. Anderson et al., *LAPACK Users' Guide*, 3rd ed., SIAM (1999), <https://www.netlib.org/lapack/lug/>).

modules.cost: (4/3)·n³ for the reduction and 2·n³ for its accumulation, charged first as 4·n³; each QR step then charges (block + 1)·(4n + 12). One working copy, the tridiagonal and Q.
modules.does: [`SymmetricEigen::factor`] reduces a symmetric n × n matrix to tridiagonal form T by n − 2 Householder similarity transformations (Golub and Van Loan's algorithm 8.3.1), then applies implicit QR steps with Wilkinson's shift (algorithm 8.3.2), chasing the bulge down T with Givens rotations, until every subdiagonal entry is negligible (|`b_i`| ≤ 2^−52·(|`a_i`| + |`a_(i+1)`|)); the diagonal is then Λ, and the accumulated transformations Q. Eigenvalues come smallest first, each with its unit eigenvector as a column of Q.
guarantees: **Symmetric or refused.** A matrix that is not square is [`LinalgError::Shape`]; one whose entries are not exactly symmetric, `a_ij` ≠ `a_ji` for some pair, is [`LinalgError::NotSymmetric`]. Only the lower triangle is read after that check.

**Deterministic.** Fixed order of reflections, rotations and deflation tests; the shift from the trailing 2 × 2 block, computed on the block scaled to magnitude 1; IEEE 754 operations in the order written and the correctly rounded square root; a stable sort of the eigenvalues with ties broken by position.

**Accuracy, checked against exact rationals.** The method is backward stable: Q·Λ·Qᵀ is a symmetric matrix within a small multiple of u·‖A‖ of A, so each eigenvalue is within that of an exact one (Golub and Van Loan, section 8.3.6). The tests check the residual and Q's orthogonality exactly and bracket each eigenvalue by exact inertia counts of A − x·I.
**Bounded.** At most 30·n QR steps, then [`LinalgError::NoConvergence`]; each step charges its work before it runs, the reduction its own first.
modules.job: The symmetric eigenproblem: A = Q·Λ·Qᵀ for a symmetric matrix, by Householder tridiagonalisation and the implicit symmetric QR algorithm with Wilkinson's shift.

method.text: G. H. Golub and C. F. Van Loan, *Matrix Computations*, 4th ed., Johns Hopkins (2013), algorithms 8.3.1 (Householder tridiagonalisation), 8.3.2 (the implicit symmetric QR step with Wilkinson shift) and 8.3.3 (the symmetric QR algorithm), and section 8.3.6 (accuracy); J. H. Wilkinson, *The Algebraic Eigenvalue Problem*, Clarendon Press (1965), chapter 8, for the shift; B. N. Parlett, *The Symmetric Eigenvalue Problem*, SIAM (1998), chapter 8, <https://doi.org/10.1137/1.9781611971163>, for the shift's convergence. Written in our own words from the books (chapter 29.4).

modules.cost: a matrix of r × c entries is one allocation of r · c doubles; access is constant time.
modules.does: [`Matrix`] is a dense matrix stored by rows, every entry a finite `f64`, made only by fallible constructors (an allocation that cannot be made is [`LinalgError::OutOfMemory`], never an abort). [`Work`] is a budget in units of one multiply-add: each factorisation knows its cost from its shape, charges it in full before touching a number, and refuses with [`LinalgError::OutOfWork`] when the budget cannot cover it, so a factorisation either finishes or never starts (chapter 15.6: "budgets in work, not time").
guarantees: **Finite.** Every entry of every [`Matrix`] is finite; a constructor refuses NaN and infinities with [`LinalgError::NotFinite`], and a factorisation whose arithmetic overflows reports it the same way instead of returning infinities.

**Charged before it starts.** A factorisation's cost is a function of its shape alone, stated on each function, and is charged before any arithmetic: the same budget gives the same answer, or the same refusal, on every target.
**No panic, no abort.** Indices are checked; allocations are fallible.
modules.job: Dense matrices of finite doubles, the errors of every factorisation, and the work budget each one charges before it starts.

method.text: row-major dense storage, as LAPACK's column-major storage transposed (E. Anderson et al., *LAPACK Users' Guide*, 3rd ed., SIAM (1999), <https://www.netlib.org/lapack/lug/>), with the work model of G. H. Golub and C. F. Van Loan, *Matrix Computations*, 4th ed., Johns Hopkins (2013), section 1.1.15 (flop counts).

modules.cost: as charged above; one copy of A and a few vectors of length n.
modules.does: [`PivotedQr::factor`] factors an m × n matrix as A·Π = Q·R, Q a product of Householder reflections, R upper triangular with diagonal magnitudes that never increase, Π the column order chosen by largest remaining norm. [`Cod::factor`] decides the rank r from R's diagonal and a relative tolerance, then removes R's trailing columns by reflections from the right, giving A·Π = Q·[T 0; 0 0]·Zᵀ with T r × r upper triangular: the complete orthogonal decomposition. From it, [`Cod::least_squares`] gives the least-squares solution of A·x = b of least norm (chapter 15.6's full step: the limit of the damped steps, never a pivot-order basic solution), and [`Cod::null_space`] an orthonormal basis of the null space. [`canonical_null_space`] turns that basis into chapter 15.8's canonical one: reduced echelon form over the variable order, each vector 1 at its own leading variable and 0 at the others', so the basis is unique.
guarantees: **Deterministic.** Plain scalar loops in a fixed order (chapter 15.6). A pivot column is the one of largest remaining norm, the first on a tie; norms are scaled by the column's largest magnitude, so they never overflow for finite entries.

**Least change, never basic.** In a rank-deficient or under-determined system the solution has the least Euclidean norm among all least-squares solutions; no free variable is set to zero in pivot order.

**Rank decided once, by the caller's tolerance.** A diagonal entry of R at most `tol` times the first ends the rank; the tolerance is the caller's (chapter 15 derives it from the tolerance ladder). Like every column-pivoted QR, it can miss a near rank deficiency that no column norm shows: Kahan's matrix is the classic case (tested).
**Charged first.** A factorisation charges 2·m·n·min(m, n) multiply-adds before it starts, the decomposition r²·n more, a solve 2·m·n, a null space n²·(n − r).
modules.job: Householder QR with column pivoting, the complete orthogonal decomposition, the minimum-norm least-squares solution, and the canonical null space.

method.text: G. H. Golub and C. F. Van Loan, *Matrix Computations*, 4th ed., Johns Hopkins (2013): algorithm 5.1.1 (the Householder vector), 5.4.1 (QR with column pivoting), section 5.4.2 (the complete orthogonal decomposition) and 5.5 (least squares in the rank-deficient case); the column norms downdated as LAPACK's `xLAQP2` does, recomputed when the downdate loses more than √u of its relative accuracy (Z. Drmač and Z. Bujanović, *On the failure of rank-revealing QR factorization software*, ACM TOMS 35 (2008), doi:10.1145/1377612.1377616); the trailing columns removed as LAPACK's `xTZRZF` does (E. Anderson et al., *LAPACK Users' Guide*, 3rd ed., SIAM (1999), <https://www.netlib.org/lapack/lug/>). Written in our own words from the books and papers (chapter 29.4).

modules.cost: constant per call; [`rotate_slices`] is linear in the vectors' length.
modules.does: [`hypot`] gives √(a² + b²) without overflow or underflow; [`givens`] gives the rotation (c, s) and r with c·y + s·z = r and −s·y + c·z = 0, which zeroes z against y; [`rotate`] applies a rotation to a pair of numbers, and [`rotate_slices`] to two vectors element by element.
guarantees: **No spurious overflow or underflow.** [`hypot`] divides both numbers by the larger magnitude before squaring, so the squares lie in [0, 1] and the sum in [1, 2].
**Deterministic.** IEEE 754 operations in the order written and the correctly rounded square root of `geom_num::math`; no fused multiply-add.
**Exact identity when nothing is to be zeroed.** A zero z gives c = 1, s = 0 and r = y, so a rotation that has nothing to do changes no bit.
modules.job: Plane rotations and the norm of two numbers, for the iterative factorisations.

method.text: Givens rotations as Golub and Van Loan compute them (G. H. Golub and C. F. Van Loan, *Matrix Computations*, 4th ed., Johns Hopkins (2013), section 5.1.8 and algorithm 5.1.3), with the norm scaled as LAPACK's `xLAPY2` does (E. Anderson et al., *LAPACK Users' Guide*, 3rd ed., SIAM (1999), <https://www.netlib.org/lapack/lug/>); written in our own words (chapter 29.4).

modules.cost: as charged above; one allocation of n² doubles for LU or Cholesky, n doubles per solve.
modules.does: [`Lu::factor`] factors a square matrix as P·A = L·U by Gaussian elimination with partial pivoting, and [`Lu::solve`] solves A·x = b with it. [`Cholesky::factor`] factors a symmetric positive definite matrix as A = G·Gᵀ, and [`Cholesky::solve`] solves with it. [`solve_lower`] and [`solve_upper`] are forward and back substitution on a triangle, and [`solve_tridiagonal`] solves a tridiagonal system by Gaussian elimination with partial pivoting.
guarantees: **Deterministic.** Plain scalar loops in a fixed order: no SIMD, no fused multiply-add, no threads (chapter 15.6). A pivot is the largest magnitude in its column, the first such row on a tie, so the same matrix gives the same factors, bit for bit, on every target.

**Refused, never guessed.** A zero pivot is [`LinalgError::Singular`], a non-positive Cholesky pivot or an asymmetric matrix [`LinalgError::NotPositiveDefinite`], an overflow [`LinalgError::NotFinite`]: no result holds an infinity or a NaN. Tiny pivots are allowed: conditioning is the caller's to judge (the complete orthogonal decomposition in [`crate::qr`] decides rank).

**Charged first.** Each factorisation charges its cost to the [`Work`] budget before any arithmetic: n³ multiply-adds for LU and Cholesky (an upper bound: n³/3 and n³/6 are the leading terms), n² for a solve with factors, n for a tridiagonal solve.
modules.job: Square systems: LU with partial pivoting, Cholesky, triangular and tridiagonal solves.

method.text: G. H. Golub and C. F. Van Loan, *Matrix Computations*, 4th ed., Johns Hopkins (2013): algorithm 3.4.1 (Gaussian elimination with partial pivoting, outer-product form), 3.1.1 and 3.1.2 (row-oriented forward and back substitution), 4.2.2 (Cholesky, gaxpy form) and section 4.3.6 with LAPACK's `dgtsv` (tridiagonal elimination with partial pivoting, which fills one extra superdiagonal; E. Anderson et al., *LAPACK Users' Guide*, 3rd ed., SIAM (1999), <https://www.netlib.org/lapack/lug/>), written in our own words from the books (chapter 29.4's row for LAPACK, Golub and Van Loan and the Thomas algorithm).

modules.cost: `n` columns and `z` entries take O(n + z) memory; construction sorts each column, O(z log z).
modules.does: [`Sparse`] is a matrix in compressed sparse column form, each column's row indices ascending. It is made from triplets in any order; repeated positions add up, in the order given. An entry that is stored stays stored when its value is zero, so a matrix's pattern depends on the positions given and never on the values: a factorisation's analysis can be reused for every matrix of one pattern (chapter 15.7).
guarantees: **Finite.** Every value is finite; a constructor refuses NaN and infinities with [`LinalgError::NotFinite`], and a sum that overflows is refused the same way.
**Canonical.** One pattern and one set of values have one representation, whatever order the triplets came in, so two matrices are equal exactly when `==` says so.
**No panic, no abort.** Indices are checked; allocations are fallible.
modules.job: Sparse matrices of finite doubles, stored by columns, with the checked steps every sparse factorisation is written in.

method.text: compressed sparse column storage, I. S. Duff, A. M. Erisman and J. K. Reid, *Direct Methods for Sparse Matrices*, 2nd ed., Oxford (2017), doi:10.1093/acprof:oso/9780198508380.001.0001, section 2.

modules.cost: as charged; O(|L| + n) memory. No recursion.
modules.does: [`SymbolicCholesky`] reads a symmetric pattern: the order, the elimination tree, and the pattern of each row of L. It is computed once for every matrix of that pattern (chapter 15.7). [`SparseCholesky::factor`] gives P·A·Pᵀ = L·Lᵀ, and [`SparseLdlt::factor`] gives P·A·Pᵀ = L·D·Lᵀ with L unit lower triangular and D diagonal, for a symmetric quasi-definite matrix: neither pivots, so the order is the pattern's alone. Each row of L is solved in turn against the rows above it.
guarantees: **Deterministic.** Plain scalar loops in a fixed order, and an order from the pattern alone (chapter 15.6).
**Symmetric, or refused.** A matrix that is not its own transpose, entry for entry, is refused: nothing is silently read from one triangle.
**Refused, never approximate.** A pivot at or below zero stops Cholesky, and a zero pivot stops L·D·Lᵀ: there is no shifting and no pivoting behind the caller's back.
**Charged first.** The analysis charges [`crate::colamd::symmetric`]'s cost and 2·z more; a factorisation Σⱼ |L₍ⱼ₎|², from the pattern alone; a solve 2·|L|.
modules.job: Sparse Cholesky and L·D·Lᵀ of symmetric matrices, the analysis kept apart from the numbers.

method.text: the elimination tree and row subtrees, J. W. H. Liu, "The role of elimination trees in sparse factorization", SIAM J. Matrix Anal. Appl. 11(1) (1990), doi:10.1137/0611010; the up-looking factorisation by rows, T. A. Davis, "Algorithm 849: a concise sparse Cholesky factorization package", ACM TOMS 31(4) (2005), doi:10.1145/1114268.1114277, read for its method only; L·D·Lᵀ of quasi-definite matrices without pivoting, R. J. Vanderbei, "Symmetric quasidefinite matrices", SIAM J. Optim. 5(1) (1995), doi:10.1137/0805005.

modules.cost: as charged; O(|R| + |V| + m + n) memory. No recursion.
modules.does: [`SymbolicQr`] reads a pattern: the column order, the elimination tree of Aᵀ·A and the pattern of R. It is computed once for every matrix of that pattern (chapter 15.7). [`SparseQr::factor`] then factors one matrix, column by column from the left: each column takes the reflections of the earlier columns R says reach it, and makes its own on the rows it holds. A row enters at the first column it touches, and each column hands the rows it did not use as its pivot to its parent in the tree. A column with nothing left, to the rank tolerance, is dead: it makes no reflection and uses no pivot, and its rows go on up, so A·Π = Q·R with R a staircase. [`SparseQr::least_squares`] solves A·x = b in the least-squares sense with the least norm. On a staircase, and on any under-determined system, it factors Rᵀ too and solves through that. Where solvi fixes its rows in its symbolic step and fails on a rank-deficient matrix, a dead column here hands its rows on and the solve stays least-norm.
guarantees: **Deterministic.** Plain scalar loops in a fixed order, the order and the tree coming from the pattern alone; a column's pivot is the lowest-numbered row it holds (chapter 15.6).

**Least change, never basic.** The solution has the least Euclidean norm among all the least-squares solutions of the kept rows: no free variable is set to zero by its place in the order. It equals the dense path, [`crate::Cod::least_squares`], to rounding, while both find the same rank.

**Rank decided once, and only roughly.** A column is dead when what is left of it is at most `tol` times the largest column of A. There is no column pivoting, so this can miss a near rank deficiency that column pivoting would find, which is why chapter 15.8's verdicts rest on the dense path.
**Never the normal equations.** Aᵀ·A is never formed; its tree is read from A's rows.

**Charged first.** [`SymbolicQr::new`] charges [`crate::colamd::colamd`]'s cost and 2·z more; [`SparseQr::factor`] charges 2·(Σⱼ |R₍ⱼ₎|·|V₍ⱼ₎| + Σⱼ |V₍ⱼ₎|) from the pattern alone, V the Householder vectors, and a staircase the second factorisation's own; a solve charges 2·(|V| + |R|).
modules.job: Sparse QR with Householder reflections, its analysis kept apart from its numbers, and the least-squares solution of least norm.

method.text: the elimination tree of Aᵀ·A, read from A's rows, J. R. Gilbert, X. S. Li, E. G. Ng and B. W. Peyton, "Computing row and column counts for sparse QR and LU factorization", BIT 41(4) (2001), doi:10.1023/A:1021943902025; R's pattern as the row subtrees of that tree, J. W. H. Liu, "The role of elimination trees in sparse factorization", SIAM J. Matrix Anal. Appl. 11(1) (1990), doi:10.1137/0611010; left-looking Householder QR with rows handed up the tree, in the structure of solvi's `decomposition/sparse/qr.rs`; dead columns and the staircase, M. T. Heath, "Some extensions of an algorithm for sparse linear least squares problems", SIAM J. Sci. Stat. Comput. 3(2) (1982), doi:10.1137/0903014; the minimum-norm solve through the QR of Rᵀ, G. H. Golub and C. F. Van Loan, *Matrix Computations*, 4th ed., Johns Hopkins (2013), section 5.6.

provenance.name: solvi (Linebender)
provenance.purpose: for its left-looking structure and the handing of rows up the tree.

modules.cost: Jacobi charges n²·(5m + 2n) per sweep and converges in a handful of sweeps; Golub–Kahan charges 8·m·n² + 4·n³ for the reduction and the accumulation, then (k + 1)·(4(m + n) + 12) per QR step. Each allocates its working copy, U and V.
modules.does: [`Svd::jacobi`] and [`Svd::golub_kahan`] factor an m × n matrix as A = U·Σ·Vᵀ, with k = min(m, n) singular values in Σ, largest first, U m × k and V n × k with orthonormal columns. A wide matrix is factored through its transpose.
guarantees: **Deterministic.** Fixed sweep order (pairs (p, q), p < q, row by row), fixed deflation and shift rules, IEEE 754 operations in the order written, the correctly rounded square root of `geom_num::math`, no fused multiply-add, and a stable sort with ties broken by column index. The same input gives the same bits on every target.

**Accuracy, checked against exact rationals.** Both are backward stable: the computed factors are those of a matrix A + E with ‖E‖ a small multiple of u·‖A‖ (Golub and Van Loan, 8.6.3), so each singular value is within that of the exact one. Jacobi does better on graded matrices A = B·D with B well conditioned: each singular value to a small multiple of u·κ(B) in relative terms, however small (Demmel and Veselić, theorem 4.4). The tests check both claims with exact rational arithmetic: the residual and the orthogonality of U and V, and each singular value bracketed by exact inertia counts of Aᵀ·A.

**Bounded.** Jacobi stops after [`MAX_SWEEPS`] sweeps and Golub–Kahan after 6·k² QR steps with [`LinalgError::NoConvergence`]; neither has ever needed it in the tests. Each sweep or step charges its work before it runs; the reductions charge theirs first.
**Typed failures.** Columns whose norms differ by more than the doubles can hold (a rotation angle that is not finite) are [`LinalgError::NotFinite`], never a silently wrong factor.
modules.job: The singular value decomposition, two ways: one-sided Jacobi, accurate to the last bits of tiny singular values of graded matrices, and Golub–Kahan, the fast general method.

method.text: M. R. Hestenes, "Inversion of matrices by biorthogonalization and related results", *Journal of the SIAM* 6(1) (1958), 51–90, <https://doi.org/10.1137/0106005>. J. Demmel and K. Veselić, "Jacobi's method is more accurate than QR", *SIAM Journal on Matrix Analysis and Applications* 13(4) (1992), 1204–1245, <https://doi.org/10.1137/0613074>. G. Golub and W. Kahan, "Calculating the singular values and pseudo-inverse of a matrix", *Journal of the SIAM, Series B* 2(2) (1965), 205–224, <https://doi.org/10.1137/0702016>. G. H. Golub and C. F. Van Loan, *Matrix Computations*, 4th ed., Johns Hopkins (2013), algorithms 5.4.2 (bidiagonalisation), 8.6.1 and 8.6.2 (the Golub–Kahan SVD step and algorithm) and section 8.6.3 (accuracy).

invariants: Every result passes all four checker groups before it is returned; inputs are never changed (principle 4, 8.3).
Primitives name their faces by role (20.2).

crates.job: The Make and Transform families of 10.2: primitives, transforms and patterns.

modules.cost: linear in the part's rows, plus publishing (a sort by name) and the checker's own cost. Recursion: none.
modules.does: a [`Part`] lists a solid's vertices, edges and faces, each with its geometry and the role it is named by (20.2), and each face's loops as edges and senses. [`assemble`] names every region, face, edge and vertex `Created { op, role, from }` (`geom_op::TopoName`), builds the rows (one solid region and the void outside it, one shell, a ring of fins round each edge), publishes them in name order (`geom_topo::Builder::publish_named`), runs the checker on the result as the operation's postcondition (8.3) and records each entity's origin. [`Made`] is what comes back: the body, its history and, from a transform, which one it was.
guarantees: **Names, not positions.** Every index of the body follows its entities' names, and every name comes from the operation's path, a role and the names it is relative to: never from the order the rows were written in (8.2, 20.2).
**Checked before returned.** A body that does not pass the checker at the build's level is never returned; the operation fails with [`MakeDetail::ResultInvalid`], a defect, instead.

**Charged by what it builds.** One meter unit ([`PER_ROW`]) and 64 logical bytes per row built, before it is built (23.10), and the publishing charges its own rows to the same meter. The postcondition check runs on a meter of its own, cancellable and without a limit: its level differs between a test build and a shipped one, and a budget must stop an operation the same way in both.
**Transactional.** Nothing the caller holds is changed; a failure, or a stop the operation did not report, returns no body (`OpContext::run`).
modules.job: Assembling what a Make or Transform operation returns: a body's rows, each entity named by its role, published in name order, checked, and the history that says where each entity came from.

method.text: chapter 8's arenas and name order (8.2), chapter 20's names by role and history records (20.2, 20.3), and the checker's postcondition (8.3) (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/08-topology.md`, `projects/engines/geometry/architecture/20-naming-history.md`).

modules.cost: one transform of the body per instance. Recursion: none.
modules.does: [`pattern`] runs one copy per [`Instance`], in key order: the body moved by the instance's transform as the Transform family moves it, each entity named `Created { op: the operation's path with the instance's key, role: copy(source), from: source }` and recorded as generated from its source with that role. It returns one [`Made`] per instance, keyed as given, and the least exact of their records.
guarantees: **One answer per key, whatever the order given.** Instances run in key order; two with one key are refused ([`MakeDetail::RepeatedKey`]), and so is an empty pattern.
**Copies, not the body.** Every copy's entities have names of their own, distinct across instances (each instance's path differs), and trace to the body's entities as copies.
**Each copy checked.** Every copy passes the checker before the pattern returns; one failure fails the whole pattern, which returns nothing.
**The transform states its own stretch.** Each copy's bound grows by what its transform can do to a length, read from the transform, never taken on the caller's word.
modules.job: Patterns: copies of one body, each by its own transform and keyed by the caller, each copy's entities named as copies of the body's (8.4's `Copied`, which a pattern's schema declares).

method.text: chapter 10.1's batch rule (an item's path is the operation's path and its key) and chapter 8.4's `Copied` event (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/10-operations.md`, `projects/engines/geometry/architecture/08-topology.md`).

modules.cost: constant per primitive; O(n log n) for a prism of n corners, whose edges are found through an ordered map. Recursion: none.
modules.does: each function checks its input, writes the solid as a [`Part`] and hands it to [`assemble`], which names, publishes, checks and records it. Lengths are whole grid steps of the frame (`geom_num::Steps`) and every vertex is a grid point; round shapes stand on the z axis through the point given, and other orientations come from the Transform family.
guarantees: **Outward and counter-clockwise.** Every face's surface normal, with its sense, points out of the solid, and every loop runs counter-clockwise seen from outside.

**Exact where it can be.** A box and a prism are recorded Exact: their planes are given by integers through grid corners. Round shapes are recorded Certified with a bound of one step of the step given, as 10.2 asks: their circles' points come from certified sines and cosines.

**Typed refusals.** A zero length, a base that is not strictly convex or not level, and a torus that would not be a ring are input errors that name the input and the nearest value that works; a corner past the grid's range is the numbers layer's `OutOfRange`.
modules.job: The primitives of chapter 10.2's Make family: box, prism, cylinder, cone, sphere and torus, each the shape 10.2's "Primitive topology" fixes, its faces, edges and vertices named by role.

method.text: chapter 10.2's primitives and their topology, accepted with piece G85 (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/10-operations.md`), on chapter 7's analytic surfaces (`geom_surface::analytic`).

modules.cost: linear in the body's rows, one meter unit each, plus each curve's and surface's transform and the checker. Recursion: none.
modules.does: each function turns its input into a `geom_math::TypedTransform` and hands it to [`moved_copy`], which copies every row of the body with its points, curves, surfaces and face boxes moved, publishes the copy under the same names, checks it and records each entity as modified from itself (20.2: a one-to-one change keeps the name). [`Motion`], in the result, says which of the four it was, for the attribute event `Transformed` (8.4).
guarantees: **Exact where the transform is.** A move by whole steps, quarter turns, mirrors across grid planes and whole-number uniform scales map grid points to grid points and keep planes given by integers: an Exact body stays Exact.

**Rounded once, and said so.** Any other rotation or scale rounds each vertex to the grid once (at most √3/2 of a step), and moves curves and surfaces by their own typed transforms, each with a certified deviation. The result's bound is the input's, stretched by the most the transform can stretch a length, plus one step if any vertex rounded, plus the largest deviation, rounded up.
**The class never rises.** The result keeps the input's class or a less exact one: an Approximate body stays Approximate whatever its bound does (principle 3).

**Accepted, or refused.** A result less exact than the input is returned only when the caller accepts it ([`Moved::accept`]): a class at least as loose and a ceiling at least the result's bound; otherwise [`MakeDetail::NotAccepted`] names the class the result would have.

**Kinds change only where the checker can follow.** A transform that does not keep circles turns them into ellipses and analytic surfaces into affine ones, which the checker cannot certify yet: on a body with curved geometry it is [`MakeDetail::KindNotCertified`] (G177).
**Mirrors keep the outside outside.** A mirror reverses orientation, so every face's sense and every loop's direction is reversed with it.
modules.job: The Transform family of chapter 10.2: move, rotate, mirror and scale a body, its entities keeping their names, its geometry changing kind only as chapter 7's typed transforms say.

errors.name: MathError

invariants: **Exact where it decides.** Grid vectors, grid and rational transforms and grid boxes use integers only, and every product's bit budget is derived in its doc comment. Arithmetic that could leave its range is checked and returns [`NumError::OutOfRange`](geom_num::NumError) instead of wrapping.

**The same result in every build profile; defects reported, never answered.** As in the numbers layer, every integer addition, subtraction, multiplication, division and negation in this crate's code is a checked method, never a native operator, and no cast loses a value silently (each cast's bound is written beside it), so nothing depends on overflow checks being on. A step that its bit budget proves fits can fail only through a defect, and is then reported as [`NumError::BudgetExceeded`](geom_num::NumError), never replaced by a guessed value: that is why exact products and classifications return a `Result`. For valid inputs every such result is `Ok`. Clippy enforces this (`arithmetic_side_effects` and the lossy-cast lints are denied); tests and the benchmark may use native arithmetic.

**Certified elsewhere.** Floating-point boxes round outward; transform classifications and orientations are decided with interval arithmetic, never with a guessed tolerance (the only tolerance used is the ladder's angular bound); conversions to the grid round exactly once and say whether they were exact.
**Never NaN, never infinite.** Every floating-point value this crate makes is finite; an operation whose result would not be returns an error.

**Deterministic.** Only IEEE 754 basic operations (which Rust never fuses into a fused multiply-add), integer arithmetic and the maths of `geom_num::math`. No hash maps, no randomness, no platform maths, no recursion; every loop is bounded, by a fixed or proven count or by the length of the caller's own input (`from_points`, [`FrameRecord::home_of`], [`Decimal::parse`]).
**Safe.** No `unsafe`, no panics, no unchecked indexing.
crates.job: points, vectors, exact and general transforms, boxes and frames, the small vocabulary every geometry crate above the numbers layer shares.

modules.cost: constant time and no allocation for every operation except `from_points`, which is one union per point. Grid boxes compare integers (at most six comparisons for a union, an intersection or a containment test); moving one by a [`GridTransform`] moves its two corners. [`FBox3::transformed`] is 18 interval operations, a product and a sum for each entry of the linear part (an interval sum is two IEEE additions, a product four multiplications and six comparisons, each followed by a one-step widening of both bounds); [`FBox3::to_grid_outward`] is six roundings and six range checks; [`FBox2`]'s operations are the same on two axes (its transform, eight interval operations).
guarantees: **Never empty, always ordered.** Every box has `min ≤ max` (`lo ≤ hi`) on every axis; constructors refuse anything else with [`NumError::EmptyInterval`], and an intersection that would be empty is `None`.
**Closed.** Boxes contain their boundary: two boxes that share only a face, an edge or a corner overlap.
**Finite.** `FBox2` and `FBox3` bounds are finite, with zero stored as +0; operations that would overflow return [`NumError::NotFinite`].
**2D in the plane only.** A 2D box is moved only by a transform that leaves z unchanged; any other is refused with [`MathError::NotInPlane`], never projected.
modules.job: Axis-aligned boxes: exact boxes on the grid, and floating-point boxes that round outward.

method.text: closed intervals per axis, so a box is the product of three intervals and every operation is per-axis interval logic; outward-rounded interval arithmetic as in R. E. Moore, R. B. Kearfott and M. J. Cloud, *Introduction to Interval Analysis*, SIAM (2009), <https://doi.org/10.1137/1.9780898717716>.

modules.cost: no allocation, constant time.
guarantees: **Map to frame rounds once.** [`FrameRecord::to_frame`] and [`FrameRecord::to_frame_decimal`] return the exact value of every coordinate rounded to the nearest step, ties to even, and say whether all three were exact, for every frame and every linear unit; never through a rounded intermediate, and never through `f64` for decimal text.

**Out of range, exactly.** A coordinate beyond ±(2^40 − 1) steps is refused with [`NumError::OutOfRange`] whose value is that coordinate, exactly rounded, and saturated only when it is beyond `i128` (and so, for inputs beyond 2^200 steps, a coordinate beyond 2^135 steps with its true sign). NaN and infinities are [`NumError::NotFinite`].
**Frame to map rounds once.** [`FrameRecord::to_map`] gives the nearest doubles to the exact map coordinates in the frame's linear unit, ties to even, with whether they are exact, for every frame.
**Certified or refused.** No conversion returns a value it could not certify, and no exact sign that fails is replaced by a guess: a defect is reported as [`NumError::BudgetExceeded`].
modules.job: Conversion between map coordinates and a frame's grid, each way rounded once and correctly: map values in the frame's linear unit, given as doubles or as exact decimal text, go to the nearest grid step, ties to even; grid points go to the nearest doubles, ties to even.

method.text: the conversion rules of chapter 17.1 (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/17-survey-terrain-civil.md`) and chapter 24's numbers to grid (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/24-file-format-exchange.md`); double-double arithmetic with `geom-num`'s proven bounds (`geom_num::dd`, piece G25); the exact settling as the filter-then-exact pattern of the kernel's predicates (chapter 6.2; J. R. Shewchuk, *Discrete & Computational Geometry* 18 (1997), <https://doi.org/10.1007/PL00009321>), with exact values of doubles read as dyadic rationals and of decimals as rationals over powers of ten (IEEE 754-2019, <https://doi.org/10.1109/IEEESTD.2019.8766229>), and numbers a + b√n compared exactly by their squares (C. K. Yap, *Computational Geometry* 7 (1997), <https://doi.org/10.1016/0925-7721(95)00040-2>).

modules.cost: [`Decimal::parse`] is one pass over the text, one checked multiplication and addition per significant digit (zeros inside the significand are multiplied in at most 38 at a time), and the standard library's parse of the exponent's digits; no allocation. `Display` writes at most 38 digits and, in plain notation, at most 30 zeros.
guarantees: **Exact.** [`Decimal::parse`] returns exactly the value the text writes, or refuses it with [`DecimalError`]; nothing is rounded.

**One form per value.** Every `Decimal` is in lowest terms, so two decimals are equal exactly when their values are, `Hash` agrees with `==`, and `Display` writes text that [`Decimal::parse`] reads back to the same `Decimal`.
**No panics, no allocation.** Every integer step is checked; `Display` writes into the given formatter.
modules.job: Exact decimal numbers: text such as `5921000.1234` or `-1.5e-3` read as significand·10^exponent with no rounding at all, so survey and map coordinates given as decimal text reach the grid through one rounding, never through `f64` (chapters 17.1 and 24).

method.text: decimal scientific notation as IEEE 754-2019 defines its character sequences (section 5.12.3, <https://doi.org/10.1109/IEEESTD.2019.8766229>), read digit by digit into an exact integer and a power of ten, with trailing zeros moved into the exponent (D. E. Knuth, *The Art of Computer Programming*, vol. 2, section 4.4, radix conversion, <https://www-cs-faculty.stanford.edu/~knuth/taocp.html>).

modules.cost: constant time; no allocation.
guarantees: **Exact identity.** Two epochs are equal exactly when their decimal values are (a [`Decimal`] is in lowest terms, so 2023.50 and 2023.5 are one epoch); two models are equal exactly when their digests are.
**In range or refused.** [`DecimalYear::new`] refuses a year below 0 or from 10000 on with [`NumError::OutsideDomain`].
modules.job: Coordinate epochs and deformation models: the two parts of a frame record that say when its map coordinates hold and how observations at other dates were carried to it (chapter 17.1, Epochs).

method.text: the coordinate epoch of a dynamic coordinate reference system and the point-motion operations of ISO 19111:2019, *Geographic information: referencing by coordinates* (<https://www.iso.org/standard/74039.html>), as chapter 17.1 records them (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/17-survey-terrain-civil.md`), with PROJ's deformation-model operation, which takes the observation date as input; content addressing by SHA-256 (FIPS 180-4, <https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.FIPS.180-4>), the digest chapters 21 and 28.13 specify.

modules.cost: constructing, copying and comparing an error is constant time; `Display` writes one short sentence and allocates nothing.
guarantees: **Plain values.** Every error is `Copy`, compares with `==` and holds only enums and integers, so it can be returned from `no_std` code, matched exhaustively and compared in tests.

**Says what went wrong.** `Display` writes one fixed sentence per variant, with the offending coordinate for `FrameRangeExceeded` and the numbers layer's own sentence for `Num`. (The numbers layer's sentence for `BudgetExceeded` names `geom-num`; reported by this crate, the defect is in `geom-math`.)
modules.job: Errors from this crate that the numbers layer has no word for.

method.text: the kernel's error model, chapter 22 of the architecture: each variant says what was wrong in plain words and carries the value that caused it (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/22-errors-queries-ai.md`).

modules.cost: no allocation. [`pow2`], [`exponent`], [`dyadic`] and [`scale_b`] are a few bit operations and at most two floating-point multiplications. [`pow2_big`], [`shl_into`], [`bit_length`], [`leading_106`] and [`round_scaled`] are linear in the number of 64-bit limbs (24 for [`Big`], at most 48 anywhere in the crate). [`pow5_big`] is one multiplication by a factor below 2^63 per 27 powers of five, each linear in the limbs. [`sign_minus_sqrt`] is three schoolbook multiplications of L-limb integers (at most L² limb products each) and one subtraction. [`rational_to_f64`] is one 128-bit division and at most 181 shift-and-subtract steps; [`quotient_to_f64`] is 58 shifts by multiplication with a power of two, each linear in the limbs, and 56 comparisons and subtractions. [`gcd_u128`] takes at most 257 remainder steps (the remainder at least halves every two steps). [`divrem_u128`] takes exactly 64·L shift-and-subtract steps.
guarantees: **Exact, or it says so.** Every integer result is exact, and one that does not fit its type is `None`, never a wrapped value. Every rounded result is rounded once, to nearest, ties to even: [`round_scaled`], [`rational_to_f64`] and [`quotient_to_f64`] also say whether they were exact, and [`scale_b`], like IEEE 754's scaleB, returns ±∞ when the exact result overflows. [`leading_106`] truncates toward zero and says by how many bits.

**The same result in every build profile.** Every integer addition, subtraction, multiplication, division by a variable and negation is a checked method that returns `None` instead of wrapping, or `abs_diff`, which is exact for every input; the only native integer operations are shifts by amounts below the width and division and remainder by the constant 64, none of which can overflow. So nothing depends on overflow checks being on. A `None` that the bounds written here rule out is passed on, and the caller reports it as [`NumError::BudgetExceeded`](geom_num::NumError), never as an answer.

**No panics.** Every shift amount is below the width it shifts (each says why), every limb access is checked, and every loop has a fixed or proven bound (below). The only casts are of values whose bound is written beside them.
modules.job: Exact helpers shared by the crate: doubles as exact dyadic numbers, exact scaling of doubles by powers of two, wide integers built from shifted products and powers of two and five, their bit lengths and leading bits, exact rounding of a wide integer divided by a power of two, the exact sign of a − b·√n, the correctly rounded double nearest a quotient of integers (128-bit or wide), and long division of a wide integer by a 128-bit one.

method.text: A double is exactly m·2^k with integer m (IEEE 754-2019, section 3.3); scaling by a power of two is IEEE's scaleB (section 5.3.3), rounded once. The quotient of two integers is rounded to the nearest double, ties to even (roundTiesToEven, section 4.3.1), by binary long division that produces the 53 bits of the significand, one or more further bits, and a sticky bit for whether anything nonzero remains (D. E. Knuth, *The Art of Computer Programming*, vol. 2, section 4.3.1); IEEE 754-2019, <https://doi.org/10.1109/IEEESTD.2019.8766229>. The sign of a − b·√n is decided by comparing a² with b²·n when a and b have the same sign: exact geometric computation with algebraic numbers of degree two, evaluated in exact integers instead of rounded square roots (C. K. Yap, "Towards exact geometric computation", *Computational Geometry* 7 (1997), 3–23, <https://doi.org/10.1016/0925-7721(95)00040-2>). Greatest common divisors by Euclid's algorithm, and long division of a wide integer one bit at a time (Knuth, *The Art of Computer Programming*, vol. 2, sections 4.5.2 and 4.3.1, <https://www-cs-faculty.stanford.edu/~knuth/taocp.html>).

modules.cost: constant time, no loops beyond the two or three components, no allocation. Arithmetic, dot and cross products are at most nine IEEE operations plus a finiteness check per result; `length` and `normalized` add a pass over the components for the largest, one exact power-of-two scaling per component (`scale_b`), the squared sum and one correctly rounded square root, then one more scaling (`length`) or one division per component (`normalized`).
guarantees: **Finite.** Every component is finite: made only by constructors that check, and by operations that check their results and return [`NumError::NotFinite`] when a result would overflow. No value here is ever NaN or infinite (chapter 21: NaN's bits are not deterministic).

**Deterministic.** Only IEEE 754 addition, subtraction, multiplication and division, each correctly rounded to nearest on every target, evaluated in the fixed order written in each function. Rust never contracts `a * b + c` into a fused multiply-add on its own, and nothing here asks for one. Square roots come from [`geom_num::math::sqrt`], correctly rounded. No `f64::max`, `f64::min` or platform maths.
**Exact conversions from the grid.** A grid point or grid vector has components below 2^42 in magnitude, so it converts to `f64` with no rounding.

**Lengths without spurious overflow or underflow.** `length` and `normalized` first scale the vector by the power of two that brings its largest component into [1, 2) (exact, except that a component more than 2^1022 times smaller than the largest may round, which changes nothing visible), so the squares neither overflow nor underflow. Where the plain formula would not overflow or underflow, the result has the same bits as the plain formula, because scaling by a power of two commutes with every rounding in the normal range. With u = 2^−53, the squared length has a relative error below 2u + u² for [`F2`] (two squares, one sum) and 3u + 3u² for [`F3`]; the square root halves it and adds its own rounding, so the length is within a relative 2.01u ([`F2`]) or 2.51u ([`F3`]) of the exact length, plus 2^−1070 relative for components that round when scaled. Only the zero vector cannot be normalized.

**Defects reported, never answered.** The one integer step of the scaling (an exponent's negation) is checked, and the maths functions' errors are passed on. None of them can occur for finite components; one that did would be [`NumError::BudgetExceeded`] or the maths function's own error, never a guessed length.
modules.job: Floating-point points and vectors, finite by construction, with deterministic arithmetic.

method.text: IEEE 754-2019 binary64 basic operations, round to nearest, ties to even, and its scaleB (<https://doi.org/10.1109/IEEESTD.2019.8766229>), under Rust's floating-point semantics, which guarantee those results on every supported target and forbid implicit contraction (Rust RFC 3514, <https://rust-lang.github.io/rfcs/3514-float-semantics.html>); the scaling before squaring is the classic remedy for overflow and underflow in Euclidean norms (J. L. Blue, "A portable Fortran program to find the Euclidean norm of a vector", *ACM Transactions on Mathematical Software* 4(1) (1978), 15–23, <https://doi.org/10.1145/355769.355771>), here with an exact power-of-two scale.

modules.cost: no allocation, and constant time for every operation except [`FrameRecord::home_of`], which is linear in the number of operands.
guarantees: **Canonical records.** Rotations, scales and linear units are stored reduced, epochs and deformation models exactly, so two records are `==` exactly when they describe the same frame.

**Frames are never mixed without an exact shift.** [`FrameRecord::shift_to`] and [`FrameRecord::home_of`] refuse frames whose coordinate reference systems, linear units, epochs, deformation models, rotations or scales differ with the matching [`FrameMismatch`], in that order, and frames off a shared lattice with [`FrameMismatch::NotOnLattice`].

**Shifts are exact.** A shift's offset is decided whole before its range is checked, so two frames off a shared lattice are refused as such however far apart they are; an offset beyond [`SHIFT_MAX`] is [`NumError::OutOfRange`] with its exact value (saturated beyond `i128`).
**Home frames.** An operation runs in the lattice frame whose cell holds the centre of its operands' combined box, or is refused with [`MathError::FrameRangeExceeded`].
modules.job: Frames: the record that ties a model's flat grid to a map projection, exact shifts between frames on a shared lattice, and the regional lattice of frames for long networks.

method.text: the frame record and lattice rules of chapter 17.1 (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/17-survey-terrain-civil.md`), with EPSG:2193 as given in PROJ's copy of the EPSG data (<https://github.com/OSGeo/PROJ/blob/5fa31c29f0a806568ed7bc76c1a557604db4a804/data/sql/projected_crs.sql#L375>); exact integer shifts, with divisibility decided by long division of a wide integer (D. E. Knuth, *The Art of Computer Programming*, vol. 2, section 4.3.1, <https://www-cs-faculty.stanford.edu/~knuth/taocp.html>).

modules.cost: constant time, no allocation. Applying is, per axis, one pick, an optional negation, one addition and one range check; composing and inverting rebuild three rows (composing checks three translations); the determinant counts at most three inversions and three negations.
guarantees: **Exact.** Applying, composing and inverting use integer arithmetic only. Composition and inversion of signed permutations are again signed permutations, so nothing ever rounds.

**Range-checked.** Applying to a point checks that the result stays within the frame's ±(2^40 − 1) steps and returns [`NumError::OutOfRange`] otherwise. Translations are kept within [`TRANSLATION_MAX`] = 2(2^40 − 1) steps per axis, the largest that can map some grid point to another; a composition whose translation would exceed it returns `OutOfRange` too.

**Orientation known exactly.** The determinant is ±1, computed from the permutation's parity and the signs; [`GridTransform::reverses_orientation`] says whether a mirror is involved, which reverses arcs, face normals and winding numbers.

**2D is the plane z = 0, with the same transforms.** The kernel has one family of transforms for 2D and 3D (principle 8). A transform that leaves every z unchanged ([`GridTransform::acts_in_plane`]) maps a 2D frame's plane onto itself, and [`GridTransform::apply_2d`] and [`GridTransform::apply_vector_2d`] give exactly what [`GridTransform::apply`] gives at z = 0; its orientation in the plane is its orientation in 3D. Any other transform is refused for 2D input ([`MathError::NotInPlane`]), never projected. Chapter 14.10's exact 2D transforms are all of this kind: translations in x and y, quarter turns about z, and mirrors about axis-aligned and 45-degree lines ([`GridTransform::mirror_diagonal`]), each composed with a translation for a line off the origin.

**The same result in every build profile.** Every integer step (a negation, a sum) is a checked method, never a native operator, so nothing depends on overflow checks being on. The bit budget below proves each fits; one that did not would be reported as [`NumError::BudgetExceeded`], never answered.
modules.job: Exact transforms of the grid: whole-step translations, quarter turns about the axes, mirrors.

method.text: the hyperoctahedral group B₃ (the symmetry group of the cube) represented as signed permutations, composed by composing the permutations and multiplying the signs, with the inverse given by the transpose, as in A. Björner and F. Brenti, *Combinatorics of Coxeter Groups*, Graduate Texts in Mathematics 231, Springer (2005), section 8.1 (the group `B_n` of signed permutations), <https://doi.org/10.1007/3-540-27596-7>; chapter 7 of the architecture names which transforms stay exact (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/07-geometry-types.md`).

modules.cost: constant time, no allocation. [`RationalTransform::apply`] is nine `i128` products and three Euclidean divisions. [`RationalTransform::compose`] is 40 `i128` products and a reduction. [`RationalTransform::inverse`] is 36 `i128` products (determinant, adjugate and scaling), nine 256-bit products, twelve greatest common divisors and six long divisions of a 256-bit integer by their result (256 shift-and-subtract steps each), and a reduction. [`RationalTransform::classify`] is at most 28 `i128` products. A reduction folds 13 values into their greatest common divisor, then divides each by it. Every greatest common divisor is Euclid's algorithm on `u128`, at most 257 remainder steps.
guarantees: a [`RationalTransform`] is exact. Its image of a grid point is computed in exact integer arithmetic and rounded once, half to even, with whether it was already on the grid; it composes and inverts exactly; its classification is decided exactly, with no tolerance; equal transforms have equal fields; and a step its budget proves fits that fails all the same is reported as [`NumError::BudgetExceeded`], never answered.
modules.job: Rational affine transforms: `p ↦ (M·p + t)/d` with an integer matrix M, an integer vector t and a positive integer d.

method.text: exact rational arithmetic on a common denominator, reduced by Euclid's algorithm (D. E. Knuth, *The Art of Computer Programming*, vol. 2, section 4.5.2, <https://www-cs-faculty.stanford.edu/~knuth/taocp.html>), the inverse by the adjugate (Cramer's rule), and the classification by the Gram matrix as in [`crate::transform`] (R. Hartley and A. Zisserman, *Multiple View Geometry in Computer Vision*, 2nd ed. (2004), section 2.4, <https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511811685>), here exactly.

modules.cost: constant time, no allocation. Applying is ten `i128` products for M(q) and nine for the image, and three Euclidean divisions; composing is sixteen products and a reduction (four greatest common divisors); a 2D search is about twenty interval operations, at most 200 steps of the simplest-rational loop and one certificate (about 60 interval operations); a 3D search is at most 36 roundings and certificates.
guarantees: a [`RationalRotation`] is exact and canonical, its image of a grid point is the exact image rounded once, ties to even, with whether it was exact; composition is exact while the product fits the budget and otherwise re-approximated once, saying by how much; every [`WithinAngle`] bound is a certified upper bound on the true angle and at most the bound asked for; and a step the budget proves fits that fails all the same is reported as [`NumError::BudgetExceeded`], never answered.
modules.job: Rational rotations: one exact rotation type for 2D and 3D, held as an integer quaternion, and the closest such rotation, or Pythagorean direction, within a requested angle (decision 32.14).

method.text: J. Canny, B. Donald and E. K. Ressler, "A rational rotation method for robust geometric algorithms", Proceedings of the 8th Symposium on Computational Geometry (1992), 251–260, <https://doi.org/10.1145/142675.142726>, for the 2D directions; the Euler–Rodrigues parametrisation of rotations by quaternions for the 3D type (decision 32.14); the simplest rational in an interval from the continued fractions of its ends (G. H. Hardy and E. M. Wright, *An Introduction to the Theory of Numbers*, 6th ed., Oxford University Press (2008), chapter 10, <https://global.oup.com/academic/product/9780199219865>); interval arithmetic as in [`geom_num::interval`]. The quaternion of a rational rotation matrix ([`RationalRotation::from_rational`]) is read from the identity d·(1 + tr R) = 4w²·d/|q|² and its companions, derived in that function's comment.

modules.cost: a value and one flag; reading either is a copy.
guarantees: **The report is the truth.** A `Rounded` is made only inside this crate, by the function that did the rounding, so `is_exact` says whether the value equals what was converted. A caller can read a `Rounded`, never build one that claims exactness for a rounded value.
**Plain value.** `Copy`, compared with `==`, hashed; no allocation.
modules.job: A value that may have been rounded, with whether it was: the report chapter 7 asks of every transform and conversion that rounds to the grid ("other rotations round to the grid and the result says so"), and chapter 6.1 of every conversion from fine to coarse.

method.text: the rounding report of chapters 6.1 and 7 of the kernel architecture (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/07-geometry-types.md`), with the same shape as the numbers layer's.

modules.cost: constant time, no allocation. [`Transform::apply_point`] is 18 IEEE operations and [`Transform::compose`] 63. [`Transform::classify`] is fewer than 100 interval operations (the determinant enclosure, then one or two Gram matrices and their row sums), each a few IEEE operations with a one-step widening. [`Transform::inverse`] is a classification, 60 IEEE operations and 18 power-of-two scalings. [`Transform::apply_grid`] decides each coordinate by the cheapest stage that can: about twenty IEEE operations in plain doubles; if those cannot decide, three exact products and three double-double additions; only then the exact sum of four shifted terms in an integer of 128 bits up to 2176 bits (34 limbs, chosen by how far apart the exponents are) and one exact rounding, each linear in the limbs. A coordinate outside the frame always takes that exact stage, which finds the rounded coordinate its error reports.
guarantees: **Finite.** Every entry is finite; operations whose results would overflow return [`NumError::NotFinite`]. Zero entries are stored as +0, so equal transforms have equal bits.
**Deterministic.** Each entry of a product is evaluated as `(a₀b₀ + a₁b₁) + a₂b₂`, in that order, with IEEE 754 operations only; no fused multiply-add, no platform maths.

**Never a wrong orientation.** [`Classification::mirror`] comes from a certified determinant sign. When the sign is not certain the transform is `Degenerate`, and [`Transform::inverse`] refuses it with [`MathError::Singular`].

**Grid points round once.** [`Transform::apply_grid`] gives the exact image of a grid point under the exact entries, rounded to the nearest grid point, ties to even, with whether it was already on the grid. An image outside the frame is refused with its exact rounded coordinate (saturated at the ends of `i128`, as [`NumError::OutOfRange`] documents), never an estimate.

**Defects reported, never answered.** The integer steps (the exponents of the row scalings and of the exact rounding) are checked methods, and the maths functions' errors are passed on. For finite entries none can fail; one that did is reported as [`NumError::BudgetExceeded`] (or the maths function's own error), never turned into a classification or a coordinate. Where a stage of [`Transform::apply_grid`] can decline (the two filters), such a failure only makes it decline, and the exact stage decides.
modules.job: General affine transforms in `f64`, classified so callers know when a kind changes.

method.text: the hierarchy of planar and spatial transformations (isometry, similarity, affinity) of R. Hartley and A. Zisserman, *Multiple View Geometry in Computer Vision*, 2nd ed., Cambridge University Press (2004), section 2.4, <https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511811685>, with each level recognised from the Gram matrix `LᵀL`; Gershgorin's theorem for the eigenvalue bound (R. A. Horn and C. R. Johnson, *Matrix Analysis*, 2nd ed., Cambridge University Press (2012), section 6.1, <https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9781139020411>); the inverse by the adjugate (Cramer's rule) on the row-scaled matrix; the certified tests by interval arithmetic (R. E. Moore, R. B. Kearfott and M. J. Cloud, *Introduction to Interval Analysis*, SIAM (2009), <https://doi.org/10.1137/1.9780898717716>); exact rounding of grid images by the filter-then-exact pattern of the kernel's predicates (J. R. Shewchuk, *Discrete & Computational Geometry* 18 (1997), <https://doi.org/10.1007/PL00009321>).

modules.cost: constant time, no allocation: that of the variant's own operation (see [`crate::grid_transform`], [`crate::rational`] and [`crate::transform`]), plus, when a result is simplified, a comparison of each of the twelve entries (with 0 and ±1, and the translations with their range), and for a certified transform three roundings to integers and a reduction to canonical form. [`TypedTransform::rotation`] for an irrational direction adds one double-double square root and two double-double divisions.
guarantees: every [`TypedTransform::apply`] returns a [`Rounded`] point, the exact image rounded once to the nearest step, ties to even, with whether it was already exact; composition keeps the most exact variant both operands allow and records a change of variant; classification is exact for the exact and rational variants and certified for the certified one.
modules.job: The typed transform: one enum for every transform the kernel applies to geometry, so that whether a transform is exact is part of its type (chapter 7: "Transforms are typed so that this is explicit").

method.text: the hierarchy of transformation groups (isometries, similarities, affinities) of R. Hartley and A. Zisserman, *Multiple View Geometry in Computer Vision*, 2nd ed., Cambridge University Press (2004), section 2.4, <https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511811685>, with each group represented in the most exact number type that holds it.

modules.cost: constant time; [`LinearUnit::new`] and [`LinearUnit::from_decimal`] reduce by a greatest common divisor (at most 129 remainder steps of 64-bit integers), and [`LinearUnit::from_decimal`] multiplies by at most 38 powers of ten.
guarantees: **Exact and canonical.** A unit is stored reduced by the greatest common divisor, so equal ratios have equal fields and `==` is equality of the ratios.

**In range or refused.** [`LinearUnit::new`] and [`LinearUnit::from_decimal`] refuse a zero part with [`NumError::Degenerate`], and a ratio outside 2^−32 to 2^32, or one whose reduced parts do not fit 64 bits, with [`NumError::OutsideDomain`]; nothing is rounded.
modules.job: Linear units: how many metres one unit of a coordinate reference system is, as an exact ratio.

method.text: exact rational arithmetic with Euclid's greatest common divisor (D. E. Knuth, *The Art of Computer Programming*, vol. 2, section 4.5.2, <https://www-cs-faculty.stanford.edu/~knuth/taocp.html>); the units as EPSG defines them: the international foot 0.3048 m and Clarke's foot 0.3047972654 m as PROJ's copy of the EPSG data gives them (<https://github.com/OSGeo/PROJ/blob/5fa31c29f0a806568ed7bc76c1a557604db4a804/data/sql/unit_of_measure.sql>), and the US survey foot by its definition, 1200/3937 m (EPSG's 12/39.37), which that copy stores only rounded, as 0.304800609601219241.

provenance.purpose: for the factors of the US survey foot (EPSG:9003), the international foot (EPSG:9002) and Clarke's foot (EPSG:9005). No code copied.

modules.cost: constant time, no allocation. A dot product is two or three checked `i128` multiplications, a 3D cross product six and a triple product nine; sums, differences and moved points are one checked `i128` addition and one range check per component.
guarantees: **Exact.** Integer arithmetic only. A dot or cross product is the exact integer, never a rounded one; its sign is an exact predicate.

**No overflow, no panic, the same result in every build profile.** Every integer step is a checked method (`checked_add`, `checked_sub`, `checked_mul`, `checked_neg`), never a native operator, so nothing depends on overflow checks being on. Products are proved to fit `i128` (|v| < 2^127) with room to spare, and a step the bit budget proves fits can only fail through a defect in this crate: it is then reported as [`NumError::BudgetExceeded`], never answered, so a defect can never pass for an exact result. For grid vectors every such result is `Ok`. Sums and differences of vectors, which can leave the vector range, return [`NumError::OutOfRange`].
**Deterministic.** The same integers on every target.
modules.job: Exact grid vectors: differences of grid points, with exact dot, cross and triple products.

method.text: these products are the building blocks of Shewchuk's determinant forms of the orientation predicates, evaluated exactly in fixed-width integers because the inputs are grid integers below 2^41, as `geom_num::predicate` does: J. R. Shewchuk, "Adaptive precision floating-point arithmetic and fast robust geometric predicates", *Discrete & Computational Geometry* 18 (1997), 305–363, <https://doi.org/10.1007/PL00009321>.

invariants: An exact mesh is exact data on the grid, decided by the same exact predicates as the rest of the kernel, with a proven bound on its distance from the shape it stands for (19).
The display copy is a different type that no operation accepts (19, 19.4).

The constrained Delaunay triangulation is unique: every tie breaks by one rule, so an incremental edit and a full rebuild give the same triangles (17.3, 19.14).
A flat map is committed and checked with exact predicates before it is used (16.4).

invariants: Every name is derived from the operation that made its entity and is hash-consed; nothing is named by position, a random suffix or a memory address (20.2).

Everything is sorted by name, never by the order an algorithm reported it; ordinals follow `NameScheme` v1's one fixed order, and an order that cannot be decided fails with `UndecidedOrder`, never a guess (20.2).
A reference resolves exactly, follows recorded history, or returns one value of the closed `Resolution` type with its reason; there is no geometric guessing (20.4).
History that was pruned resolves to `HistoryPruned`, never `Deleted` (20.4, 24.4).
Attribute classes are applied in one shared, pure step from the history; no operation writes attribute code of its own (8.4).
