provenance.purpose: the problem statements of `N_FitCrvApproxLstSq`, `N_FitCrvApproxKnots` and `N_FitCrvWeightedLstSq` (which end points are fixed, what is weighted, which constraints are allowed), solved by `geom-linalg`'s QR instead of `NLib`'s banded normal equations; constraints of any derivative order at any parameter; rank checked; every fit returns its certified error.

modules.cost: the curve operation's cost times the number of lines, each twice; the new net and its enclosure are allocated once, and each line's result once.
modules.does: each surface algorithm of the book is its curve algorithm applied to every column of the net (direction u) or every row (direction v), with the same coefficients, because the coefficients depend only on the knots of that direction. So [`Surface::insert_knot`], [`Surface::refine`], [`Surface::to_bezier`] and [`Surface::elevate`] run the curve kernels of `crate::insert`, `crate::bezier` and `crate::elevate` on each line of the net, in doubles for the result and in intervals for its certified rounding (`crate::ops`).
guarantees: **The same surface, within the reported deviation.** In real arithmetic these operations do not change the surface; the reported deviation bounds, with certainty, how far rounding moved it, by the partition of unity of the tensor-product basis.
**The curve operations' conditions, in the direction asked for.** Each refusal is the curve operation's, for the basis of that direction.
**Line by line, as the book.** Every line gets exactly the operations its curve would, in the same order, so a surface's line equals the curve operation on that line, bit for bit.
modules.job: Knot insertion, refinement, Bezier extraction and degree elevation of NURBS surfaces (The NURBS Book, algorithms A5.3, A5.5, A5.7 and A5.10).

method.text: Piegl and Tiller's algorithms A5.3, A5.5, A5.7 and A5.10 (The NURBS Book, 2nd ed., sections 5.2 to 5.5, <https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-59223-2>), which apply the curve algorithms A5.1, A5.4, A5.6 and A5.9 to the rows or columns of the net, as `NLib`'s surface tools do with its curve routines.

provenance.name: NVIDIA USD `BRep` `NLib`
notice: SPDX-FileCopyrightText: Copyright (c) 2026 NVIDIA CORPORATION & AFFILIATES. All rights reserved.
provenance.purpose: `NLib`'s surface insertion, refinement, Bezier extraction and elevation are rebuilt on the ported curve kernels applied line by line, in place of its separate surface loops, with the curve kernels' changes; every result carries its certified deviation.

modules.cost: linear in the number of control points; [`homs`] and [`split`] make one allocation each.
modules.does: a knot operation returns a [`Changed`] value: the new curve, curves or surface, and `deviation`, an upper bound on the distance between the new shape and the old one at every parameter of the domain. For an operation that is exact in real arithmetic (insertion, refinement, Bezier extraction, degree elevation) the deviation is only the rounding of the new control points; for an approximation (knot removal, degree reduction) it also holds the approximation's own error. [`rounding`] turns the interval run of an operation (`crate::arith`) into the rounding part: chapter 7's rule that a conversion "returns the NURBS, whether it is exact, and its maximum error".
guarantees: **Certified.** For a nonrational result with control points Q̂ whose exact counterparts are Q, the shapes differ by Σ `N_i`·(`Q̂_i` − `Q_i`), at most `max_i` |`Q̂_i` − `Q_i`| because the basis functions are not negative and sum to 1; the interval run bounds each |`Q̂_i` − `Q_i`| by the Euclidean norm of its interval's widths, rounded up. For a rational result, S = A / W and Ŝ − S = ((Â − A) − S·(Ŵ − W)) / Ŵ, so |Ŝ − S| ≤ (max |Δ(w·Q)| + `P_max`·max |Δw|) / min ŵ, where `P_max` bounds |S| (the largest distance of an input control point from the origin, by the convex hull property) and min ŵ is the smallest weight of the result, which bounds Ŵ below. Every step is computed in interval arithmetic and its upper bound taken.
**Refused, never weak.** A result with a weight that is not positive is [`NurbsError::Weight`]; a bound that is not finite is [`NurbsError::NotFinite`].
modules.job: What every knot operation returns, and the certified bound on how far its result lies from the curve or surface it was given.

method.text: the partition of unity and the convex hull property of B-splines (The NURBS Book, 2nd ed., Springer (1997), properties P2.4, P3.4 and P4.4, <https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-59223-2>), with interval arithmetic for every bound (`crate::arith`).

modules.cost: constant; nothing allocates.
modules.does: one algorithm serves 2D and 3D (chapter 7: "One curve family serves 2D and 3D"). Curves and surfaces are generic over the dimension D and store coordinates as `[f64; D]`; [`Point`] converts `geom-math`'s [`F2`] and [`F3`], and arrays, to and from those coordinates.
guarantees: **Exact both ways.** `coords` copies the components, and `from_coords` builds the point from them unchanged.
**Finite.** `from_coords` refuses a coordinate that is NaN or infinite with [`NurbsError::NotFinite`], as `geom-math`'s constructors do.
modules.job: The control points the NURBS algorithms accept and return: `geom-math`'s finite points in two and three dimensions, and plain coordinate arrays.

method.none: a trait and its implementations, which only copy components.

modules.cost: a product of degrees (p1, q1) and (p2, q2) takes O((p1 + 1)(p2 + 1)(q1 + 1)(q2 + 1)·D) interval operations; a rational normal patch three products of degree (3p − 1, 3q − 1); one allocation per result, charged first.
modules.does: the product of two polynomials in Bernstein form is a polynomial of the summed degree in Bernstein form, coefficient k being Σ C(p, i)·C(q, k − i)/C(p + q, k) · `a_i`·`b_(k−i)` (and the same in each direction of a patch). On that rule, [`BernsteinCurve::scaled_by`], [`BernsteinCurve::dot`] and [`BernsteinCurve::cross`] multiply curves exactly, as polynomials, and [`BernsteinPatch::scaled_by`], [`BernsteinPatch::dot`] and [`BernsteinPatch::cross`] patches. [`BernsteinPatch::normal`] builds the normal patch: `S_u` × `S_v` for a nonrational patch, and for a rational one S = A / W the polynomial N = W·(`A_u` × `A_v`) − `W_v`·(`A_u` × A) − `W_u`·(A × `A_v`) = W³·(`S_u` × `S_v`), a positive multiple of the normal. [`Surface::normal_patches`] gives the normal patch of every Bezier patch of a surface, and where a boundary edge of the surface is collapsed to one point (a pole, an apex) divides the factor that vanishes along it out of the patches on that edge, so the bound keeps the normals' directions instead of containing zero.
guarantees: **Exact products, enclosed.** Each coefficient of a product is computed in interval arithmetic from enclosures of its factors' exact coefficients and of the binomial ratios, so it encloses the exact coefficient of the exact product. The binomials come from Pascal's rule in intervals, exact while they stay below 2^53.

**The normal patch's sign and direction.** For a nonrational patch the normal patch's value at (u, v) is `S_u` × `S_v`; for a rational one W³ times it, W > 0. Either way the hull of its coefficients bounds the normals' directions (the Gauss map).

**Collapsed edges divided exactly.** An edge counts as collapsed only when the surface's stored control points along it are one point exactly: identical doubles, or for a rational surface identical quotients w·P / w, compared through exact products (`geom-num`'s `two_prod`). Then S along the edge is a constant, the partial derivative along it vanishes there, and so does N, exactly: N = v·T (edge v = v0), and T's coefficients are N's with the vanishing row dropped and row j scaled by q/(j + 1) (q/(q − j) for v = v1; likewise in u). Chapter 12.9 names this derivation as ours, to be proven in its build piece: the proof is these lines and `tests/bernstein.rs`.
**Typed refusals.** Products of rational forms are [`NurbsError::Rational`] (multiply their numerators and weight functions); factors on different domains are [`NurbsError::Domains`].
**Deterministic.** Sums in index order; no fused multiply-add.
modules.job: Symbolic products of Bernstein forms, and the normal patch of a surface with its collapsed edges divided out: the Gauss-map bound of chapter 12.6.

method.text: products of polynomials in Bernstein form (R. T. Farouki and V. T. Rajan, "Algorithms for polynomials in Bernstein form", *Computer Aided Geometric Design* 5(1) (1988), 1–26) as Piegl and Tiller use them for symbolic operators on NURBS (L. Piegl and W. Tiller, "Symbolic operators for NURBS", *Computer-Aided Design* 29(5) (1997), 361–368, <https://doi.org/10.1016/S0010-4485(96)00074-7>) and `NLib` implements them; the normal patch for Gauss-map bounds (T. W. Sederberg and R. J. Meyers, "Loop detection in surface patch intersections", *Computer Aided Geometric Design* 5(2) (1988), 161–171, <https://doi.org/10.1016/0167-8396(88)90029-5>).

provenance.name: NVIDIA USD `BRep` `NLib`
notice: SPDX-FileCopyrightText: Copyright (c) 2026 NVIDIA CORPORATION & AFFILIATES. All rights reserved.
provenance.purpose: translated to safe `no_std` Rust from `N_BezFuncMultiplyBezCrvMatrix`, `N_BezFuncMultiplyBezFunc`, `N_BezSrfFuncMultiply`, `N_BezCrossProduct`, `N_BezSrfCrossProduct` and `N_BezSrfDotProduct`, in interval arithmetic so every coefficient is certified; the binomial ratios from Pascal's rule in intervals instead of `NLib`'s table of 18 rows; the normal patch of rational patches and the division of collapsed edges are ours.

modules.cost: O(s·p²) operations for s spans to reduce, and an elevation and a refinement of the result in intervals to certify, O(s·p²) more; the candidate and the enclosures are allocated once each.
modules.does: [`Curve::reduce_degree`] walks the knot vector as Bezier extraction does (A5.6), reduces each Bezier piece from degree p to p − 1 (the book's equations 5.41 to 5.44: points solved from both ends, the middle one averaged for odd degree), and removes one copy of each knot again, averaging the two estimates where the removal sweeps cross with `NLib`'s weight λ = α / (α + β) (`NLib`'s `N_CrvReduceDegreeOnce`). Every distinct knot loses one copy, so knots of multiplicity 1 disappear. Whether the result is kept is not decided by `NLib`'s error estimate but certified: the candidate is raised back to degree p (A5.9) and the knots it lost are inserted (A5.4), both exact operations run in interval arithmetic, which gives the input's knots and an enclosure of the control points the candidate has on the input's basis; their largest distance from the input's points bounds the distance between the curves (`crate::remove`'s difference bound, with the rational form of `crate::ops`).
guarantees: **Within the tolerance, certified.** A returned curve differs from the input by at most the returned deviation everywhere in the domain, and the deviation is at most `tol`; the bound includes the rounding of every returned control point. Otherwise the result is [`NurbsError::OutsideTolerance`], also when a weight of the candidate is not positive.

**Where it applies.** The curve has degree 2 or more ([`NurbsError::Degree`]), is clamped ([`NurbsError::NotClamped`]) and has no interior knot repeated p + 1 times ([`NurbsError::Discontinuous`]), as A5.11 and `NLib` assume; the tolerance is finite and not negative ([`NurbsError::Tolerance`]).
**Budgeted.** The candidate and its certification are charged to the meter first.
modules.job: Degree reduction of NURBS curves (The NURBS Book, algorithm A5.11), certified: the curve of degree p − 1 is returned only when it provably lies within the tolerance of the input.

method.text: Piegl and Tiller's algorithm A5.11 with Bezier degree reduction by equations 5.41 to 5.44 (The NURBS Book, 2nd ed., section 5.6, <https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-59223-2>; L. Piegl and W. Tiller, "Algorithm for degree reduction of B-spline curves", *Computer-Aided Design* 27(2) (1995), 101–110, <https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-4485(95)92147-K>), as `NLib` implements it, certified by exact elevation and refinement in interval arithmetic (`crate::elevate`, `crate::insert`, `crate::arith`).

provenance.name: NVIDIA USD `BRep` `NLib`
notice: <https://github.com/NVIDIA-Omniverse/usd-brep/blob/c9c5979f04cea8c38213004d4f04df0dcfb40d05/source/SMLib/src/NL_Bezier.cpp>
SPDX-FileCopyrightText: Copyright (c) 2026 NVIDIA CORPORATION & AFFILIATES. All rights reserved.
provenance.purpose: translated to safe `no_std` Rust from `N_CrvReduceDegreeOnce`, `N_BezDegreeReduceCoefs` and `N_BezReduceDegree`; `NLib`'s error estimate (Bezier error terms and basis maxima from a numerical search) and its weight range are replaced by the certified bound above, so the square root of its odd-degree estimate is not needed; a new curve is returned with its deviation instead of a flag.

modules.cost: each removal takes O(n·D) operations to copy the points, O(p·D) to solve, and O(n + p²) in intervals to certify; at most min(times, multiplicity) removals are tried.
modules.does: [`Curve::remove_knot`] removes the knot u up to `times` times. Each removal solves for the new control points from both ends of the affected run, as A5.8 and `NLib`'s `N_CrvRemoveKnot` do (`P_i` = `α_i`·`Q_i` + (1 − `α_i`)·`Q_(i−1)` solved for Q), and where the two sweeps cross it averages their two estimates with `NLib`'s weight λ = α / (α + β). Whether a removal is kept is not decided from those formulas: the candidate curve is re-inserted (u put back as many times as it was removed, Boehm's algorithm) in interval arithmetic, which gives the input's knots and an enclosure of the control points the candidate has in the input's basis; the two curves differ by Σ `N_l`·(`P̃_l` − `P_l`) on that basis, so the largest enclosed |`P̃_l` − `P_l`| bounds their distance (with the rational form of `crate::ops`). A removal is kept only while that certified bound stays within the tolerance; the bound of the last removal kept is the deviation returned.
guarantees: **Within the tolerance, certified.** The returned curve differs from the input by at most the returned deviation everywhere in the domain, and the deviation is at most `tol`. The bound covers the removal's own change and the rounding of every new control point, because it is measured on the doubles returned.

**Never worse than asked.** Where `NLib`'s test can pass a knot whose true change exceeds the tolerance (its basis maxima come from a numerical search, and its rational test uses the input's weights), this one cannot; it may remove fewer knots than an uncertified test.

**Typed refusals.** A tolerance that is negative or not finite is [`NurbsError::Tolerance`]; u not an interior knot is [`NurbsError::KnotOutside`]; u repeated p + 1 times (where the curve may jump) is [`NurbsError::Discontinuous`]. A removal that would make a weight not positive is not kept.
**Budgeted.** Each attempt is charged to the meter before it is computed.
modules.job: Knot removal of NURBS curves (The NURBS Book, algorithm A5.8), certified: a knot is removed only while the curve provably stays within the tolerance asked for.

method.text: Tiller's knot removal (W. Tiller, "Knot-removal algorithms for NURBS curves and surfaces", *Computer-Aided Design* 24(8) (1992), 445–453, <https://doi.org/10.1016/0010-4485(92)90012-Y>) as Piegl and Tiller's algorithm A5.8 gives it (The NURBS Book, 2nd ed., section 5.4, <https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-59223-2>) and `NLib` implements it, with the change bounded through re-insertion and the partition of unity (properties P2.4 and P4.4 of the book) in interval arithmetic (`crate::arith`).

provenance.name: NVIDIA USD `BRep` `NLib`
notice: SPDX-FileCopyrightText: Copyright (c) 2026 NVIDIA CORPORATION & AFFILIATES. All rights reserved.
provenance.purpose: translated to safe `no_std` Rust from `N_CrvRemoveKnot`, one removal at a time; the decision to keep a removal uses a certified bound from re-insertion in interval arithmetic in place of `NLib`'s distance test with basis maxima from a numerical search, its rescaled tolerance for rational curves and its weight range; a new curve is returned with the deviation instead of being edited in place.

modules.cost: O(p²·D) interval operations per subdivision; a patch O(p·q·(p + q)·D); one allocation per row of coefficients.
modules.does: [`BernsteinCurve::restrict`] gives the Bernstein form of a piece over a sub-span [lo, hi] of its domain, and [`BernsteinPatch::restrict`] of a patch over a sub-box, by de Casteljau subdivision at the sub-span's ends, each a local parameter (t − a)/(b − a) enclosed in an interval. [`BernsteinCurve::value_at`] and [`BernsteinPatch::value_at`] give the homogeneous value and the weight at a parameter, the last point of a subdivision there.
guarantees: **Enclosures of the exact.** Subdivision is linear in the coefficients with weights 1 − s and s; computed with s an interval holding the exact local parameter, and every operation rounded outward, each new coefficient holds the exact coefficient of the exact sub-piece (inclusion monotonicity), so the convex hull bounds of `crate::bernstein` hold for the sub-span.
**Homogeneous.** Rational forms are cut with their weights as a last coordinate, so the weights of the result are the exact weights of the sub-piece's homogeneous form.
**Typed refusals.** A sub-span outside the domain, unordered, or a single value, is [`NurbsError::KnotOutside`]; a parameter outside it [`NurbsError::ParameterOutside`].
modules.job: Bernstein forms cut down to a sub-span and evaluated at a parameter, in interval arithmetic: the de Casteljau steps the kind contract's bounds and enclosures need (piece G60).

method.text: de Casteljau's algorithm and subdivision (The NURBS Book, 2nd ed., section 1.3 and algorithm A1.5, <https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-59223-2>), in interval arithmetic.

modules.cost: construction is linear in the control points and makes one allocation (two if rational). [`Surface::point`] takes O(p² + q² + p·q·D) operations; [`Surface::derivs`] O(p² + q² + du·dv·(p·q·D + du·dv·D)); neither allocates.
modules.does: a [`Surface`] holds two bases, one per parameter direction, and a net of (n + 1) × (m + 1) control points stored row by row (row i follows u, column j follows v), with weights if it is rational, in homogeneous form w·P as for curves. [`Surface::point`] sums, for each row of the p + 1 rows that matter, the q + 1 points against the v basis, then the rows against the u basis (A3.5, as `NLib` does it), and divides by the weights summed the same way for a rational surface (A4.3). [`Surface::derivs`] does the same with basis derivatives (A3.6) and applies Leibniz's rule to w·S = A for a rational surface (A4.4), for every order k ≤ du in u and l ≤ dv in v.
guarantees: **Well formed or refused.** A surface has exactly one control point (and one weight) per pair of basis functions, every coordinate finite, every weight positive and finite, and every weighted coordinate finite.

**Points.** A nonrational point is within `γ_(7p+7q+2)` · `Σ_i` `NU_i` `Σ_j` `NV_j`·|`P_ij`|; a rational one within `γ_(14p+14q+5)` times the same sum over |w·P| divided by Σ `NU_i` `NV_j` `w_ij`. Each inner sum carries `γ_(7q+1)`, and each product with a u basis value and the outer sum add `γ_(6p)` and p + 1 roundings.

**Underflow.** These bounds are relative, so where a product falls below 2^−1022 (gradual underflow) a rounding may also err by up to 2^−1075 absolutely: each bound gains n·2^−1074 for its count n of roundings (7p + 7q + 2 for a point, 7p + 7q + 6 or e below for a derivative); for a rational surface, whose weights are taken in the normal range, n·2^−1074·(1 + 1 / `Σ_i` `NU_i` `Σ_j` `NV_j`·`w_ij`) (piece G69).

**Derivatives.** A nonrational derivative is within `γ_(7p+7q+6)` · `Σ_i` `MU_(k,i)` `Σ_j` `MV_(l,j)`·|`P_ij`|. A rational one is within `γ_e` · `MS_(k,l)`, e = (D + 1)(14p + 14q + 2D + 12), where `MS` is A4.4's recurrence run on magnitudes (every subtraction an addition, with the magnitude sums in place of A and of the weight derivatives); each step of the recurrence adds the error of the sums, two products per term, its sums and subtractions and the division to the largest error of the lower orders, and a chain of steps from order (0, 0) has at most D of them. The value of order (0, 0) has the same bits as [`Surface::point`].

**Typed failures.** A parameter outside its domain is [`NurbsError::ParameterOutside`], a result that overflows [`NurbsError::NotFinite`], an order above [`MAX_DEGREE`] [`NurbsError::DerivativeOrder`].
**Deterministic.** Fixed summation order (v inside u, by increasing index), no fused multiply-add, no platform maths.
modules.job: NURBS surfaces in two and three dimensions: construction under chapter 24.7's rules, points and partial derivatives (The NURBS Book, algorithms A3.5, A3.6, A4.3 and A4.4).

method.text: Piegl and Tiller's algorithms A3.5, A3.6, A4.3 and A4.4 (The NURBS Book, 2nd ed., sections 3.4, 3.5 and 4.4 to 4.5, <https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-59223-2>), with `NLib`'s order of summation for points; the error bounds follow Higham (*Accuracy and Stability of Numerical Algorithms*, 2nd ed., SIAM (2002), chapter 3, <https://doi.org/10.1137/1.9780898718027>).

provenance.purpose: translated to safe `no_std` Rust from `N_SrfEvalPtImpl` and `N_SrfDerivs`, for any dimension D instead of `NLib`'s homogeneous 4D points with its "no z" and "no w" markers; derivatives summed in the same nested order as points (v inside u), where `N_ComputeDerivativeMatrixSpec` sums products of the two bases' derivatives in one double loop, so the value of order (0, 0) equals the point; rational derivatives by the book's A4.4 on the stored homogeneous points, where `NLib` forms rational basis derivatives against points divided by their weights; parameters outside the domains and orders above the maximum are typed errors; each overflow is checked.

errors.doc: A failure of the numbers layer (`geom-num`'s `NumError`), named and mapped by what it means for the operation (chapter 22).

kinds.doc: A coordinate would leave ±(2^40 − 1) grid steps of its frame's origin (`NumError::OutOfRange`).
kinds.name: OutOfRange

kinds.doc: The inputs are degenerate for a construction: collinear points for a plane, or three planes that do not meet in exactly one point (`NumError::Degenerate`).
kinds.name: Degenerate

kinds.doc: A value or a result was not finite: a pole, such as a division by zero or the logarithm of zero, or an overflow (`NumError::NotFinite`). Base kind `Degenerate`, decided by this piece: kernel values are bounded (coordinates within ±2^40 steps), so on valid input a computation leaves the finite doubles only at a singularity of the configuration, which is chapter 22's "degenerate for this operation"; an operation that reads a caller's number checks it first, and reports a non-finite one as its own `InvalidInput` detail.
kinds.name: NotFinite

kinds.doc: A maths function was asked for a value it does not have: the square root or logarithm of a negative number, the arcsine of a number beyond ±1 (`NumError::OutsideDomain`). Base kind `NoSolution`, decided by this piece: no real value exists, so no result meets the input, which is chapter 22's `NoSolution`; it is not a malformed input, because the argument was computed from valid ones.
kinds.name: OutsideDomain

kinds.doc: An interval division by an interval that contains zero (`NumError::DivisorContainsZero`). Base kind `Undecided`, decided by this piece: the enclosure cannot say whether the divisor vanishes, so the decision cannot be certified at this resolution; an exact zero is found by the exact predicates first, and is `Degenerate`.
kinds.name: DivisorContainsZero

kinds.doc: An interval square root of an interval with negative values in it (`NumError::NegativeSqrt`). Base kind `Undecided`, decided by this piece for the reason [`NumDetail::DivisorContainsZero`] gives: the enclosure cannot say whether the value is negative.
kinds.name: NegativeSqrt

kinds.doc: An empty interval was asked for: a lower bound above its upper bound (`NumError::EmptyInterval`). Base kind `Internal`, decided by this piece: the kernel builds intervals from bounds it computed, so an empty one is a defect; a range a caller gives is checked by the operation as its own input.
kinds.name: EmptyInterval

kinds.doc: A conversion between grid steps was asked to go the wrong way (`NumError::WrongDirection`). Base kind `Internal`, decided by this piece: the direction is chosen by kernel code, never by data, so going the wrong way is a defect.
kinds.name: WrongDirection

kinds.doc: An exact computation did not fit the width its proven bit budget gives it (`NumError::BudgetExceeded`). Only a defect can cause it, so its base kind is `Internal`, never `BudgetExceeded` (chapter 22).
kinds.name: BitBudget

kinds.doc: A certified bound would pass the ceiling it was checked against (`NumError::ToleranceExceeded`): the result would be less exact than accepted, so its base kind is `ExactnessNotAccepted`, never `ToleranceExceeded` (chapter 22).
kinds.name: BoundOverCeiling

kinds.doc: An enclosure needs a maths function whose error is not proven (`NumError::UnprovenMaths`). The wrapping operation names the function and the piece that adds its proof (chapters 12.16 and 22).
kinds.name: UnprovenMaths

errors.doc: The shared base of every error (chapter 22): one of a closed set, each kind defined once.

kinds.doc: An input breaks the operation's preconditions: it fails the checker, is malformed, or repeats a key. The caller can fix or replace the input.
kinds.name: InvalidInput

kinds.doc: A valid input is degenerate for this operation: a zero length, angle or radius, coincident anchors, a folded arc, a singular start. The caller can change the value it names.
kinds.name: Degenerate

kinds.doc: The input is valid, but no result meets it and the rules the caller set. The caller can change a value; the remedies give the nearest one that works.
kinds.name: NoSolution

kinds.doc: More than one result fits, and nothing given chooses between them. The caller can choose, or add what decides.
kinds.name: Ambiguous

kinds.doc: A decision the result needs can be neither made exactly nor certified at the data's own resolution. The caller can move things apart, close the gap explicitly, or take another route.
kinds.name: Undecided

kinds.doc: The result would be less exact than the caller accepted: a lower class, a certified bound past the accepted one, or a commit to the grid that would flip a decision. The caller can accept explicitly the class and bound it would reach, or make the change that keeps it exact.
kinds.name: ExactnessNotAccepted

kinds.doc: For Tolerant data only: an operation would need a larger tolerance than a Tolerant body carries, or healing would need to close a gap wider than `ε_heal` allows. The caller can heal first, or raise `ε_heal` up to its cap.
kinds.name: ToleranceExceeded

kinds.doc: A coordinate would leave ±(2^40 − 1) steps of its frame's origin. The caller can work in a frame placed at the overlap or on the lattice, split, or ask for a coarser step.
kinds.name: FrameRangeExceeded

kinds.doc: A deterministic work or logical-memory budget ran out. The caller can raise the budget, split the call, or ask for a preview.
kinds.name: BudgetExceeded

kinds.doc: The caller's cancellation token, or a deadline it set, stopped the operation. Not deterministic, so never logged or cached; there is nothing to do.
kinds.name: Cancelled

kinds.doc: The machine refused a large allocation. Not deterministic, so never logged or cached; there is nothing to do.
kinds.name: OutOfMemory

kinds.doc: No route exists yet for this input. The caller can take a route that exists, or wait for the build piece that adds one.
kinds.name: Unsupported

kinds.doc: An invariant broke: a bug, never a panic and never a success. The caller can report it, with what reproduces it.

invariants: `OpContext` holds no randomness and no clock that can affect a result (10.1).
`ErrorKind` is section 22's closed set of base kinds and is not `#[non_exhaustive]`; every `OpError` is built from its detail, so its kind always agrees with the detail's base kind (22).
A `NameId` is the 128-bit hash of the one canonical encoding of a `TopoName` under a versioned `NameScheme`; nothing is named by position, memory address or a random suffix (20.1, 20.2).

History records keep section 20.3's laws: a deleted input has no modified outputs, an input's generated and modified sets do not overlap, every output traces to an input or is generated, and histories compose across operations.
Batch items are keyed by the caller's stable key, never by position: an item's `OpPath` is the batch's `OpPath` plus that key (10.1).
Evidence carries only `geom-num` values, so this crate needs no geometry crate (27).
crates.job: The operation contract every crate shares: `OpContext`; the shared parts of `OpOutput` (history, names, exactness, diagnostics); the `OpError` base (`ErrorKind`, `Evidence`, `Remedy`); the exactness class, `OpId` and `OpPath`; the `NameId` value and its hashing under `NameScheme`, `TopoName`, `Role` and `PieceKey`; the history records of 20.3; the operation schema types.

modules.cost: linear in what is encoded; one allocation for the encoding.
modules.does: [`encode_exactness`], [`encode_evidence`], [`encode_diagnostic`] and [`encode_error`] write each in SKG's canonical CBOR (24.3), the parts chapter 28.13's canonical output hashes: an output's exactness class and diagnostics, or an error's kind, entities and evidence. `geom-test`'s canonical-output hasher combines them with the bodies, names and history (piece G96).
guarantees: **Values, never words.** A warning is its code, entities and evidence; an error its base kind, entities and evidence (28.13). Messages are plain words that may be reworded or translated, so they are never hashed, and two runs that fail the same way hash the same.

**One encoding per value**: integers in the shortest form, doubles as the shortest finite float that holds them, lists in the order the operation gave them (a deterministic operation fixes it), and names as 16-byte strings.
modules.job: Canonical encodings of what an operation reports besides its bodies: exactness classes, evidence, warnings and errors, so a result and a failure hash the same on every machine.

method.text: chapter 28.13's canonical output and 24.3's canonical CBOR (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/28-testing.md`, `projects/engines/geometry/architecture/24-file-format-exchange.md`).

modules.cost: linear in the bytes written, with one amortised `Vec` growth; [`Encoder::set`] and [`Encoder::sorted`] sort their elements, O(n log n) comparisons of their encodings. Memory is the output plus one small frame per open array or map. No recursion: open containers are an explicit stack.
modules.does: an [`Encoder`] writes exactly one CBOR data item (RFC 8949) from SKG's subset of values, in the core deterministic encoding of RFC 8949 section 4.2.1 with chapter 24.3's rules on top, and [`Encoder::finish`] hands it back as an [`Item`]. The subset is what chapter 24.3 stores: unsigned and signed integers (big ones as bignums), finite doubles, byte strings, UTF-8 text, arrays, maps keyed by unsigned integers (24.3's extension maps), sets and sorted lists (arrays sorted by the bytes of each element's encoding, 32.19), and coordinate columns as RFC 8746 typed arrays of little-endian `i64` (tag 79) and `f64` (tag 86). An [`Item`] can only be made by an encoder, so an item placed inside another ([`Encoder::item`], [`Encoder::set`], [`Encoder::sorted`]) is canonical by construction. Persistent names (G87) and the native format's records and decoder (G91, G92) are built on it, and never encode a value a second way.
guarantees: **One encoding per value.** Every head carries its argument in the fewest bytes (RFC 8949 sections 4.1 and 4.2.1); lengths are always definite; an integer is a bignum (tag 2 or 3) only when it does not fit major type 0 or 1, and then with no leading zero byte (24.3, RFC 8949 section 3.4.3); a double is written as the shortest of binary16, binary32 and binary64 that holds its value bit for bit, so −0.0 stays −0.0 (RFC 8949 section 4.1; 24.3); map keys are written in ascending order, which for unsigned keys is the bytewise order of their encodings that RFC 8949 section 4.2.1 asks for; a set's elements are sorted by their encodings' bytes, without repeats, and a sorted list's the same way with repeats kept (32.19).

**Only the subset, and only well-formed items.** NaN and the infinities are refused, as a double and inside an `f64` column (24.3); a map key that is not greater than the one before it, an item where a map wants its key, a key anywhere else, a second top-level item, a set with a repeat, and a finish before the item is whole are each refused with their own [`EncodeError`]. A refused call writes nothing and leaves the encoder as it was, so the caller can still finish the item correctly. An array or map closes as soon as it holds the items it declared, so the next item belongs to the container around it.

**The same bytes on every target.** The bytes depend only on the calls made: every step is integer and bit work on the value's own bits (`f64::to_bits`), with no float arithmetic, no hash-map order and no platform width beyond `usize` lengths, which fit `u64` on every target Rust supports.
**No panic.** Nothing here indexes, unwraps or overflows: lengths are counted with checked arithmetic and a length too large for the format is refused with [`EncodeError::TooLong`].
modules.job: Deterministic CBOR for SKG's subset: the one encoding every stored and hashed value has (24.3).

method.text: RFC 8949 (CBOR, IETF STD 94), sections 3 (the head and its argument), 3.4.3 (bignums), 4.1 (preferred serialization, shortest floats) and 4.2.1 (core deterministic encoding), <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8949>; RFC 8746 section 2 (typed arrays: tag 79 for little-endian `sint64`, tag 86 for little-endian binary64), <https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc8746>; IEEE 754-2019 section 3.4 for the binary16 and binary32 interchange formats the shortest-float test narrows to; and the kernel's rules in `projects/engines/geometry/architecture/24-file-format-exchange.md` (24.3) and `projects/engines/geometry/architecture/32-decisions.md` (32.19 and 32.20).

provenance.name: ciborium-ll
provenance.purpose: its choice of the shortest float that keeps a double's bits; used as a test oracle only.

modules.cost: a context is a path (one vector of labels) and a few machine words; making one and reading it never allocates beyond the path it is given.
modules.does: every operation has chapter 10.1's shape, `fn operation(ctx: &OpContext, input: &OpInput) -> Result<OpOutput, OpError>`. An [`OpContext`] carries the operation's [`OpPath`] (its permanent ID from the operation log, and the step or batch item it is), its [`Budget`] of work units and logical bytes (chapter 23.10), the caller's [`Cancel`], and its [`Precision`]: final, or a coarser preview the caller asked for (chapter 23.6).
guarantees: **No clock and no randomness.** An `OpContext` holds a path, a budget, a precision and the caller's cancellation, and nothing else; none of them reads a clock or draws a random number. A time limit reaches an operation only as the caller's [`Cancel`] (owner action G71, section 32.15), whose only effect is to stop it, and a stopped operation publishes nothing.
**Final unless asked.** A context is made with [`Precision::Final`]; only [`OpContext::with_precision`] asks for a preview.
**Shown as its value.** `Debug` prints the path, the budget, the precision and whether a cancellation is attached, never the cancellation's address or state.
modules.job: What every operation is given besides its input: which operation it is, its budgets, the caller's cancellation and the precision asked for.

method.text: chapter 10.1's operation contract and chapter 23.10's budgets and cancellation, as decided in owner action G71 (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/10-operations.md`, `projects/engines/geometry/architecture/23-performance.md`, section 32.15 of `projects/engines/geometry/architecture/32-decisions.md`).

modules.cost: constant; the details are a few machine words, and only [`OpErrorDetail::remedies`] allocates, the vector it returns.
modules.does: [`OpErrorDetail`] has one variant per family of details (chapter 22), and grows with the kernel: each operation family adds its own enum as a variant, as its piece lands. This module holds the two every operation can meet. [`RunDetail`] is a stop from `geom-run`: a budget that ran out, the caller's cancellation, a refused allocation, or a broken invariant of the helper. [`NumDetail`] is a failure of `geom-num`, wrapped by meaning rather than by name (chapter 22: "A crate's own error type never reaches a caller"). Every detail says its base kind through its `kind` function, which the map reads to list each detail with its base kind (chapter 26.3), and gives the remedies it knows.
guarantees: **One base kind per detail.** Each variant maps to exactly one [`ErrorKind`] in its `kind` function, written as a match the map reads; a family variant of [`OpErrorDetail`] takes the kind of the detail it holds.

**The numbers layer maps by meaning** (chapter 22, and the open question of section 31.7 that names this piece): an exact computation over its proven bit budget is a defect, so [`NumDetail::BitBudget`] is `Internal`, never `BudgetExceeded`; a certified bound over its ceiling is [`NumDetail::BoundOverCeiling`], `ExactnessNotAccepted`; a coordinate past the frame is `FrameRangeExceeded`; a degenerate construction is `Degenerate`; maths with no proven enclosure is `Unsupported`. The six section 22 left open are decided here, each with its reason on its variant: a value that is not finite is `Degenerate`; an argument outside a function's domain is `NoSolution`; an interval divisor that contains zero and the square root of an interval with negative values are `Undecided`; an empty interval and a grid-step conversion the wrong way are `Internal`.

**The helper's stops keep their meaning.** A budget failure keeps its `{ budget, kind, phase, used }` record, and a batch's total stays the batch's ([`RunDetail::BatchTotal`]), never cached as an item's result; cancellation and refused allocations stay `Cancelled` and `OutOfMemory`, which are never stored (chapter 23.10).
modules.job: Error details: each operation family's own typed failures, each mapped to one base kind; and the two the whole kernel shares, the parallel helper's stops and the numbers layer's failures.

method.text: chapter 22's shared base and per-operation detail, and its mapping of the numbers layer's errors (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/22-errors-queries-ai.md`), with chapter 23.10's budget and batch rules (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/23-performance.md`).

modules.cost: an error is one box holding its path, its message and three short vectors; making one allocates them, once. Errors are made only on failure, and the box keeps every operation's `Result` one pointer wide on the error side.
modules.does: an [`OpError`] is chapter 22's structured error, the same for people and for AI agents: `kind`, `detail`, `op`, `entities`, `at` (evidence), `message` and `remedies`. It is built from its detail ([`OpError::new`]), which fixes its kind, its first message and the remedies the detail knows; the operation then adds the entities it names, the values that explain it, a fuller message and the remedies only it knows.
guarantees: **The kind always agrees with the detail.** [`OpError::kind`] is the detail's base kind, read from the detail every time; nothing can set one without the other (chapter 22).
**Never empty of meaning.** Every error has a message in plain words, the detail's own until the operation gives a fuller one, and the remedies its detail knows.

**Additions keep their order.** Entities, evidence and remedies are kept in the order the operation gave them; a deterministic operation gives them in a deterministic order, so equal inputs give equal errors (chapters 21 and 28.13).
**Replayable unless stopped.** [`OpError::is_replayable`] is false exactly for `Cancelled` and `OutOfMemory`, which are never logged, stored or cached.
modules.job: The error every operation returns: its base kind, its own typed detail, where it happened, the entities and values involved, plain words, and what would make it succeed.

method.text: chapter 22's `OpError`, a closed base kind with an open, typed detail that the kind is read from (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/22-errors-queries-ai.md`).

modules.cost: a few machine words per value; nothing allocates.
modules.does: an [`Evidence`] is one named [`Value`]: a point, a coordinate, a length, a parameter, an exactness class and its bound, or a count, such as "largest radius: 4.2 mm" or "station: 3.40 m" (chapter 22's `at: Vec<Evidence>`). Values are `geom-num` values only, so this crate needs no geometry crate (chapter 27, "Who owns what").
guarantees: **Numbers layer values only.** Every [`Value`] holds `geom-num` values or plain integers, in the kernel's own units: grid steps with their step, parameters as certified intervals.
**A length always carries its step.** A count of steps means nothing alone (64 steps of `Q0` are 10 µm, of `Q1` 0.4 µm), so [`Value::Length`] holds both, as an exactness bound does.
**Plain words.** `Display` writes the name and the value, a length with its step, so a message can be read without the code.
modules.job: Evidence: the values an error or a warning points at, each named for what it is.

method.none: the values chapter 22's `Evidence` carries, written as data (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/22-errors-queries-ai.md`), in `geom-num`'s own types.

modules.cost: linear in the message, one compression per 64-byte block; the state is a fixed 112 bytes or so, and nothing is allocated.
modules.does: [`Sha256`] takes a message piece by piece and gives its 32-byte digest, or the digest's leftmost 16 bytes; [`sha256`] and [`sha256_128`] hash one buffer. The owner chose SHA-256 for both uses (owner action G79, 32.20): a content ID is algorithm 1, the whole digest of a record's payload (24.2), and a `NameId` is the leftmost 128 bits of the digest of a name's domain prefix and canonical bytes (32.19, piece G87). The hashing itself is the `RustCrypto` project's `sha2` crate, the implementation 32.20 approves, at the release `Cargo.lock` pins.
guarantees: **The digest FIPS 180-4 defines.** For every message, in whatever pieces it is written, the digest is the standard's SHA-256: the tests check NIST's published test vectors (the Cryptographic Algorithm Validation Program's byte-oriented short and long messages and its Monte Carlo chain, and FIPS 180-4's examples), whole and written in pieces.
**The 128-bit cut is the digest's first 16 bytes**, the leftmost 128 bits NIST SP 800-107 section 5.1 allows a truncated SHA-256 to keep, and nothing else.

**The same digest on every target and build.** `sha2` uses a processor's SHA instructions where it has them and portable code elsewhere, WebAssembly included; each computes the one function FIPS 180-4 defines, so the choice changes speed, never bits (its audit, cited in `deny-no-std.toml`, reads each path).

**No panic, no `unsafe` here.** Writing and finishing never panic, and this module has no `unsafe` code. The crates' own `unsafe` code (`sha2`'s processor backends and its software path's table read, `block-buffer`'s buffer, `hybrid-array`'s array casts and `cpufeatures`' processor probe) is read site by site in their audit.
modules.job: SHA-256, the kernel's one hash: for content IDs and, cut to 128 bits, for persistent names.

method.text: NIST FIPS 180-4, *Secure Hash Standard* (2015), <https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/fips/180-4/upd1/final>, computed by the `sha2` crate (`RustCrypto`, MIT OR Apache-2.0, a dependency, not a port); the cut follows NIST SP 800-107 Rev. 1 section 5.1, <https://csrc.nist.gov/pubs/sp/800/107/r1/final>. The owner's choice and its reasons are `projects/engines/geometry/architecture/32-decisions.md` (32.19 and 32.20). The test vectors are NIST's, <https://csrc.nist.gov/projects/cryptographic-algorithm-validation-program/secure-hashing>.

modules.cost: making a history sorts its records and changes, `O(n log n)` in their number; a check and a composition are `O(m log m)` in the number of relation pairs, on sorted vectors searched by bisection, never hashed sets. Recursion: none.
modules.does: a [`History`] holds one [`Record`] per output entity, sorted by name, saying whether the output passed through unchanged, was modified from inputs, generated from inputs (or from nothing) in a role, split from one input by cutting faces, or merged from several (chapter 20.3); the set of inputs it deleted; and the [`TopologyChange`]s of chapter 13.14 it made. [`History::check`] tests the laws every operation's history keeps. [`Relations`] is the same history as three relations between inputs and outputs (modified, generated, deleted), the form in which histories compose ([`Relations::then`]) across a chain of operations.
guarantees: **Sorted by name, never by report order.** Records are in output-name order, each output once; changes and every set in them are in name order (20.2). Two operations that report the same history in different orders hold equal histories.

**The four laws hold** for every history and composition. Law 1 (a deleted input has no modified output) and law 3 (every output traces to an input or is generated, and every input a record names is an input of the operation) are checked ([`History::check`], [`Relations::check`]). Law 2 (an input's generated and modified outputs do not overlap) holds by construction: a history gives each output one origin, and composition takes the modified pairs out of the generated ones. Law 4 (histories compose, keeping the others) is [`Relations::then`]; `geom-test`'s history kit checks laws 2 and 4 on generated chains.

**Every topology change is recorded in the history** (13.14): a vanished face or an overshoot removed is deleted, faces merged are one `Merged` output of exactly those faces, and a face added is generated in the role the change gives.

**Composition is associative and keeps the laws.** Composing follows the method note's three rules, with one more where a part reaches an input by both relations through a chain: there it is modified, not generated, because it carries on a part of that input (the "two paths" case, decided here and written into 20.3). Grouping a chain either way gives the same relations.
modules.job: History: how every output of an operation relates to its inputs, which inputs it removed and what topology changes it made; the four laws of chapter 20.3; and how histories compose.

modules.cost: IDs and names are sixteen bytes, copied by value. A path holds its labels in one vector; a child path copies its parent's labels once and adds one, so it allocates once.
modules.does: an [`OpId`] is the permanent 128-bit ID of one operation, set when the operation is authored and kept in the operation log forever (architecture chapter 20.1). An [`OpPath`] adds sub-step labels to it: a [`Label::Step`] named by the operation, or a [`Label::Key`], the stable key the caller gives a batch item (chapter 10.1), so an item's path is the batch's path plus that key and never its position. A [`NameId`] is the 128-bit value of a persistent name (chapter 20.1), held here as its sixteen bytes so that errors and diagnostics can name the entities they concern; computing one from a `TopoName` under `NameScheme v1` is piece G87's.
guarantees: **Nothing is named by position or by chance.** An [`OpPath`] holds only the [`OpId`] and the labels given to it, in the order given; a batch item's label is the caller's key, so adding an item to a batch changes no other item's path.

**Every label hashes the same everywhere.** A step label is 1 to [`STEP_MAX`] bytes of printable ASCII or spaces, not starting or ending with a space. ASCII text is in Unicode Normalization Form C under every Unicode version, so a step label meets section 32.19's rule for text hashed into a name without a normalisation table.

**Order is byte order.** IDs, names and paths compare by their bytes and labels (a step before a key at the same depth, then by bytes), the order section 32.19 sorts names in: the order of their canonical encodings, which for sixteen-byte strings is the order of the bytes.

**Shown as their value.** `Debug` and `Display` print an ID or a name as 32 lowercase hexadecimal digits, the most significant byte first, and a path as its ID followed by its labels; nothing prints an address.
modules.job: Operation identity: an operation's permanent ID, the path to one of its steps or batch items, and the value of a persistent name.

modules.does: [`ErrorKind`] is the shared base of every [`OpError`](crate::OpError). Generic code (the command layer, the MCP tools, AI agents, the test harness) can handle any error by its kind alone; each operation's own detail says the rest (chapter 22). Each kind's doc comment is its definition and what the caller can do, which the map lists as the base of the error catalogue (chapter 26.3).
guarantees: **Closed.** `ErrorKind` is not `#[non_exhaustive]`, so callers handle every kind; a new failure is a new detail, never a new kind (chapter 22). [`ErrorKind::ALL`] lists every kind once, in chapter 22's table order.

**Only two kinds are not replayable.** [`ErrorKind::Cancelled`] and [`ErrorKind::OutOfMemory`] depend on the caller and the machine, so they are never logged, stored or cached; every other kind is a deterministic answer (chapters 22 and 23.10).
**Named as chapter 22 names them.** [`ErrorKind::name`] is the kind's name in chapter 22, for logs, schemas and the map.

modules.cost: encoding a name allocates its bytes once and one small item per element of each set; hashing is one SHA-256 pass over at most a few hundred bytes. The NFC check is linear in a role name's length. Recursion: none; a name refers to other names by `NameId`, never by nesting.
modules.does: a [`TopoName`] says how an entity was made: created by an operation step in a [`Role`], split from one input by cutting faces ([`PieceKey`]), merged from several, bounded by the faces it lies between and those that end it, or, where entities would still collide, the [`Ordinal`]-th of a [`TopoName::Weak`] group (chapter 20.2). [`TopoName::encode`] writes its canonical bytes and [`TopoName::id`] hashes them to the 128-bit [`NameId`] (32.19): the first 16 bytes of SHA-256 over [`NAME_SCHEME_V1_PREFIX`] and those bytes. Sets of names are [`NameSet`]s, sorted lists [`NameList`]s, both in name order. A [`Stamp`] fills in the names a name-free run made with its path and input names left blank (23.8).
guarantees: **One name, one encoding, one `NameId`.** A `TopoName` can only hold sets without repeats, lists in order, ordinals with `n < of` and role names in Normalization Form C, so its encoding is a pure function of the name, and so is its `NameId`, on every target.

**Text is NFC under Unicode 18.0.0** (32.19): a role name not in Normalization Form C is refused when the role is made, never normalised behind the caller's back. Step labels are printable ASCII ([`crate::id`]), which is NFC under every Unicode version.

**A stamped name is the name a run with those names would make.** [`Stamp::name`] writes the real path and names where the blanks stood and hashes the result the usual way, and it refuses a name that refers to anything it has not stamped.
**Names never collide with other hashes.** The prefix `SKG NameScheme v1` and a zero byte go before every name's bytes, so no name hashes like a content ID (32.20) or a later scheme.

modules.cost: [`Charge::charge`] is constant: at most two charges on the meter whatever the count. [`reserve`] is one charge and one allocation. [`OpContext::run`] adds one meter and one read of the cancellation to the body.
modules.does: every operation runs inside the budgets its [`OpContext`] carries (chapter 23.10). A [`Charge`] is one line of an operation version's charge schedule: in one phase, so many work units per counted thing (an input face, a pair of overlapping boxes, a Newton step), fixed by the operation's version and listed in its schema (chapter 26.2). [`Charge::charge`] charges a count of them exactly as a serial loop charging one at a time would. [`reserve`] reserves room for a number of values: their logical bytes on the meter first, then the real allocation, fallibly. [`OpContext::run`] runs an operation's body with a meter over the context's budget and cancellation, and publishes its result only if the meter never stopped and no cancellation was asked for by the time it returned.
guarantees: **Counts a serial loop would make.** Charging `count` things at `units` each passes exactly when charging them one by one would, and on failure the meter has used exactly what that loop had used up to and including the first thing over the cap: never more, never a saturated total. So a `BudgetExceeded` is the same on every target, thread count and build, and may be stored (chapter 23.10).

**Large reservations are fallible.** [`reserve`] charges the logical bytes first, so a budget failure comes before any allocation and is the same everywhere; a count the target cannot address, or an allocation the machine refuses, stops the meter with `OutOfMemory`, which is never stored. Nothing aborts.

**A stopped operation publishes nothing.** [`OpContext::run`] returns the body's result only when the body succeeded, its meter never stopped, and a last read of the caller's cancellation finds no request; otherwise it returns the stop as an error at the context's path. A body that ignored a stop cannot publish a result past it.
modules.job: Running an operation inside its context's budgets: the charge schedule, fallible reservations, and a run that publishes nothing once stopped.

modules.does: an [`OpSchema`] is chapter 22's description of one operation: its name, version and family; its inputs and outputs, each with a type and a unit; the roles it names; the errors it can return, each detail with its base kind and its data; the warnings it can give; the exactness classes it can return; its charge schedule; whether it has a batch entry; and an example. The types here are the vocabulary; the facade, `engine-geometry`, holds every operation's schema as data and generates from them (piece G100).
guarantees: **Constant data.** Every schema type is made of `&'static` strings and slices, so a schema is a constant, compiled in, with no allocation and nothing to initialise.
**Errors name their base kind.** An [`ErrorSpec`] gives each detail its [`ErrorKind`], as chapter 22 asks every error table and schema to.
**Classes without bounds.** A schema states which [`Class`]es its operation can return; the bound is a property of each result, and [`Class::of`] reads the class of one.

invariants: It only runs tasks: it implements `geom-run`'s `Pool` trait, and the fixed chunks, ordered results, ordered errors and order-free combines are the helper's, so every result is the same bits with this pool, on any number of threads, as with no pool at all (23.4, 21).

Every task it is handed runs exactly once, on any thread and in any order, and the pool is re-entrant: a task may call the helper again without blocking a thread, so one pool serves a program's per-element work and an operation's inner work (23.4).
It never panics, except to pass on a task's panic (23.4).
In a browser it starts Web Workers only where shared memory is allowed; elsewhere the kernel runs serially, with the same answer (23.4, 29.4).

It is the one `geom-*` crate that ships and may use `std`, because threads need it (the development crates use it too, and never ship); it still forbids unsafe code and carries `geom-num`'s lint posture (27).

The only published crates it may name are rayon and, for Web Workers, wasm-bindgen-rayon, each by its row of section 29.4. It names rayon, on native targets only ([`native`], piece G33); wasm-bindgen-rayon waits for piece G456, and until then WebAssembly runs serially.

modules.cost: one scope and one spawned job per task, each a small heap allocation inside rayon, and the pool's threads, started once when it is built and stopped when it is dropped.
modules.does: [`Rayon`] owns a `rayon::ThreadPool` of a fixed number of threads and implements [`Pool`]: [`Pool::run_all`] spawns every task into one scope of that pool and returns when all of them have finished. The helper (`geom_run::Exec::with_pool`) decides everything else: the fixed chunks, the order results are read in, the lowest-numbered failure, so every answer is the serial executor's, bit for bit, whatever the pool does (23.4).
guarantees: **Every task runs exactly once**, on some thread of the pool, in any order: each is spawned once into the scope, and the scope returns only after every spawned job has finished.

**Re-entrant.** A task may call the helper again with the same pool. The nested scope runs on the worker thread that opened it, and while it waits that thread runs other jobs of the pool, rayon's work stealing, instead of blocking; so a nested call makes progress on any number of threads, one included.

**No panic of its own.** `run_all` panics only to pass on a task's panic, after every task has finished: rayon's scope catches a job's panic and resumes it when the scope ends. Building a pool reports a failure to start its threads as [`PoolError`], never a panic.

**The thread count is the caller's.** It is fixed when the pool is built and never read by the helper, whose chunks do not depend on it (23.4); rayon's own environment variable (`RAYON_NUM_THREADS`) is not consulted, because the count is set explicitly.
modules.job: rayon's work-stealing pool behind `geom-run`'s `Pool` trait, for native targets.

method.text: rayon's scoped spawning, `ThreadPool::in_place_scope` and `Scope::spawn`, whose documented contract is that the scope returns when every job spawned into it, and every job those spawned, has completed, and that a panic in a job is propagated when the scope ends (<https://docs.rs/rayon/1.12.0/rayon/struct.ThreadPool.html#method.in_place_scope>), over its work-stealing scheduler, after Blumofe and Leiserson, "Scheduling Multithreaded Computations by Work Stealing", Journal of the ACM 46(5), 1999 (`doi:10.1145/324133.324234`). rayon's audit is `projects/kit/notes/G33-rayon-audit.md`.

modules.cost: for n items, at most n calls of the function, each with a fresh meter, and one read of the cancellation every [`POLL_EVERY`](crate::POLL_EVERY) items of each chunk. Room for a chunk's results is reserved when the chunk starts, since every item has a result, and the n results are gathered in the order the items run; the items past the crossing that never ran get copies of the one failure. On a pool, at most one wave of chunks past the crossing is run. With a total, add the key sort (`crate::sort`: O(n log n) comparisons, each calling `key` twice, and two buffers of n index–reference pairs, the first kept while the items run), and n slots and the n results again to put the results back in item order.

The result has exactly one entry per item, in item order. A broken count is [`Interrupted::Internal`], never a short or misplaced result.

method.text: the lowest-index rule of rayon's `find_first`, which returns the first match in input order however the work was split (<https://github.com/rayon-rs/rayon/blob/ee0a00bdb1ab039e178a215ad5712fb7fa58e58f/src/iter/mod.rs#L1675-L1680>), applied to failures, and chapter 22's error kinds and remedies.

provenance.purpose: for the lowest-index rule of `find_first`, which this crate applies to failures. No code copied.

modules.cost: for n items in c chunks, [`map`](Exec::map), [`try_map`](Exec::try_map), [`find_first`](Exec::find_first) and [`filter_ordered`](Exec::filter_ordered) make at most n calls of the function, each with a fresh meter of a few words, and read the cancellation once per [`POLL_EVERY`](crate::POLL_EVERY) items of each chunk; they allocate their result as items run and, on a pool, the bookkeeping of one wave (`crate::pool`). [`map_each`](Exec::map_each) costs the same, with one result per item, plus a sort by key when the batch has a total (`crate::batch`). [`scan_exclusive`](Exec::scan_exclusive) makes 2n + c additions; [`count_then_fill`](Exec::count_then_fill) is two phases and a scan (`crate::scan`); [`sort_stable`](Exec::sort_stable) makes O(n log n) comparisons and holds 2n index–reference pairs (`crate::sort`). A call made inside an item costs what it costs at its own level, and is charged to the item's meter.
guarantees: Every answer is decided by a serial walk over chunk results in index order (`crate::phase`; for a batch's total, in key order, `crate::batch`), so it cannot depend on the pool, the thread count or the order chunks finished in.

Every allocation the helper makes that grows with the input is fallible, so a refused one is [`RunError::OutOfMemory`], never an abort; and a phase whose items may stop early reserves room only as its items run (amortised doubling, so at most about twice what they need), never for the whole input up front.
No `unsafe`, no panics, no recursion, no lock, no atomic counter.
modules.job: The helper: the one way kernel code spreads work over threads (architecture chapter 23.4).

method.text: the deterministic parallel helper of chapter 23.4, after rayon's indexed parallel iterators, which keep input order when collecting and report the first match in input order (<https://github.com/rayon-rs/rayon/blob/ee0a00bdb1ab039e178a215ad5712fb7fa58e58f/src/iter/mod.rs#L1675-L1680>), but without rayon's unordered `sum`, `reduce` and `fold`, whose grouping is unspecified (evidence note 05, section 7); fixed-size chunks as in the chunk-size form of OpenMP's worksharing-loop `schedule` clause (OpenMP API 5.2, section 11.5.3, <https://www.openmp.org/spec-html/5.2/openmp.html>); and thread-count determinism tested as Rapier tests it (<https://github.com/dimforge/rapier/blob/475caa3ff4646fd9a796b67d14116256f4962bc7/crates/rapier3d/tests/thread_count_determinism.rs#L274-L295>).

modules.cost: a meter is a few machine words and never allocates. Each charge or reservation is one `u128` addition and comparison, plus one call of the caller's [`Cancel::requested`] every [`POLL_EVERY`] charges; [`WorkMeter::poll`] makes that call at once.
guarantees: A meter that has not stopped has used no more than its cap of either kind.
A stop is never undone, and the first stop is the one kept.
Cancellation is read every [`POLL_EVERY`] charges, counted from the meter's creation, and whenever [`WorkMeter::poll`] is called: fixed points, whatever the timing.
modules.job: The work meter: counts work units and logical bytes against a cap, and polls the caller's cancellation at fixed intervals (architecture chapter 23.10).

method.text: fuel metering with periodic interruption checks, as Wasmtime separates fuel (counted, deterministic) from epoch interruption (polled at fixed points, not deterministic) (<https://docs.rs/wasmtime/50.0.0/wasmtime/struct.Config.html#method.consume_fuel>), and cooperative cancellation polled at fixed points as in .NET's `CancellationToken` (<https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/dotnet/standard/threading/cancellation-in-managed-threads>).

modules.cost: per item, one fresh meter (a few words, no allocation), one call of the function and, for a value kept, an amortised push onto its chunk's list; per chunk, one task and one read of the cancellation every [`POLL_EVERY`] items. The walk appends each chunk's list to the result in index order, so a kept value is moved twice. Nothing else is allocated but the pool's wave bookkeeping (`crate::pool`).
guarantees: Every item runs under a fresh meter capped at R, so an item's verdict never depends on the other items or on how they were chunked.
The meter, not the item's return value, says whether an item stopped.
Results are gathered in index order; a chunk result missing from a wave is computed on the calling thread, so the walk never skips one.
modules.job: The engine under every helper call: run a phase's items chunk by chunk, then decide the answer as a serial loop would.

method.text: the serial-equivalence rule of chapter 23.4 ("Ordered results", "Ordered errors": the error reported is the lowest-numbered failure, as in rayon's `find_first`, <https://github.com/rayon-rs/rayon/blob/ee0a00bdb1ab039e178a215ad5712fb7fa58e58f/src/iter/mod.rs#L1675-L1680>) and the phase rule of chapter 23.10.

modules.cost: a plan is one machine word. [`ChunkPlan::count`], [`ChunkPlan::chunk`] and each step of [`Chunks`] are a fixed number of integer operations; nothing allocates.
guarantees: Every chunk holds at least one item; only the last chunk of a problem may hold fewer than the chunk size.
Chunks are contiguous, in index order, and together cover every item exactly once.
No arithmetic here can overflow, whatever the length and size, including `usize::MAX`.
modules.job: Chunk plans: where a problem of a given size is cut into chunks.

method.text: fixed-size static chunking, the boundaries of Rust's own [`slice::chunks`] (<https://doc.rust-lang.org/core/primitive.slice.html#method.chunks>) and of the chunk-size form of OpenMP's worksharing-loop `schedule` clause (OpenMP API 5.2, section 11.5.3, <https://www.openmp.org/spec-html/5.2/openmp.html>). The tests check the boundaries against `slice::chunks` for every size and length they try.

modules.cost: a phase of c chunks runs in at most 7 + ⌈c / `WAVE_MAX`⌉ waves (six doublings from `WAVE_FIRST` reach `WAVE_MAX`). Each wave of w chunks costs two lists of w entries (the tasks and the handles passed to the pool) and one barrier; the slots of the current wave, each a chunk's payload and output, are the only other storage. With no pool there is no list and no barrier: each chunk runs just before it is read.
guarantees: Whatever a pool does, the answer is right. A task run twice writes its slot once (a filled slot is skipped); a task never run is run on the calling thread when its result is read. Only a panic inside the pool escapes, and pools must not panic.
Results are read in index order, never in the order tasks finished.
modules.job: Threads come from the caller: the [`Pool`] trait, and how the helper hands a pool its work.

method.text: the superstep of Valiant's bulk-synchronous parallel model ("A bridging model for parallel computation", Communications of the ACM 33(8), 1990, <https://doi.org/10.1145/79173.79181>): independent work, a barrier, then a serial step that reads the results. No atomic counter, lock or shared mutable state is used; each task writes only its own slot.

modules.cost: for n counts in c chunks, `scan_exclusive` makes n checked additions to sum the chunks, c to turn the sums into bases and n to write the offsets; it reads the cancellation once per chunk in each pass and allocates the n offsets and the c bases. `count_then_fill` adds a count phase and a fill phase (n calls each, as in `crate::phase`) and room for the n counts. Each item's outputs are made in a buffer of exactly its count, with one `U::default()` per output, then moved onto its chunk's outputs and those onto the result.
guarantees: Offsets are exact. A total past `usize::MAX` is [`RunError::OutOfMemory`]: no result of that size can exist on this target, and the limit differs between 32-bit and 64-bit targets, so the failure is never stored.
`count_then_fill` gives each item a slice of exactly the length it counted, so no item can write outside its own range.
modules.job: Exclusive prefix sums of counts, and `count_then_fill`: how new entities get their indices.

method.text: the parallel scan in its blocked form, for fewer processors than elements (sum each block, scan the block sums, then scan within each block from its base), and its use to give each element its output positions, as in Blelloch, "Prefix Sums and Their Applications" (Technical Report CMU-CS-90-190, Carnegie Mellon University, 1990; the 1993 book-chapter version is at <https://www.cs.cmu.edu/~guyb/papers/Ble93.pdf>).

modules.cost: for n items in chunks of s, at most n · (⌈log₂ s⌉ + ⌈log₂ ⌈n / s⌉⌉) comparisons, so O(n log n), each calling `key` twice; two buffers of n (index, reference) pairs and the result of n indices; one read of the cancellation per chunk and per merge.
guarantees: Every merge writes each element of its two runs exactly once into a destination of exactly their combined length, so the result is always a permutation of the indices.
No recursion: every loop is bounded by the number of items.
modules.job: `sort_stable`: the stable sorted order of items by a total key, the same whatever the chunks.

method.text: bottom-up two-way merge sort (Knuth, The Art of Computer Programming, volume 3, 2nd edition, 1998, section 5.2.4, "Sorting by merging", straight two-way merging; the book's page is <https://www-cs-faculty.stanford.edu/~knuth/taocp.html>), first within chunks, then across them. Written here rather than taken from `core`'s sorts so that nothing allocates infallibly and no comparison, even of an `Ord` that breaks its contract, can make the helper panic.

invariants: Never moves fixed, reference or model geometry (15.18).
Never drops, relaxes or reorders a constraint silently, and never returns a partly solved sketch as a success (15.18).
Constraints refer to entities by persistent name, never by position (15.14, 15.18).
Convergence is measured in grid steps and budgets in work, not time; running out returns `BudgetExceeded` or `Cancelled`, never a best-so-far answer (15.6).
Never flattens arcs, ellipses or splines to solve them, and never uses hand-typed or finite-difference derivatives or platform maths (15.18).
crates.job: The constraint solver, in 2D and 3D.

modules.cost: [`fix_entity`] is linear in the sketch's variables and [`offset_chain`] in its pieces. No recursion.
modules.does: [`fix_entity`] gives the constraints that hold a whole entity at its values, and [`offset_chain`] the ones that tie each piece of a chain of lines and arcs to its offset copy: parallel and a distance apart for a line, concentric and a radius apart for an arc (chapter 15.2).
guarantees: **Plain constraints.** A macro returns constraints a caller could write by hand, and changes nothing, so a refusal leaves the sketch as it was.
**Replayable.** Keys run up from the caller's `first_key`, in the pieces' order, so one replay authors one set of ids.
**One distance.** Every piece of an offset takes one [`Amount`], so changing a chain's distance is a change of value (chapter 15.7).
modules.job: Authoring macros: the plain constraints a named operation writes for its caller.

method.text: section 15.2's offset chains and section 15.3's fixing (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/15-sketches.md`).

modules.cost: [`Assembly::new`] sorts the Jacobian's entries once; [`Assembly::evaluate_at`] is linear in the rows, with no allocation. No recursion.
modules.does: a kind implements [`Residual`]: its residual function, a length that is zero exactly when the constraint holds, and the part of its inputs where it has no derivative. Its derivatives come from running that one function on dual numbers (`geom_num::dual`), never from a second text. A kind's inputs are [`Slot`]s: a sketch variable, or a constant, such as a dimension's value or the characteristic length of an angle, which carries no derivative. A dimension given as a named scalar is the same kind with a variable in that slot. [`Assembly::new`] lays out the rows of the driving constraints and of each arc's two ends, in authoring order, and the Jacobian's stored entries. [`Assembly::evaluate`] then fills the residuals and the Jacobian, in the variables the solver sees: each divided by its power of two, so each column is multiplied by it. It checks the inputs against each singular set first.
guarantees: **Derivatives are generated.** A Jacobian entry is the dual number's, and tests hold it to central differences of the same residual, on every kind (chapter 15.4).

**Every residual is a length, with a gradient near one.** A distance's gradient has length one at its solution; an angle's or an incidence's is scaled by a characteristic length of its lines, a power of two fixed at the start, so one tolerance serves every constraint.
**Smooth forms.** A distance d uses (|PQ|² − d²) / 2d, a polynomial in the points. Square roots appear only in a point's distance from a line, and a sweep's length.

**Singular sets are declared.** [`Residual::singular`] is checked before differentiating, and an input on one is [`SketchError::Degenerate`], naming the constraint. The remedy of section 15.4, a perturbation derived from keys, is the solver's (G222).

**The rows are structure alone.** The Jacobian's pattern depends only on which items a sketch has. [`Assembly::rescale`] reads values, once, at the start of a solve; those lengths then stay fixed through it, so the residuals are one function of the variables.
**Deterministic.** Rows run in authoring order, and a NaN anywhere is [`SketchError::Numeric`] from the operation that made it.
modules.job: Equations: each constraint kind's residual, written once over [`Scalar`], its singular set, and the assembly of a sketch's residuals and Jacobian.

method.text: section 15.4 (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/15-sketches.md`), on the forward mode of `geom_num::dual`; each residual is elementary coordinate geometry, H. S. M. Coxeter, *Introduction to Geometry*, 2nd ed., Wiley (1969), <https://archive.org/details/introductiontoge0000coxe>, chapter 1; the angle between two vectors as a rotated cross product, which has no square root and no branch.
