modules.cost: adding an item costs a binary search and a move of the items after it, nothing when items arrive in order; O(n) memory. No recursion.
modules.does: a [`Sketch`] holds a plane, its [`Entity`]s and its [`Constraint`]s, each named by an [`ItemId`], the sequence number and key the caller stores with it. Everything is kept sorted by that id, older first, so plan order, factorisation order and every floating-point result that follows depend on stored data alone (chapter 15.2). [`Sketch::variables`] lays the entities' unknowns out in that order, each with the power of two that makes it act as a length (chapter 15.4). A constraint is driving, which the solver must meet, or reference, which is measured and never solved; its priority orders pivots and removal suggestions and nothing else (chapter 15.3).
guarantees: **One order.** The items' order depends only on their ids, never on the order they were added in, so a shuffled authoring gives the same sketch.
**Finite.** Every value is finite, and a radius, a length or a distance that must be positive is, or the item is refused.
**References resolve.** An item that names another names one that exists and of the right kind, and an item with the id of another is refused.
**Exact scales.** A variable's scale is a power of two, so dividing by it rounds nothing.
**Reference only where it means something.** Only a dimension can be a reference.

**Root choices are stored.** A side, a sense or a tangency is a field of its constraint, and [`Sketch::drawn_side`], [`Sketch::drawn_outside`] and [`Sketch::drawn_touching_outside`] read it off a drawing by exact predicates, or say it cannot be read (chapter 15.3).
modules.job: The sketch model: entities and their variables, constraints and their standing, in authoring order.

method.text: section 15.2's table of entities and variables, and sections 15.3 and 15.4 (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/15-sketches.md`).

modules.cost: a lattice's construction takes O(log n) divisions and O(log n) reduction steps; every map is constant time. No allocation; no recursion.
modules.does: a [`SketchPlane`] holds a [`PlaneFrame`]. A [`Lattice`] frame is exact both ways: a sketch point (s, t) is origin + s·u + t·v, whole numbers throughout, and every grid point of the plane is one (s, t). Axis-aligned planes have unit vectors for u and v. A plane with a small whole-number normal, such as a 5-in-12 roof, takes the two shortest vectors of its grid ([`Lattice::of_normal`]), and the sketch measures through their Gram matrix, so a rafter measures its true length ([`Lattice::length_squared`]). A [`Rotated`] frame serves every other plane: its axes are orthonormal doubles, and placing a point in 3D rounds it to the grid.
guarantees: **The class is stated.** [`SketchPlane::place`] gives the point and its class: `Exact` on a lattice, `Certified` to one step on a rotated frame, where the rounding is at most √3/2 of a step and the arithmetic adds under 2^−11 of one.

**Exact both ways on a lattice.** [`Lattice::locate`] returns the (s, t) of a grid point of the plane, the inverse of [`Lattice::place`], and refuses a point off the plane. u and v must be a basis of the plane's whole grid, which their cross product being primitive says, so no grid point of the plane falls between lattice points.
**A cell of at most 16 steps.** A lattice whose cell's longer diagonal passes [`LATTICE_CELL`] is refused: the commit rung section 15.1 proposes. Above it, the plane takes a rotated frame.
**Orthonormal or refused.** A rotated frame's axes must be unit and at right angles to within 2^−40.
**Checked.** Every integer step is checked; a point outside the grid's range is refused.
modules.job: Sketch planes: how 2D sketch coordinates map into the 3D frame, and how lengths are measured on a plane whose grid is not square.

method.text: sections 15.1 and 6.1 (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/15-sketches.md`). The grid of a plane n·x = d from Bézout's identity on n (D. E. Knuth, *The Art of Computer Programming* vol. 2, 3rd ed., section 4.5.2, algorithm X), and its two shortest vectors by Lagrange's reduction (P. Q. Nguyen and D. Stehlé, "Low-dimensional lattice basis reduction revisited", ACM Trans. Algorithms 5(4) (2009), doi:10.1145/1597036.1597050). The extended Euclidean step is written here since a kernel crate takes no integer library (chapter 27).

modules.cost: each iteration of a stage is one factorisation of its rows, charged to the work meter with the rows' evaluation, and the meter is checked once an iteration. No recursion.
modules.does: a plan is what depends on a sketch's structure alone: the merged variables, the Jacobian's pattern, the stages in solve order and an analysis of each. Each stage is a component's over-determined part, one of its square blocks, or its under-determined part, and holds everything before it fixed. [`solve`] runs every stage from the sketch's values until each residual is within a 64th of a grid step, and returns the sketch at those values with a [`Report`]. [`continue_to`] moves the changed values along a straight path instead of jumping, solving at each step from the last, and halves a step that does not converge, puts a stored sense at risk or nears a singular configuration.
guarantees: **Least change.** The full step is the least-norm least-squares step, the limit of the damped steps as the damping goes to zero, so a free variable does not jump (chapter 15.6). Every variable has weight one: after the scaling of chapter 15.4 each acts as a length. Weights of their own are the dragging piece's (G228).
**QR, never normal equations.** A damped step is the least-squares solution of J stacked on √λ·I, by `geom_linalg`'s sparse QR; the pattern of each is analysed once, in the plan.

**Convergence in grid steps.** A stage has converged when each of its residuals is at most [`TOLERANCE`]. Every residual is a length with a gradient near one, so that means the same at any size, and no further division by the block's size would change a step.
**Never a partial answer.** A block that does not converge is [`SketchError::Unsolved`], naming its worst rule, and running out of budget is [`SketchError::Stopped`]; neither returns a sketch.

**A singular start is nudged once.** A rule on its singular set has its points moved by small amounts derived from its id alone, which the report records; a rule still on it is [`SketchError::Degenerate`] (chapter 15.4). A square block whose Jacobian is singular at its start, though no rule of it is on its own singular set, is started again with every rule's inputs nudged if it does not converge: no step leaves such a start.

**The branch is followed.** Each stored sense is checked after each step of a path with interval arithmetic, and a sign that cannot be certified counts as at risk; the smallest pivot of each square block is held at or above [`INDEPENDENT`], and the sign of its determinant is kept: a step that changes it has jumped to another branch. After [`MOST_HALVINGS`] halvings at one place the answer is [`SketchError::BranchLost`], with the rule and how far along the path it stopped. A step is halved after a failure and doubled after a success, and the halvings are those that brought the step to its size: a failed step of 2^-10 of the path loses it. Read as halvings since the last success, 15.7's rule would let a path creep up on a singular place in ever smaller steps that each succeed, and never end. So a path takes at most about 2,000 steps: each success moves at least 2^-10 of it, and each failure undoes at most one doubling.
**Deterministic.** Stages, rows and steps run in an order that depends on stored data alone, and the schedule of a path on the stored state and the new values alone (chapter 15.7).
modules.job: The block solver and continuation: Gauss–Newton steps with Moré's damping on each block of a sketch, least change where it is under-determined, and a followed path when its values change.

method.text: Levenberg–Marquardt as J. J. Moré, *The Levenberg–Marquardt algorithm: implementation and theory*, Numerical Analysis, Springer LNM 630 (1978), <https://doi.org/10.1007/BFb0067700>: accept a step on the ratio of actual to predicted reduction, and move the damping by a factor of four on the same ratio. The trust-region radius of that paper is replaced by the damping itself, as in Marquardt's original. Continuation is section 15.7 (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/15-sketches.md`).

provenance.name: fiksi (Endoli)
provenance.purpose: for solving the stacked system instead of the normal equations; no code is taken.

modules.cost: O(z√n) for the matching and O(z + n log n) for the rest, z the graph's edges and n its nodes; O(z + n) memory. No recursion.
modules.does: [`Graph`] is the bipartite graph of equations and variables. [`substitute`] builds it from a sketch, merging the two variables of every equality between single variables, such as coincident points or a horizontal line. [`analyse`] splits the graph into connected [`Component`]s, finds a largest matching of equations to variables by Hopcroft and Karp's method, and from it the Dulmage–Mendelsohn decomposition of each component: an over-determined part, an under-determined part, and square [`Part`]s in the order to solve them.
guarantees: **From structure alone, in exact integers.** No value is read, so the plan is the same on every machine. Every tie goes to the lower index, and indices are authoring order.

**Parts are exact.** The over-determined and under-determined parts do not depend on which largest matching was found, and neither do the square blocks as sets. The order of the blocks is the one that takes, of those ready, the block with the lowest equation.
**Iterative.** Every graph walk has an explicit stack charged to the meter, so a chain of any length cannot overflow the machine's stack (principle 13).
**A solve order.** Each square block's equations touch only variables of its own block, of earlier blocks, and of the under-determined part.
**Exact counts.** A component's `freedoms` is its under-determined variables less equations, and its `excess` its over-determined equations less variables.

method.text: section 15.5 (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/15-sketches.md`): J. E. Hopcroft and R. M. Karp, "An n^(5/2) algorithm for maximum matchings in bipartite graphs", SIAM J. modules.does: [`write`] prints a sketch: its plane, then each entity and constraint in authoring order, one to a line. [`parse`] reads that back. An id is written `sequence.key`; a number as the shortest decimal that reads back to the same double, so a grid value is a whole number of steps; an amount as a number, or `@sequence.key` for a named scalar.
guarantees: **Round trip.** `parse(write(s)) == s`, bit for bit, for every sketch.
**Canonical.** A sketch has one text: `write(parse(t))` is the same whatever order `t`'s items came in, once they name only what came before them.

**Never a panic.** Any text at all gives a sketch or [`SketchError::Text`] with its line, or the refusal [`Sketch::add_entity`] gives: the parser's fuzz target holds it to that (`geom-fuzz`'s `sketch_text`). A value the model refuses is refused here too.
**Versioned.** The first line names the grammar. A later grammar is a new tag, and this one keeps reading its own (chapter 26.2).

invariants: Each kind is stored as itself in a closed enum; conversion to NURBS is on demand and states whether it is exact and its maximum error (7).

modules.cost: constant per evaluation; a bound O(1) per piece (at most 64 pieces); a conversion O(m·n) for its control net.
modules.does: each kind writes its surface in the shared form c + Σ f(u)·g(v)·W (`crate::terms`), with angles in half-turns on an exact [`Frame`] (x̂, ŷ, n̂), and a sign s = ±1 on its axial term so that reversing either parameter is exact:
guarantees: **Stored as themselves.** Centres, radii, slopes and frames are the stored doubles, exactly.

**Certified, or refused.** Enclosures and bounds are the terms' closed forms in interval arithmetic; the normal bound is the closed-form direction, which survives the poles of a sphere and the apex of a cone (where its sign may be either: then both).

**Exact NURBS forms.** Each converts to a tensor-product rational surface (a circle in each angular direction, a line in each linear one) with a parameter map per direction, its deviation 0 where the doubles hold it exactly (a whole cylinder on an axis-aligned frame).

**Transforms change kinds explicitly.** A similarity keeps the kind (lengths times its scale, the frame carried, a mirror flipping the axial sign); any other transform gives the moved NURBS form. A plane takes every affine map. A grid transform that moves the centre exactly is exact: deviation 0 (chapter 7; piece G69).
**Exact split and reversal.**
modules.job: The analytic surface kinds: plane, cylinder, cone, sphere and torus, each stored as itself.

method.text: the elementary surfaces of ISO 10303-42 (`plane`, `cylindrical_surface`, `conical_surface`, `spherical_surface`, `toroidal_surface`), parametrised in half-turns, with the kinds and the lemon and apple forms of chapter 7 (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/07-geometry-types.md`); their normals by the cross product of the closed-form partials.

modules.cost: per try, (cells·n + 1)² samples and as many interpolation solves' worth of O(n) work, plus one certificate per span (the kind's partials to order 6 at a point, 7 along a line and 4 over a box, and O(p²) interval operations to sum them); at most four tries (n = 4 to 32); knot removal O(knots · rows · n).
modules.does: [`same_parameter`] cuts the kind's domain at its breaks into smooth cells, samples the kind on an n × n grid of equally spaced parameters in each cell, and interpolates the samples with a bicubic B-spline surface on those parameters (A9.4, through `geom-nurbs`'s `Curve::interpolate_at` along u and then along v), each cell's knots those averaging (9.8) gives its equally spaced parameters, joined C⁰ at the breaks, so the surface's spans never straddle a break. It then certifies the surface against the kind span by span, and samples twice as densely while the certified error is above half the target and still falls by at least a quarter with each doubling (the error itself falls about sixteen times for a smooth kind; where the certificate stops falling, rounding or a jump of the kind is what is left). Last, it removes knots (A5.8 on every row of the net at once, `geom-nurbs`'s certified `Curve::remove_knot`) while the removals' certified changes fit in what the target leaves, and returns the surface with its deviation: the certified error plus the removals' changes.
guarantees: **Certified.** |O(u, v) − N(u, v)| is at most the deviation returned at every (u, v) of the domain: on each span the remainder form holds because both are smooth inside it (no span meets a break of the kind inside), every term is an outward-rounded enclosure, and knot removal adds no more than its own certified change (the triangle inequality; a row's change bounds the net's, since the other direction's basis functions are a partition of unity).

**Within the tolerance, or refused.** Asked for a tolerance, the result is within it or the call fails with [`NurbsError::OutsideTolerance`]; without one, the target is the fit bound `ε_fit` (`geom_num::ladder::FIT`, 64 grid steps: chapter 13 certifies a procedural kind's cache within it), and the deviation returned is what the densest sampling certified when the target is not reached: honest, never assumed.
**Same parameter.** The surface at (u, v) is within the deviation of the kind at (u, v), so both maps are `ParamMap::Same`.
**Deterministic.** Fixed sampling, fixed orders.
modules.job: A NURBS cache of a surface kind on its own parameters, by Piegl and Tiller's sample, interpolate and remove-knots method, certified by interval bounds.

method.text: L. Piegl and W. Tiller, "Computing offsets of NURBS curves and surfaces", Computer-Aided Design 31(2) (1999), 147–156, <https://doi.org/10.1016/S0010-4485(98)00066-9> (sample, interpolate, remove knots), with The NURBS Book's A9.4 and A5.8 (2nd ed., <https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-59223-2>) as `geom-nurbs` implements them; the error certified instead of estimated from samples, by Taylor's theorem in several variables with the Lagrange remainder in interval arithmetic (R. E. Moore, R. B. Kearfott and M. J. Cloud, *Introduction to Interval Analysis*, SIAM (2009), <https://doi.org/10.1137/1.9780898717716>, on Taylor forms).

modules.cost: for each parameter pair, a few enclosures and bounds (the partials to order 2 among them), a split, a reversal and a transform.
modules.does: [`check`] runs a kind through the laws of `geom-curve`'s [`Law`], read for surfaces, at the parameter pairs given, and returns the first law broken. As for curves, the laws compare certified objects: enclosures of one exact value must overlap after widening by the stated deviations (the partials of every order among them: [`ParamSurface::partials_over`]'s first three are the enclosure's, and its partials at a pair meet those over the box around it, as the second partials' and the unit normal's partials' bounds do, piece G68); the normal bound must keep the sign of every coordinate it decides; doubles must lie in the certified enclosures within 2^−30 of the largest value there (a wrong formula, not rounding).
guarantees: **Sound.** A law reported broken is broken (two certified enclosures of one value that miss each other, a sign the normal bound decides that the exact normal contradicts, or a refusal that did not come).
**Deterministic.** Parameters in the order given, laws in a fixed order.
modules.job: The kind contract for surfaces: the laws every surface kind must keep, as a check any kind's tests run (`projects/engines/geometry/AGENTS.md`, "How to add a geometry kind").

method.text: as `geom-curve`'s contract (chapter 28.2's contract laws, applied to the behaviour of chapter 7), on the inclusion property of interval arithmetic (Moore, Kearfott and Cloud, <https://doi.org/10.1137/1.9780898717716>).

modules.cost: one call of the kind's partials to order 2 over the box, then a fixed number of interval operations: O(1).
modules.does: [`second_partials`] reads `S_uu`, `S_uv` and `S_vv` over a box from a kind's partials to order 2 ([`crate::ParamSurface::partials_over`]) as boxes, and [`SecondPartials::chord`] gives chapter 19.3's M = max(`M_uu`, `M_vv`) + `M_uv`, each M an upper bound on its box's Euclidean norm: M bounds ‖`d_u`²·`S_uu` + 2·`d_u`·`d_v`·`S_uv` + `d_v`²·`S_vv`‖ for every unit direction (`d_u`, `d_v`), because 2·|`d_u`·`d_v`| ≤ 1, and so the chord bound ½·M·r² of tessellation. [`normal_partials`] bounds the partials `N_u` and `N_v` of the unit normal N = n/|n|, n = `S_u` × `S_v`: from the partials to order 2, the jets of `S_u` and `S_v` (order 1), their cross product's jet, its length's by the root recurrence and N's by the quotient recurrence, N's value cut to [−1, 1] in each coordinate since N is a unit vector. Each of `N_u` and `N_v` is then cut to the box ±|`n_u`|/|n| (or ±|`n_v`|/|n|): `N_u` = (`n_u` − (N·`n_u`)·N)/|n|, the part of `n_u` across N divided by |n|, is no longer than |`n_u`|/|n|.
guarantees: **Certified.** Each box holds the exact partial at every point of the box, from both sides of a break inside it, as the kind's partials do: every step is interval arithmetic rounded outward on enclosures of exact values (inclusion isotonicity), and every cut intersects two enclosures of one value.

**Unbounded, never a guess.** Where n may vanish over the box (a pole, an apex, a degenerate point), N has no derivative to bound there, and the result is `Unbounded`; so it is for a kind whose partials cannot be bounded over the box (an offset where its base normal vanishes, a swept kind on an unbounded profile).
**Deterministic.** A fixed sequence of operations.
modules.job: Certified bounds on a surface's second partials and on its unit normal's partials over a parameter box, for every kind, from the kind's partials there (piece G68).

method.text: the second-derivative bound and the chord bound of chapter 19.3 (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/19-meshes-spatial-clash.md`); the derivative of a normalised vector, (n/|n|)′ = (n′ − (N·n′)·N)/|n| (M. P. do Carmo, *Differential Geometry of Curves and Surfaces*, 2nd ed., Dover (2016), section 3-2, the differential of the Gauss map), in two-variable interval jets (A. Griewank and A. Walther, *Evaluating Derivatives*, 2nd ed., SIAM (2008), chapter 13, <https://doi.org/10.1137/1.9780898717761>; R. E. Moore, R. B. Kearfott and M. J. Cloud, *Introduction to Interval Analysis*, SIAM (2009), <https://doi.org/10.1137/1.9780898717716>).

modules.cost: at most three extents in one parameter per coordinate, or one per piece (at most 64) on the last route.
modules.does: a coordinate of ∂^{i+j}S/∂u^i∂v^j of a kind written in `crate::terms`' form is Σ M_{fg}·f(u)·g(v) over f and g each 1, t, cos πt or sin πt: a grid of coefficients, each the enclosure of an exact real. [`terms`] reads the grid's shape and takes the closed form that fits it:
guarantees: **Certified.** Every route holds every value of the coordinate over the box: the extents in one parameter are certified (`geom_curve::extent`), and each step's reduction is exact over the reals: a function affine in a parameter takes its extremes over a span at the span's ends; a function affine in G takes them over [G₋, G₊] at its ends, and [G₋, G₊] holds G's values; on a piece, Taylor's theorem with the remainder ½δ²·`S_vv`(u, ξ) for some ξ in it.

**The kinds' own extents.** Every route but the last gives the coordinate's extent over the box up to rounding; the last within ½r² times the second v-derivative's size, about 10⁻³ of it on pieces of a thirty-second of a half-turn.
**Deterministic.** The same terms and box give the same bits on every target.
modules.job: Closed-form extents of the analytic surface kinds: the range of each coordinate of a partial derivative over a parameter box, from `geom-curve`'s closed-form extents in one parameter.

method.text: separation of the parameters by linearity (a bilinear or affine function's extremes on a box lie on its edges), then `geom-curve`'s closed-form extents in one parameter (`geom_curve::extent`), all in interval arithmetic (R. E. Moore, R. B. Kearfott and M. J. Cloud, *Introduction to Interval Analysis*, SIAM (2009), <https://doi.org/10.1137/1.9780898717716>).

modules.cost: constant for a plane: nine interval operations.
modules.does: [`ImplicitBound::enclose_box`] gives enclosures of F and of its gradient over a box of points, and whether F is smooth throughout it. `geom-num`'s exact [`Plane`] implements it, F(x) = n·x + d, its first implementor; quadrics and tori come with their kinds (G65) and fields with `geom-field`.
guarantees: **Enclosures.** For every point x of the box, F(x) lies in `value` and ∇F(x) in `gradient`; computed in interval arithmetic rounded outward. A plane's coefficients are integers below 2^126, each held exactly (an integer whose double is not exact is widened by its rounding).
**Smoothness stated.** `smooth` is true only where F is continuously differentiable over the whole box; a kind that cannot tell says false.
modules.job: Implicit surfaces F(x) = 0 seen through one trait: the interval value and gradient of F over a 3D box (chapter 12.1), so planes, quadrics, tori and fields take part in intersection without `geom-intersect` depending on them.

method.text: interval extensions of F and ∇F (R. E. Moore, R. B. Kearfott and M. J. Cloud, *Introduction to Interval Analysis*, SIAM (2009), <https://doi.org/10.1137/1.9780898717716>), the operand form chapter 12.1 gives implicit surfaces.

modules.cost: O(K²) for a sum; O(K⁴) for a product, quotient or root (each coefficient sums over the coefficients below it); K is at most a few in the kernel's uses.
modules.does: a [`Jet`] of total order K holds enclosures of the Taylor coefficients f^(i, j)/(i!·j!), where f^(i, j) = ∂^{i+j}f/∂u^i∂v^j and i + j ≤ K, at every point of a box (a point, for an enclosure; a box, for a bound), listed as [`crate::param::partial_index`] lists partials. Sums, products, quotients and square roots of jets are the jets of the sums, products, quotients and roots, by the two-variable recurrences of automatic differentiation; [`Jet::du`] and [`Jet::dv`] differentiate. A quotient whose value is known from elsewhere (a rational patch's convex hull, a unit vector's [−1, 1]) starts from that value ([`Jet::div_valued`], piece G68), so its derivatives do not inherit the width of the value's quotient of boxes. So the jet of an offset surface's formula, S + d·(`S_u` × `S_v`)/|`S_u` × `S_v`|, gives all of its partials to order K from the base's partials to order K + 1: its higher derivatives come from the formula's exact rules (Leibniz's rule and the quotient and root recurrences), never from a finite difference.
guarantees: **Certified.** If each input coefficient encloses its function's coefficient at every point of the box, so does each output coefficient: every recurrence is a polynomial or a quotient in the inputs, evaluated in outward-rounded interval arithmetic (inclusion isotonicity).

**Refused where undefined.** A quotient by, or a root of, a jet whose value may be zero (or, for the root, not positive) is [`CurveError::Unbounded`], never a guess; an order above 18, where the factorials stop being exact doubles, is [`NurbsError::DerivativeOrder`].
modules.job: Truncated two-variable Taylor series in interval arithmetic: every partial derivative of a formula built from surfaces' partials, enclosed, without differentiating the formula by hand.

method.text: the Taylor-coefficient recurrences of automatic differentiation in several variables (A. Griewank and A. Walther, *Evaluating Derivatives*, 2nd ed., SIAM (2008), chapter 13, <https://doi.org/10.1137/1.9780898717761>: the Cauchy product of multivariate Taylor series and the division and square-root recurrences it gives), evaluated in intervals as in interval automatic differentiation (R. E. Moore, R. B. Kearfott and M. J. Cloud, *Introduction to Interval Analysis*, SIAM (2009), <https://doi.org/10.1137/1.9780898717716>); the one-variable form is `geom-curve`'s jet, which this extends to two parameters.

modules.cost: a bound or enclosure runs Bezier extraction in intervals, O(`s_u`·`s_v`·(p + q)·p·q) for s spans, plus O(p·q·(p + q)) per patch cut; the normal bound three products per patch; a split O(n·m); a reversal or transform O(n·m).
modules.does: implements [`ParamSurface`] for [`Surface`]. Points and partials are A3.5, A3.6 and A4.4 (`geom-nurbs`). Enclosures and bounds come from the surface's Bernstein patches in interval arithmetic (piece G59): the patch holding (u, v), or each patch meeting the box cut down to it, its box from the convex hull; partials from the patch's partial forms, and for a rational surface `S_d` = (`A_d`·W − A·`W_d`) / W². The normal bound is the hull of the normal patches (`Surface::normal_patches`, collapsed edges divided out) cut down to the box. Partials of any order are the patch's repeated partial forms, at the point or bounded by their hulls, and for a rational surface the jet quotient A/W (`crate::jet`). Conversion to NURBS is the surface itself. A split inserts the parameter until its multiplicity is the degree in that direction and parts the net; a reversal negates and reverses one knot vector; a transform maps the control points with the weights kept.
guarantees: **Certified.** Every enclosure and bound holds the exact value; a split's deviation is the certified rounding of the knot insertion; a transform's the largest certified error of a control point's image (a surface point is a weighted average of its control points).
**Exact where the operation is.** Conversion and reversal change no bit; a grid transform of control points whose images are exact reports 0.
**Refused outside the domain.** Never clamped.
modules.job: The NURBS surface kind: `geom-nurbs`'s [`Surface`] under the kind contract.

method.text: The NURBS Book, 2nd ed. (<https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-59223-2>): A3.5, A3.6, A4.4, A5.3, de Casteljau subdivision and affine invariance, on `geom-nurbs` (G56, G59) and the normal patch of Sederberg and Meyers (<https://doi.org/10.1016/0167-8396(88)90029-5>).

modules.cost: an evaluation of order k is the base's of order k + 1 plus O(k⁴) interval operations (a box's twice, for its centred form); a bound O(1) evaluations per piece (each smooth part of the box cut into four by four), a normal bound up to 64 more per piece where the fold factor's sign needs smaller boxes (an explicit stack, three halvings deep: no recursion) and two of the base's normal bounds; the cache as `crate::cache` states.
modules.does: [`Offset`] stores its base, any [`SurfaceKind`] (an offset too), the part of the base's domain it covers, and the distance d; a positive distance moves along `S_u` × `S_v`. It is procedural (chapter 7): its points and its partials of every order come from the base's partials one order higher through two-variable interval Taylor jets (`crate::jet`), so its second and third derivatives, which Class-A blends need (chapter 13.10), are the formula's exact derivatives, never finite differences. Its NURBS form is a cache on the same parameters, built by Piegl and Tiller's sample, interpolate and remove-knots method and certified box by box in interval arithmetic (`crate::cache`), computed on demand or kept with [`Offset::cached`]; [`Offset::to_nurbs_within`] asks for a stated error.
guarantees: **Certified, or refused.** Every enclosure holds the exact offset of the stored base. Where the base's normal may vanish (a pole, a cusp, or a box too wide to separate it from zero) an enclosure is refused and a derivative bound is `Unbounded`; a bound on the points still holds there, from the base's bound widened by |d|, and the normal bound is then the whole space, which decides no sign. Elsewhere the normal bound is the base's, turned over where the offset folds, wherever the sign of 1 − 2Hd + Kd² is certified (Maekawa's identity below), and the cross product of the enclosed partials where it is not.

**Offset by d, then by −d, is the base.** Where the offset is regular (d·κ < 1 for both principal curvatures κ on the side it moves to), the offset's normal is the base's, so the offset by −d of the offset by d is the base itself, and its enclosures hold the base's points.
**Exact split and reversal.** A split narrows the domain on the same base (deviation 0); a reversal reverses the base and negates the distance (`S_u` × `S_v` turns over).

**Transforms keep the kind only when exact.** A grid transform (a signed permutation and a whole-step translation, so lengths are kept) of an offset whose base moves exactly gives an offset, a mirror negating the distance; any other transform gives the moved NURBS cache, with both deviations.
modules.job: The offset surface kind: a base kind moved along its unit normal, O = S + d·n with n = (`S_u` × `S_v`)/|`S_u` × `S_v`|, with symbolic higher derivatives and a certified NURBS cache.

method.text: the offset surface as ISO 10303-42 defines it (`offset_surface`, the base moved along its normal by a distance), its derivatives by automatic differentiation in interval arithmetic (Griewank and Walther, *Evaluating Derivatives*, 2nd ed., SIAM (2008), <https://doi.org/10.1137/1.9780898717761>), which re-derives what `SMLib`'s offset surface gets wrong in its third derivatives (chapter 13.11); the identity `O_u` × `O_v` = (1 − 2Hd + Kd²)·(`S_u` × `S_v`) for the regular offset (T. Maekawa, "An overview of offset curves and surfaces", Computer-Aided Design 31(3) (1999), <https://doi.org/10.1016/S0010-4485(99)00013-5>); the cache by L. Piegl and W. Tiller, "Computing offsets of NURBS curves and surfaces", Computer-Aided Design 31(2) (1999), <https://doi.org/10.1016/S0010-4485(98)00066-9>.

modules.cost: none here; each kind's implementation states its own.
modules.does: [`ParamSurface`] is the trait chapter 12.1 names: evaluation, first partial derivatives, certified enclosures, conservative bounds on the value and the partials over any parameter box, a bound on the normals' directions (the Gauss map), conversion to NURBS with an error, split, reverse and transform; with every partial derivative of any order enclosed at a point or over a box ([`ParamSurface::partials_over`], listed by [`partial_index`]) and the parameters where a kind may not be smooth ([`ParamSurface::breaks`]), which chapter 13's offsets and Class-A blends need (piece G66), and, from those partials, bounds on the second partials and on the unit normal's partials over any box ([`ParamSurface::second_derivative_bound`], [`ParamSurface::normal_derivative_bound`], piece G68), which tessellation's chord and normal-angle bounds rest on (chapter 19.3). [`SurfaceKind`] is the storage enum, one variant per kind, which dispatches to it. New surfaces come back as [`SurfaceKind`] inside `geom-nurbs`'s [`Changed`], with a certified bound on their distance from the exact result. Errors are `geom-curve`'s [`CurveError`], shared by every kind (a span there is a box here).
guarantees: **Certified, or refused.** Every bound and enclosure holds the exact value for the surface the stored data define; a derivative that cannot be bounded over a box is [`DerivativeBound::Unbounded`], and the normal bound then still bounds the directions.
**Closed and exhaustive.** Matching on [`SurfaceKind`] is exhaustive; a new kind is a new variant (the playbook in `projects/engines/geometry/AGENTS.md`).
**Trimming is not here.** A surface kind is a carrier; trimming belongs to the topology's loops (chapter 7).
modules.job: The behaviour every surface kind has (chapter 7), and the closed enum that stores every kind.

method.text: the operations of chapter 7 and the trait names of chapter 12.1 (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/12-intersections.md`), with the normal bound in place of an unbounded derivative as chapter 12.1 asks.

modules.cost: an evaluation is the profiles' plus O(1); a bound O(1) profile bounds per piece; a conversion O(m·n) for its control net, plus the profiles' conversions.
modules.does: each kind is a placement c + L·X(u, v) of an unplaced shape X, with L a stored 3 × 3 matrix (the identity when built) and c a stored point (when built, the origin, or a revolution's axis point a, about which X turns), so every affine transform keeps the kind on the same parameters (c′ = M·c + t, L′ = M·L):
guarantees: **Certified.** Every enclosure and bound holds the exact value of the surface the stored profiles and placement define.
**Transforms keep the kind, on the same parameters**, with the rounding of c′ and L′ as the deviation: |Δc| + ‖ΔL‖·sup|X|.
**Exact split and reversal**: a split trims a profile or cuts the linear direction; a reversal flips the axis (revolution, in u), reverses the profiles, or negates d or σ (in v).
modules.job: The swept surface kinds: surface of revolution, linear extrusion and ruled surface, each built on `geom-curve`'s trimmed curves and stored as itself.

method.text: the surfaces of ISO 10303-42 (`surface_of_revolution`, `surface_of_linear_extrusion`) and the ruled surface; their NURBS construction from L. Piegl and W. Tiller, *The NURBS Book*, 2nd ed., sections 8.3 to 8.5 (<https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-59223-2>).

modules.cost: O(T) interval operations per evaluation of T terms; a conversion O(m·n·T) for an m × n control net.
modules.does: [`Fun`] names the scalar functions (1, t, cos πt, sin πt; angles in half-turns, the kernel's proven angle form), and [`Terms`] holds a kind's c and terms in doubles and as enclosures of the exact values its stored data define. It evaluates every partial derivative ∂^{i+j}S/∂u^i∂v^j in closed form: in doubles at a point, and in intervals over any box, which is both the certified evaluation and the bound. [`Terms::distance`] bounds how far two surfaces of the same terms lie apart over a box, and [`Terms::to_nurbs`] writes them as one tensor-product NURBS surface: each direction's functions are the coordinates of a unit circle (cos, sin and 1, the exact rational quadratic of `geom-curve`) or of a line (t and 1), and a product of two such curves is a tensor product (The NURBS Book, section 8.2, on surfaces of revolution, the same construction).
guarantees: **Certified.** An enclosure holds the exact value at every point of its box: `geom-num`'s proven `sinpi` and `cospi` enclosures, π between its neighbouring doubles, and `geom-curve`'s exact-where-it-can interval arithmetic.
**Derivatives in closed form.** A derivative of cos πt or sin πt shifts it a quarter turn and gains π; never a finite difference (chapter 7).

**Conversion with its error.** The NURBS surface differs from the terms by at most the direction curves' own deviations, multiplied out over the terms, plus the rounding of its control points and weights (the rational bound of `geom-curve`'s conics).
modules.job: The certified evaluation the analytic surface kinds share: each is S(u, v) = c + Σ f(u)·g(v)·W, fixed vectors W times products of scalar functions of one parameter each.

method.text: direct evaluation of the closed forms in interval arithmetic (R. E. Moore, R. B. Kearfott and M. J. Cloud, *Introduction to Interval Analysis*, SIAM (2009), <https://doi.org/10.1137/1.9780898717716>); tensor-product rational surfaces from rational curves (L. Piegl and W. Tiller, *The NURBS Book*, 2nd ed., chapter 8, <https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-59223-2>).

invariants: **Development only.** No kernel crate depends on it except as a development dependency; the [`deps`] check enforces that. It may use `std` (chapter 27 exempts the development crates from `no_std`).

**No randomness of its own.** The kernel has no randomness, and seeds belong to test generators only (28.17). This crate never reads the operating system's random source or a clock: a seed is a test's fixed default, a seed the test fixes, or the value of `SPAREKIT_SEED`, and every one is printed.

**The same data on every target.** Test data comes from integer arithmetic only, and every word drawn from proptest's stream is a whole `u64`, so a seed gives the same inputs on every target, 32-bit and 64-bit, and only the kernel's results can differ. Golden hashes in [`grid`] and [`prop`] check it, and CI runs them natively and under wasm32-wasip1.
**The kernel's lints.** `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]`, and no `unwrap`, `expect`, `panic!` or indexing outside tests. A helper fails with a typed error and the test decides.

modules.cost: linear in the outcome; one encoding and one hash.
modules.does: [`canonical_output`] encodes one operation's [`Outcome`], a success or a failure, in SKG's canonical CBOR and hashes it with SHA-256 after the domain prefix [`PREFIX`]. A success is its result bodies (each by the SHA-256 of its native canonical encoding, in the operation's order), its new names (a set), its history with the operation's path, its exactness class and its diagnostics; a failure is its error's base kind, entities and evidence. [`canonical_bytes`] gives the encoding the hash is taken over, for a test that needs to see the difference.
guarantees: **Errors hash as deterministically as results**: an error is encoded from values only (kind, entities, evidence), never from its words, so the same failure hashes the same on every target, as 28.13 asks: AI agents replay errors.

**One hash per outcome**: every part has one encoding (`geom-op`'s canonical encodings and `History::encode`), names are a set, and the prefix keeps these hashes apart from names' (32.19) and content IDs (24.2).
modules.job: The canonical output of one case and its SHA-256: what a fixture's golden hash is taken over (chapter 28.13; piece G96).

method.text: chapter 28.13's canonical output (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/28-testing.md`), hashed with SHA-256 (FIPS 180-4) as every golden is, through [`crate::golden::sha256`].

modules.cost: linear in the register to parse; [`tree_digest`] reads every byte of the tree; [`fetch`] costs the download.
modules.does: [`Manifest::parse`] reads the register (`corpora/manifest.json`, [`MANIFEST_PATH`]) into typed records and checks the rules below. [`tree_digest`] gives a folder's one digest. [`fetch`] brings a corpus into a cache, from its pinned source, unmodified, and refuses it unless its digest is the register's. [`check_vendored`] holds the corpora folder itself to the register. The binary `corpus` lists the register, checks it in CI (`-- check`), fetches (`-- fetch`) and prints the digest a new entry needs (`-- digest`).
guarantees: **Nothing ambiguous parses**: unknown fields, a missing field, a malformed id or digest, or two entries with one id are each a [`CorpusError`].
**One digest per tree**: [`tree_digest`] depends only on each file's path and bytes, in byte order of path, never on a machine, a clock or an archive's layout.
**A hash-checked fetch or none.**
modules.job: The corpus register and its fetcher: every outside collection of models the tests run over, with its source, version, SHA-256, licence, and whether we may store it (chapter 28.12; piece G114).

method.text: chapters 28.12 and 29.15, rule (i) of decision 32.11 (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/28-testing.md`, `projects/engines/geometry/architecture/29-sources-licences.md`). A folder's digest is SHA-256 over one line per file, `<sha256> <size> <path>\n`, as `sha256sum` lists a tree. Downloads run `curl` and `git` as programs, with their standard flags; the register adds no network code of its own.

modules.cost: linear in the size of the LCOV files and the crates' sources.
modules.does: [`parse_lcov`] reads the LCOV file cargo-llvm-cov writes for one crate (`cargo llvm-cov -p <crate> --branch --lcov`). [`measure`] counts, for every file under the crate's `src/`, the lines and branches outside test code (found by [`crate::rust_source`]) and how many of them the crate's tests ran. [`judge`] applies the bars of [`crate::foundation`]: in the foundation set every line run and every branch taken both ways; elsewhere at least 90% of lines. [`check_marks`] checks every `coverage(off)` mark in the kernel's crates against [`crate::quality_ledger::Ledger::coverage_off`].
guarantees: **Test code is not counted.** Lines of items behind `#[cfg(test)]` are left out of both the lines found and the lines run, so tests cannot pad a crate's numbers.

**A line with no code is not counted.** llvm-cov can give a line holding only a comment or an attribute (`#[must_use]` above a `const fn`) a count of 0 though the function runs ([`no_code_lines`]); such a line has nothing to run, so it is left out of both counts.

**Nothing is skipped silently.** A source file that defines a function but has no coverage data was never compiled into the measured tests, and fails; so does a crate with no LCOV file at all, and a foundation crate whose code has `if` or `while` but whose data holds no branch record (the run was made without `--branch`).

**A missing foundation module fails.** A crate of [`crate::foundation::FOUNDATION_MODULES`] with code but no file of its foundation module fails, so moving the module cannot drop it from the foundation bar.

**Every mark cites a checked proof.** A `coverage(off)` mark must have a comment right above it citing `proof: <path>::<name>`, the same proof as its ledger entry, and the cited file must define that function as a Kani harness (`#[kani::proof]`) or a Verus `proof fn`. A ledger entry with no mark is stale and fails.

**Waiting lines are named, and can only go.** A foundation line the tests do not run passes only while the ledger's `awaiting_proof` names it, with the piece that proves it unreachable or tests it ([`excuse_awaiting`]); an entry that matches more or fewer missed lines than it says fails. When every kernel branch outcome of a file with a count of 0 waits so, which of them llvm-cov folded no longer matters, and the file's folding note is not a failure.
**Exact arithmetic.** Percentages are compared as integers: hit × 100 ≥ found × bar.
modules.job: The coverage gate: line and branch coverage of each kernel crate by its own tests, against the bars of section 28.8, and every `coverage(off)` mark against the proof it cites.

method.text: the LCOV tracefile records (`SF`, `DA`, `BRDA`, `BRF`, `end_of_record`) that `llvm-cov export -format=lcov` writes (<https://llvm.org/docs/CommandGuide/llvm-cov.html#llvm-cov-export>), each read by the `lcov` crate 0.8 (MIT OR Apache-2.0, <https://docs.rs/lcov/0.8.2/lcov/>); cargo-llvm-cov 0.9.1 (<https://docs.rs/crate/cargo-llvm-cov/0.9.1>) runs it. Branch coverage is rustc's `-Z coverage-options=branch`, nightly only (<https://doc.rust-lang.org/rustc/instrument-coverage.html>), which cargo-llvm-cov's `--branch` turns on.

modules.cost: O(K × (P + D)) for K kernel crates, P packages in the graph and D dependency entries, declared and resolved, with a logarithmic factor for the ordered maps; plus one `cargo metadata` run, which resolves the workspace from `Cargo.lock`.
modules.does: [`check`] reads the output of `cargo metadata` (which [`cargo_metadata`] runs with every feature of every workspace member on and every platform's dependencies in) and follows every kernel crate's normal and build dependencies through the whole dependency graph, reporting every chain that reaches `geom-test`, `geom-fuzz`, `geom-gen` or `geom-bench`. It also lists every manifest of this repository the answer depends on ([`Report::manifests`]), so CI can check that a change to any of them reruns the rule.
guarantees: **It never passes by accident.** Metadata it cannot read (a missing field, a field of the wrong type, an unknown dependency kind, a resolved edge without its kinds, or no resolved graph, which is what `cargo metadata --no-deps` gives) is an error, not a pass, and so is a workspace with no kernel crate, because a check that checked nothing must not pass.
**Deterministic.** Kernel crates are visited in name order, declared dependencies in manifest order and resolved ones in name order; the report lists violations in that order.
**Every chain is shown** from the kernel crate to the development crate, with the kind of each edge, so the fix is obvious.
**It changes nothing.** [`cargo_metadata`] runs cargo with `--locked`, so it fails rather than write a `Cargo.lock`.
modules.job: The dependency rule: no kernel crate depends, normally or at build time, on a development crate.

method.text: breadth-first search (Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest and Stein, *Introduction to Algorithms*, 3rd edition, section 22.2) over the union of the declared and resolved graphs from each kernel crate, on the JSON format documented at <https://doc.rust-lang.org/cargo/commands/cargo-metadata.html>. Breadth-first search finds a shortest chain to each development crate. The metadata is read into the typed model of the `cargo_metadata` crate (MIT, <https://docs.rs/cargo_metadata/0.23.1/>), which also builds the `cargo metadata` command: piece G12a put it in place of the field-by-field reading of the JSON that was written here (chapter 29.1). [`check`] takes the JSON itself, not the model, so the tests can seed a violation into real metadata as a manifest would and hand it over.

modules.cost: a product or quotient of k-bit numbers is O(k²) at these sizes; [`cos_sin`] and [`exp`] about 150 terms each; no recursion.
modules.does: an [`IBig`] n stands for n / 2^400. [`of`] reads a double exactly but for the bits below 2^−400, [`mul`] and [`div`] cut their results to a whole number of 2^−400, [`sqrt`] is the floor of the root, [`cos_sin`] and [`exp`] sum their Taylor series until a term vanishes, and π is read from its first 100 decimal places. [`cos_sin_pi`], [`tan_pi`] and [`tanh`] are built on them, for the half-turn angles and the tangent half-angle maps of the kinds. [`rational`] and [`of_rational`] pass values to and from the exact rationals of [`crate::nurbs_reference`], and [`within`] decides whether two points are at most a distance apart.
guarantees: **Far finer than a double.** Each cut is below 2^−400; a series of up to a few hundred terms adds a few hundred cuts; π's 100 decimal places err by less than 2^−332, which [`cos_sin_pi`] carries once after reducing t exactly to [−1, 1). Values from a few operations on arguments below 2^20 are within 2^−300 of the exact ones, against the 2^−53 relative of a double, so a law checked with a margin of 2^−200 is never decided by the truth's own error.
**Independent of the kernel.** Integer arithmetic and series only: no call into a kernel crate and no `f64` maths.
**The same bits on every target.** Integer arithmetic throughout.
modules.job: Fixed-point numbers of 400 fractional bits: the higher precision of the law catalogue's dense refutation sampler (piece G69, chapter 28.3), in which every bound a kind or a NURBS operation states is refuted if it is wrong.

method.text: the Taylor series of cos, sin and exp in fixed point, the argument of exp halved until it is at most 1 and the result squared back (R. P. Brent, "Fast multiple-precision evaluation of elementary functions", *Journal of the ACM* 23 (1976), 242–251, <https://doi.org/10.1145/321941.321944>); the integer square root of dashu; the fixed point of piece G61's attack tests (`geom-curve`'s `tests/attack_g61.rs`), which this module generalises for the law catalogue of chapter 28.3 (`projects/engines/geometry/architecture/28-testing.md`).

modules.cost: linear in the fixture for a parse or a write.
modules.does: a [`Fixture`] is one permanent test case: its [`Source`], its [`OpLog`] in the native format, one [`Expect`] per kernel edition and set of operation versions, and its [`Status`]. [`Fixture::parse`] reads one from its JSON text and checks every rule below; [`Fixture::to_json`] writes the one spelling that text may have. The submodules hold the rest:
guarantees: **Nothing ambiguous parses**, each break a [`FixtureError`], never a silent choice: unknown fields, a missing field, a malformed id, digest, name or edition label, a log that is not its one canonical encoding, two entries with one key, and text that is not [`Fixture::to_json`]'s one spelling are all refused.

**Only a typed error can be `Known`.** A `Known` fixture expects `Err` under every key, never of kind `Internal`, and wants a success. A panic, a hang, an invalid body, a broken law, a wrong but valid result, or a disagreement with an exact oracle can never be `Known` (28.16).
**Only what replays is stored.** `Cancelled` and `OutOfMemory` depend on the caller and the machine and are never logged (chapter 22), so no expectation may name them.
**The log and the keys agree.** Every key names exactly the operations the log runs, and the log's own versions are one of the keys.
modules.job: Fixtures: the stored test cases every failure ends as, and the rules they keep (chapter 28.16, piece G97).

modules.does: a [`Call`] is one replayable operation of the kernel: its name, its version and its inputs in their own types. [`Call::params`] writes the operation record's `params`, one item of SKG's canonical CBOR: an array of the fields of the operation's schema, in the schema's order, without the bodies it takes, which the record's `inputs` carry. [`Call::read`] reads them back, and [`Call::run`] runs the operation.
guarantees: **One writing.** [`Call::read`] writes what it read and refuses anything that does not come back byte for byte, so a log has one spelling of every call.
**An unknown operation is refused, never guessed**: a name or version that [`Call::read`] does not know is an error, which the kernel turns into a refusal no fixture status accepts.

modules.does: [`Kernel`] finds an operation by its name and version ([`Call::read`]), takes the bodies it names from the results so far, runs it, and keeps each result under its content ID, so a later operation of the log can name it. Each piece that adds an operation adds its row to [`Call`]. A case an oracle raised on a function no operation holds yet replays through `oracle::geomdl`.

**No state survives [`Engine::start`]**: a fresh run begins from the log's own inputs.
**A body is its stored bytes.** A result's hash in the step is its content ID (24.2).
**Counts are the kernel's own**: each operation's work and logical bytes come from its meter through `OpContext::with_tally`, the same charges that decide a budget (G98).

[`OpLog::encode`] writes the file: the header, the inputs, one operation record each, then END; [`OpLog::decode`] reads it back.
guarantees: **The native format, and nothing else.** The file is what `geom_format::file` writes, so a log also seeds the readers' fuzz corpora and lands in the format museum unchanged.
**One encoding.** Inputs come before operations, and [`OpLog::decode`] refuses bytes that are not [`OpLog::encode`]'s, so a log has one spelling and a fixture's text one form.
**Versions come from the log**: [`OpLog::versions`] and [`OpLog::at_versions`] are how a fixture's keys and a replay at another version are found.

modules.cost: each pass tries every unit once, so `O(n^2)` predicate calls for `n` units in the worst case and `n + 1` when nothing can go.
modules.does: [`minimise`] takes a log and a predicate that says whether a log still fails, and tries, in a fixed order, removing each operation, each input of each operation and each stored input, keeping every removal after which the predicate still holds. It repeats until a whole pass removes nothing. [`same_failure`] is the usual predicate: the log, run as the fixture's, fails in the same class of way.
guarantees: **The result still fails**: the predicate held for it, on the last removal kept or on the first call, which refuses a log that does not fail.

**1-minimal**: removing any one operation, input or stored input from the result makes the predicate false. The method is delta debugging's end state, reached by single removals, which is what the chapter asks for; a log is short, so nothing is gained from removing chunks.
**Deterministic**: the order of trials is fixed, so one failure minimises to one log.
**Removal only**: nothing is added or reordered, and no parameter is changed.
modules.job: The operation-log minimiser: `geom-test` removes operations and inputs one at a time while the failure persists (chapter 28.16, step 1; piece G97).

Written here: the units are this crate's, and the loop is shorter than any adapter to a delta-debugging crate.

modules.does: [`seeded`] draws a family's logs from [`SEED`]: `box` is one box of known size, `make` runs every primitive, `transform` builds a body and moves, mirrors and rotates it, and `budget` runs out of its work and of its logical memory, so a stop by a budget is held to one hash on every target. [`digest`] replays the corpus and hashes what it gave: each case's id, its hash and its two counts, in order. `tests/determinism.rs` holds that digest as the golden `geom-test/replay-corpus`, which `golden run` then carries through every target and build mode, the release build as shipped among them, whose checker runs only the cheap groups: one digest across the legs proves the checker changes nothing (28.4).
guarantees: **Fixed seeds.** The corpus is a pure function of [`SEED`] and the stored fixtures.
**Work and logical bytes are in the digest**, so a count that moves is a changed golden.
**Budget stops are errors like any other**: the two `budget` logs end in `BudgetExceeded`, and their hashes go into the digest.
**A broken case stops the corpus**, so a digest never hides one.
modules.job: The replay corpus: every fixture and a seeded operation log per family, the determinism matrix's input (chapters 21 and 28.13; piece G98).

[`must_fail_on_base`] lists the fixtures a pull request adds whose source records a fix.
guarantees: **The compiled copy is the tree's**: `build.rs` walks the folder and reruns when it changes, and the binary's `check` compares the two, so a stale build cannot pass.
**Every problem is listed**, not only the first.
**Files in byte order**, so a run reads the same on every machine.

modules.cost: the log's cost twice per key, plus the perturbations.
modules.does: [`replay`] runs a log through an [`Engine`], operation by operation, hashes each operation's canonical output ([`crate::canonical`]) and combines them into the log's hash; the first operation that fails ends the log. [`judge`] compares a [`Replayed`] with a fixture's expectation. [`run`] runs one fixture under every key of an edition, twice on two perturbed heaps, and returns its [`Verdict`].
guarantees: **Exact.** A `Pass` fixture must match `expect` exactly: hash and measures, or kind and entities in order.

**Only what 28.16 allows is `Known`.** A `Known` fixture passes while it gives its expected typed error, is [`Verdict::Improved`] once it gives its wanted result, and fails on anything else: another error, another success, a panic. A panic or a log the engine refuses is [`Replayed::Broken`], which no status accepts.

**Twice, on two heaps.** As every golden does (28.13), each key runs [`REPEATS`] times, each time from a fresh [`Engine::start`] on a differently perturbed heap, and every run must agree before the store's value is looked at; a run that differs is [`Failure::Repeat`].
**Nothing is written**: judging never changes a fixture.

The mutation gate ([`crate::mutants`]) and the coverage gate ([`crate::coverage`]) both classify with these, so the two gates can never disagree about what the foundation set is.
